finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/dr.headline: Drugmakers Shrug Off Trump Pricing Pressure With Record Revenue
finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/dr.author: Madison Muller, Robert Langreth and Rachel Cohrs Zhang

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump has spent the past year touting lower drug prices he's negotiated with pharmaceutical companies. The world's biggest drugmakers aren't yet feeling the pain.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Three of the largest US drugmakers reported record quarterly revenue on Thursday. Eli Lilly & Co., Merck & Co. and Bristol Myers Squibb Co. all raised their forecasts for the year. They cited strong demand for new treatments and established blockbusters like Lilly's weight-loss powerhouse Zepbound.

The cost of medical care is a focus for cash-strapped voters days before a US midterm election that will be a referendum on Trump's second term. The drugmakers' results offer a split-screen view from Washington, where the administration has promised some relief from high prescription drug prices.

It may take longer for the policy changes underway to hit drugmaker's income statements. For now, the booming business is making money for investors, who see the pharmaceutical sector as a haven from the volatile tech trade. Shares of Lilly rose 6.7% at 12:40 p.m. in New York, while Merck was up 4.9%.

The administration struck so-called most favored nation agreements with virtually every large pharmaceutical company to bring US prices more in line with what other developed nations pay. Trump hosted Oval Office ceremonies with chief executives who promised lower costs in exchange for avoiding threatened tariffs. The administration also launched TrumpRx, a clearinghouse to help Americans find discounted cash prices for certain medications, and crafted new Medicare and Medicaid programs aimed at controlling costs.

Strong demand is helping drugmakers shrug off that mounting pressure, allowing pharmaceutical giants to keep reaping profits. Lilly's finance chief told analysts in a call Thursday that volume growth would more than make up for any pressure on prices.
White House spokesperson Allison Schuster touted savings through TrumpRx, Medicare's GLP-1 coverage program, and all states signing up for a Medicaid discount program as accomplishments.

"President Trump did what no President before him could in securing Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing deals to offer Americans substantial savings that are driving the biggest drop in drug prices in decades," Schuster said in a written statement.

Some drugmakers cut deals with Trump to lower prices in exchange for expanding markets they can reach. Medicare is technically barred from covering weight-loss treatments, but the Trump administration created a workaround in exchange for price concessions from Lilly and Novo Nordisk A/S.

Lilly US chief Ilya Yuffa said the company's obesity drugs will be more widely available in Medicare and Medicaid next year at a lower price. The drugs' prices in the commercial market, where most working-age adults get coverage, will remain "overall stable," he said on a call with analysts.

The company's Zepbound pricing is "holding in strong" around $580 a prescription, excluding Medicare prescriptions dispensed at less than half that price, Evercore ISI analyst Umer Raffat wrote in a note to clients. Based on conversations with the company, he wrote, "they do not expect it to drop off anytime soon."
Most of the price concessions the Trump administration negotiated do not affect the private insurance market where drug companies make much of their money.
Signing White House deals also allowed companies to skirt threatened cuts to prices in the larger Medicare program that would have had more substantial impacts on their bottom lines.

Trump's bargaining followed efforts by former President Joe Biden to use the vast buying power of the Medicare program to drive down prices for older drugs that don't face generic competition. Biden's 2022 Inflation Reduction Act introduced Medicare price cuts on select medications for the first time in history.

By some measures, US drug prices are declining, though the slipperiness of pricing in the industry makes it hard to get a clear picture. The Consumer Price Index, which shows what patients and insurers pay for retail prescription drugs when they're dispensed, suggests medication prices are falling.

That gauge doesn't reflect the net cost of drugs after rebates, so it's an imperfect measure. It also doesn't capture the price of medicines administered in hospitals or clinics, like many of the most expensive, complex medicines for cancer or immune disease.

Those nuances may explain some of the dissonance voters express. Healthcare costs are among the top financial worries for Americans, with drug prices specifically preventing some from filling prescriptions, according to polling from health researcher KFF.
--With assistance from Chloé Meley.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.headline: SEC Eyes Manipulation, Insider Risk in Prediction Markets
finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.author: Nicola M White and Rebecca Klar (Bloomberg Law)

paragraphs.text: Nicola M White and Rebecca Klar (Bloomberg Law)
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 8:45 AM MST 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Add another regulator to the list of watchdogs monitoring risks in the fast-growing prediction market industry: the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Trades tied to companies' key performance indicators or earnings measures can fall under the Wall Street regulator's turf and SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency is watching out for signs of foul play.

"We're following that very closely," Woodcock said in an interview with Bloomberg. "We have to be ready to act when people are committing fraud or committing other securities violations, and I think we are going to be. I suspect you will see activity in that space."
Insider trading and market manipulation are the SEC's main concerns, Woodcock said, adding that enforcement activity is likely "in the future, for sure."

Oversight of prediction markets like Kalshi and the US arm of Polymarket largely falls to the smaller Washington financial regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which views the platforms' wagers on everything from sports to elections as financial swaps under its purview.

That agency has brought several prediction market enforcement cases so far this year. Former Congressman George Santos agreed to pay more than $35,000 to settle allegations he manipulated Kalshi wagers and a White House teleprompter operator settled with the CFTC over allegedly using insider information to rack up wins on Kalshi.

In April, the CFTC and federal prosecutors alleged a US soldier used classified information about the timing of the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to make more than $400,000 on Polymarket. That case is ongoing and the soldier has pleaded not guilty.
Kalshi and Polymarket have said they are against insider trading, monitor their platforms for potential risks and flag suspicious activities to regulators.

The CFTC views the platforms as derivative exchanges but some states argue prediction markets are illegal gambling operations shirking local laws. That has led to a high-stakes legal fight that will likely end up at the US Supreme Court.

Trading products become the SEC's turf when they are tied to securities. The agency put out a joint request for comment with the CFTC on the definitions of certain swaps and derivatives products as part of a bid to clarify the two agencies' jurisdictions.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/hong-k.headline: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/hong-k.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.
The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.
Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.

Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.

Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.
Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.
The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.

Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.
Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.
“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.

But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.
She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism rather than addressing the causes of the disaster.
Since a National Security Law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.
In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.
China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.
On Thursday Lee promised that ““similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.
Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.
Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.
The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”

npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-6019228/manx-sh.headline: Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-6019228/manx-sh.author: Geoff Brumfiel

paragraphs.text: New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.

A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.
Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.
Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.
For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.
Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.
Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?

To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.
He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.
"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.

In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.

That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.
"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.

Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.
"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.

wsj.com/business/cleveland-cliffs-to-ret.headline: Cleveland-Cliffs to Retain Stelco Amid Jobs Dispute With Canadian Government

paragraphs.text: By Robb M. Stewart and Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Cleveland-Cliffs is ruling out selling Stelco until the business improves production and 175 laid-off workers return to their jobs, an effort Chief Executive Lourenco Goncalves said hinges on Canadians buying the company's steel products.
The workers who have been laid off at operations in Ontario could be back on the job before Christmas if the actions work, Goncalves said.

The comments come amid an escalating war of words between Goncalves and Melanie Joly, Canada's industry minister, who has been critical of the layoffs and accused Cliffs of breaching undertakings around jobs and advocacy for trade policy made to secure approval for its roughly $2.4 billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024. Joly last week gave Cliffs 15 days to act or risk fines and even a possible forced sale of Stelco.

In a letter Thursday to Stelco President Paul Simon, Joly demanded Cliffs immediately recall all workers at Stelco as a condition to a meeting proposed by Simon with himself and Goncalves. Joly said she expects the steelmaker and its parent company to provide a "clear and credible plan for the re-engagment of those workers."

The minister has said a legal process has began to protect the jobs. She last week said the federal government was aware of some potential buyers for the Canadian assets of Stelco, but declined to offer names.

"Stelco is not for sale and I do not believe that what Minister Joly is doing, when she openly solicits buyers for a company the government does not own, is a good course of action. In countries other than Canada, that would be illegal," Goncalves said in an email to The Wall Street Journal.

The chairman and CEO of Cliffs said he also didn't believe that the government "engaging with the union to jointly attack in the media both the parent company and its CEO is constructive to attract foreigners to invest in Canada."

Goncalves said he wouldn't talk to any suitors for Stelco "real or imaginary" now or within one calendar year. "Conversely, after we demonstrate one year of higher production numbers, and also have brought all the 175 workers back to their jobs, I will be glad to sell the company, and only if I decide to do so by then," he said.

Cliffs has blamed weak demand for galvanized steel and Canadian imports of foreign steel it said have flooded the market for forcing it to lay off workers at Stelco and idling cold-rolled and coated steel operations in Hamilton, Ontario, so that it can concentrate on hot-roll products.

Early this week, Cliffs delivered a letter to Ottawa stating an exhaustive review confirmed Stelco was in full compliance with each of the 34 undertakings agreed to with the takeover and that it expected to close the reporting period having exceeded commitments on overall unionized and salaried worker numbers.

Joly in her letter said Cliffs interim compliance report wasn't satisfactory and that it needed to address directly her demands with underlying data, documents and evidence to substantiate what she described as assertions.

"The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition," Prime Minister Mark Carney said. "That's enough. [There is] a legal process underway."

Goncalves said that before the acquisition Stelco was flooding the U.S. hot-rolled steel market with Canadian rolled products at prices well below what his company was charging. Cliffs bought business, Goncalves said, because he believed in its cost structure and that prices could be increased while at the same time still selling the same tonnage to the same U.S. buyers.

With cold-rolled steel, where Stelco isn't a significant supplier to the automotive industry or into the U.S., he said the plan was different. "We believed that we could sell cold rolled and galvanized steel within the Canadian domestic market, and that part did not materialize and has not improved yet," he said.

Goncalves said that since the Canadian government won't block imports of cold-rolled and galvanized steel, Stelco would rely only on self-help and Canadian customers. "Going forward, it will depend exclusively on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco."

cnbc.com/2026/10/29/starbucks-sbux-q4-20.headline: Starbucks is about to report earnings. Here's what to expect
cnbc.com/2026/10/29/starbucks-sbux-q4-20.author: Amelia Lucas

paragraphs.text: Starbucks is set to report its quarterly earnings after the bell on Thursday.
Here's what Wall Street is expecting the company to report, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
• Earnings per share: 72 cents expected
• Revenue: $9.23 billion expected

Wall Street is also projecting that the coffee giant will report its fifth straight quarter of same-store sales growth, as its U.S. turnaround takes hold. Analysts expect Starbucks to post a same-store sales increase of 6%, fueled by its North American cafes, according to StreetAccount estimates.

As its U.S. business improves, Starbucks is closing underperforming locations, which could boost same-store sales numbers. In September, the company announced it would shutter about 1% of its North American footprint, representing about 250 cafes. The company expects to incur about $300 million in restructuring charges related to the closures.

The company's earnings report also comes weeks after Starbucks quashed speculation that it will buy Chipotle Mexican Grill, CEO Brian Niccol's former employer. While Chipotle investors cheered for the rumored acquisition, industry analysts said that a merger would distract Starbucks from its turnaround.
Starbucks stock has climbed about 24% this year, raising its market cap to roughly $119 billion.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/jd-van.headline: JD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and Iran
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/jd-van.author: Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: Lingering hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, offering to restart diplomacy.

The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei on Sunday and requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief.

A reply is imminent, but Iran is reluctant to give upfront and irreversible commitments on its nuclear programme, such as exporting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, if the compensatory US steps, such as lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, are reversible.
Some form of third-party guarantee that both sides will adhere to their commitments has been discussed, with China often mentioned as the only country of sufficient status to underwrite it.
The return of Vance, a sceptic about the war, to the negotiations is significant and a sign that the US has not abandoned diplomacy.

One Democrat senator briefed on the targets the US military had identified in Iran said described the plan for a renewed attack as “insane and likely lead to the destruction of our commitment to the rule of law”.

In a sign of Iran’s reluctance to meet US demands about sequencing, its chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, wrote on X: “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators. The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.”
Those conditions include the lifting of sanctions, ending asset freezes and the end to the war on all fronts, a phrase that requires an Israeli ceasefire in Lebanon.

The US wants front-loaded, specific commitments about the removal of Iran’s stockpile of highly-enriched uranium. Tehran is reluctant to give up its bargaining leverage, and also resists the return of UN nuclear inspectors for fear they might provide the US with intelligence on the whereabouts and state of the stockpile.
It has proposed blending the stockpile down inside Iran so it is no longer useable to make a nuclear weapon.

The Vance letter was sent to Rezaei rather than Ghalibaf or the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, because Washington judged that decision-making power rests with those closest to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. In practice, Iran tries to reach decisions through consensus at the highest level of government in a six strong committee.

Ghalibaf and Rezaei met the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, last week to discuss the risk of a new war. Khamenei has said he would like an end to the current state of no war, no peace. Iran has well laid plans ready to strike back against US interests in the region by hitting desalination plants, internet cables and electricity grids across the Gulf.

For a third US attack in two years to have any rationale or prospect of inducing Iran’s capitulation, the plan would require the US, probably in conjunction with a caretaker government in Israel, to mount attacks on previously off-limits targets. Europe would not join the attacks, but the views of the Gulf states, the chief targets of Iran reprisals, would be key.

The Connecticut senator Chris Murphy told a briefing at the Middle East Institute: “I did get a fairly detailed conversation about what the war plan would be … I will just say this their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.

“There has been open reporting as to the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting … I think the plan they have developed will lead in my judgement to a prolongment [sic] and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our security interest”.

Although Tehran trusts Vance marginally more than most White House politicians and envoys, the Iranian high command is still suspicious about his status after he negotiated a 14-point memorandum of understanding which then fell apart when other members of the US administration took charge of its implementation.

That led to unilateral US steps to reopen the strait of Hormuz that Iran said contravened the terms of the agreement. Trump also came to detest it because it delayed the start of nuclear talks for as long as 60 days.

In an offer made by Tehran on the margins of the UN general assembly, it proposed foreshortening the timeframe before nuclear talks started, saying they could start withinsix or seven days of the US restoring the sanctions waiver on its oil exports and the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Strategy Shifts to Daily Payments to Jumpstart Funding Machine
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: David Pan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Strategy Inc.'s flagship preferred shares will soon begin paying a daily dividend, the latest maneuver by Michael Saylor to revive the Bitcoin accumulator's sputtering fundraising machine.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Shareholders approved the change Wednesday, the second attempt in less than five months to jumpstart demand for what Saylor — the co-founder and chairman — has designated as the company's main funding source. In June, Strategy shifted to semi-monthly payments from monthly while the price of the STRC preferred issue tumbled along with the value of the cryptocurrency.

Saylor is counting on the daily payments to be enough of an incentive to restart demand from individual investors, who were among the biggest buyers of the securities when they were first introduced last year. Strategy needs the securities — which offer a 12% annual yield — to trade at par or higher to make them economical to issue. Daily payments are scheduled to begin Nov. 1.

In a statement Thursday, Strategy reiterated that it returned to profitability in the third quarter after registering a $21 billion unrealized gain from the increase in the value of its holdings during crypto's late summer rally. Net income was $19.5 billion.

The road back hasn't been easy. Last week, the biggest corporate holder of Bitcoin increased the size of its STRC buyback by 50% to $3 billion. In the meantime, it has continued to sell common stock to buy Bitcoin, diluting existing shareholders.

While the common stock rallied around 75% in the third quarter, it remains roughly 70% below the historic all-time high established during the post-election euphoria of November 2024. The stock was little changed in after-hours trading.

"The improved financing position came at a cost," Managing Director Brian Dobson and Equity Research Director Greg Pendy at the investment bank Clear Street, wrote in a recent report. "The repurchases lowered the preferred dividend burden, but came at a cost to common shareholders, as share issuance outpaced Bitcoin accumulation during the quarter."

Strategy has been seeking to tap the enduring appetite for income, especially among retail investors. For companies accumulating Bitcoin, which generates no income of its own, that demand offers a way to keep raising capital despite growing strains on the model pioneered by Saylor.

That retail demand hasn't been missed by others, with some competitors even paying dividends higher than the 12% offered on STRC. Strive Inc. sold $630 million in preferred shares with a 15% annual dividend last week. That's more than triple what you earn on a top-rated one-year US Treasury note, and comparable to distressed debt returns.

Returning to the $1 billion or more weekly Bitcoin purchases by Strategy that captured the attention of the crypto market in the first half of the year may not happen soon, according to Pendy and Dobson.
"We assume no new preferred issuance in the fourth quarter and $1.59 billion per quarter in 2027," Clear Street wrote. "The pace and cost of issuance remain important to our outlook."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Roblox Users Miss Estimates Despite Hit Game, ‘Steal An Egg’
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Cecilia D'Anastasio

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Roblox Corp. reported third-quarter users that missed analysts' expectations amid questions about whether a new hit game could reverse a recent slowdown in user engagement triggered by more robust child-safety measures.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The video-game company's 138 million daily active users fell short of analysts' estimates of 145.8 million. That's a 9% decrease year-over-year. Bookings, a measure of sales, came in at $1.7 billion, compared with Wall Street's expectations of $1.63 billion.

Roblox shares have lost about 37% of their value this year. In July, Roblox said that investments in AI-powered initiatives were expected to result in higher infrastructure costs and that the company would be withholding full-year guidance amid increased variability.
The shares fell as much as 12% in after-hours trading Thursday.

For years, Roblox has faced scrutiny over predators who use the platform to groom children, culminating in multiple lawsuits from state attorneys general. To reduce the threat, Roblox began implementing dozens of safety changes, including verifying users' ages, which wound up negatively impacting growth in the first two quarters. The company is betting that the changes will bring in more people to the platform over the long term.

The company attracts new players with hit games produced by third-party developers, and analysts have pointed out that it's difficult to anticipate when a new popular title will launch. In 2025, Roblox's user engagement soared, in large part, thanks to hit games Steal A Brainrot and Grow A Garden, which generated huge amounts of traffic and broke industry records. During the first half of 2026, no new games managed to reach the same level of attention.

Then over the summer, a new title called Steal An Egg caught fire with Roblox players, accounting for as much as half of the platform's concurrent users on some days, according to Freedom Capital Markets analyst Nick McKay. But optimism over the game's overall impact on Roblox could be "overdone," he cautioned, because its popularity might be coming at the expense of the vintage viral games, such as Steal A Brainrot.

finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.headline: Reddit to Limit Access for Logged-Out Users in Strategy Shift
finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.author: Riley Griffin

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Reddit Inc. said it plans to shift to a primarily logged-in user experience as the social forum seeks to deepen engagement and improve the advertising business that continues to drive its solid earnings results.
Most Read from Bloomberg

On Thursday, as the company posted third-quarter sales that beat analyst expectations, Chief Executive Officer Steve Huffman announced that Reddit will eventually limit how much of the platform people can access without an account. The company plans to start testing different approaches in markets outside of the US throughout the fourth quarter, and hasn't decided yet which parts of its site will remain available to logged-out visitors.

The strategy marks a big shift for the company, which has allowed users to explore its forums without an account for two decades. Reddit executives are willing to sacrifice some of the platform's reach to engage a smaller but more engaged audience with insights that will be valuable to advertisers.

In an interview on Thursday, Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong acknowledged the potential for the move to limit Reddit's reach in the short term but said it would eventually lead to more growth. "I think that's a trade that makes sense for the long term."

Since going public in early 2024, the San Francisco-based company's digital advertising business has grown rapidly. For the first time, Reddit on Thursday forecast $1 billion-plus in quarterly sales. But investors' expectations are high. Though the company said it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, the outlook missed the average Wall Street estimate of $1.05 billion.

Reddit reported third-quarter sales of $895 million, beating the average analyst estimate compiled by Bloomberg, largely driven by the continued growth of its advertising business. Daily active users increased 12% year-over-year to 130.3 million, missing the average analyst estimate of 133.5 million.

Shares of Reddit, which recently joined the S&P 500, fell as much as 13%. They were down 44% before the market close on Thursday. Even as the ads business grows, Wall Street is hyper-focused on how Reddit will attract and retain users in the age of artificial intelligence.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Ares CEO Says It’s Avoiding Backing AI Chips, Citing Complexity
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Amanda Cantrell and Laura Benitez

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Ares Management Corp. is avoiding financing deals to back the high-powered processing units that run sophisticated AI models, opting to invest in the data centers that house them instead.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The asset manager has concerns that if it backs graphics processing units, it could get stuck holding assets that may be obsolete not long after they're released, said a person close to the firm, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

"It's frankly a simpler underwriting with really attractive relative value," Chief Executive Officer Michael Arougheti said on a call with analysts Thursday, referring to financing data centers versus the computer chips known as GPUs.
"Without casting aspersions on GPU financing," Ares is finding more attractive investments in data centers and adjacent power infrastructure, he added.

The market for financing data centers is huge relative to the capital available to back them, according to Arougheti. The firm estimates AI capital expenditure needs to be around $5 trillion, with roughly $2 trillion needed for the build-out of physical AI buildings and adjacent infrastructure and $3 trillion for GPUs.

Arougheti's remarks come at a time of heightened investor anxiety around the AI sector, with both stocks and corporate bonds taking a beating in recent weeks on concerns that the massive spending on the sector may outstrip future revenues.

Almost every US bank and alternative asset manager has participated in the AI financing boom, on deals including Broadcom Inc.'s roughly $60 billion debt financing for chips that will be leased to Anthropic PBC and SpaceX's talks to raise about $40 billion for Nvidia Corp. chips. These chips cost multiples more than the data centers that house them, but typically depreciate over roughly five to six years.
Arougheti said on the firm's earnings call that he doesn't know "how to underwrite the decline and depreciation curves on that type of technology."
"At least for the time being, we're kind of sticking to the half of the market that we understand best and where our capability set is the deepest," he said

The bonds of CoreWeave Inc., the most well-known of the so-called neoclouds that lease GPUs to AI developers, plunged this month to levels that usually indicate distress. The cost to insure its debt has also spiked, reflecting concerns about the growing amount of borrowing underpinning the AI boom.

paragraphs.text: Thu, October 29, 2026 at 3:02 PM MST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Oil rose on signs the US may resume military strikes against Iran, risking fresh turbulence in the region that may hurt energy flows.

West Texas Intermediate gained toward $103 a barrel, after swinging more than $3 in the previous session, while Brent settled near $115. In Iran, one of the country's top negotiators, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested the Islamic Republic's positions on ending the war will not be compromised. His remarks followed confirmation from Tehran that officials had received a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance.

finance.yahoo.com/small-business/article.headline: McDonald’s Tests Out Value Deal Bundles at Select US Stores
finance.yahoo.com/small-business/article.author: Daniela Sirtori

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- McDonald's Corp. is rolling out a new mix-and-match bundle at select US stores to draw value-conscious diners.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The bundle would allow customers to pick two items from a lineup that includes the McDouble burger, the McChicken sandwich, six pieces of chicken nuggets and fries, according to people familiar with the matter. The deal would cost $3.50 to $4 depending on the market. The chain is also testing breakfast options.

It's one of the alternatives McDonald's is working on to sharpen its value menu, following the slowest growth for established US locations in more than a year last quarter. A prior promotion featuring about 10 items under $3 didn't draw as many diners as expected, Chief Executive Officer Chris Kempczinski said on the company's August earnings call. The chain named a new chief for its US business, Skye Anderson, to bring "focus and urgency" to the segment.
A McDonald's spokesperson said the company is looking to offer choice and value, including by testing a variety of meal bundles at select locations.
McDonald's shares rose as much as 0.7% at 4:12 p.m. Thursday in New York after the close of regular trading. The stock has fallen 16% this year, trailing the 13% rise in the S&P 500.

In September, Kempczinski told investors that having a new entry-level value program was a "big part" of McDonald's plan to strengthen the US business as it heads into 2027. The details of the value menu have not been previously reported.

The mix-and-match bundle resembles a prior "buy one, get one for $1" promotion that attracted diners but was nixed for the under $3 menu. Burger King, which grew US same-store sales faster than expected last quarter, offers a similar deal where diners can choose two items for $5.

McDonald's has tinkered with its value menu in recent years as it tries to counter the perception that its food has become too expensive. In 2024, it got a boost from its $5 meal deals. It recently brought back some app-only offers, such as free fries with a $1 minimum purchase. And it's currently advertising "extra value" meals nationwide, such as a Quarter Pounder with cheese combo that goes for $8.39 at a Chicago location.

Sales at established McDonald's US restaurants grew 0.8% in the second quarter, the weakest result since the start of 2025. Those sales likely declined in the quarter through Sept. 30, according to analysts polled by Bloomberg. The company reports earnings next week.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/png-el.headline: El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms fail
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/png-el.author: Graham Readfearn

paragraphs.text: Extreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people in Papua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.

An influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”

Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.

Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.
“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.

“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”
The El Niño climate pattern is gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will be the strongest ever recorded with its impacts worsened by global heating.
Some parts of PNG have had less than a quarter of their usual rainfall since August.

The PNG National Weather Service declared the onset of El Niño in June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.
Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.
“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.
PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.
“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.
In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.
Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.

Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.
“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”
Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.

Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.

In the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.

Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.

Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.
Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, that scientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.

Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.

“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/china-.headline: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/china-.author: Amy Hawkins

paragraphs.text: China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.

A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/sin.headline: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/sin.author: Rachel Savage

paragraphs.text: Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/sudane.headline: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/sudane.author: Carlos Mureithi

paragraphs.text: Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck8dz8j5n993o.headline: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck8dz8j5n993o.author: Lana Lam

paragraphs.text: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.

Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.

In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.
Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.
"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.
Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.
She promptly launched an appeal against her convictions, with her legal team in August arguing seven grounds for her appeal.
They claimed a hotel booking mishap - which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media - was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial.

They also argued certain pieces of evidence shown to the jury were irrelevant and prejudicial - such as cell tower data suggesting Patterson visited areas where death cap mushrooms might be found and Facebook posts where she complained about her in-laws.
Meanwhile, the judge wrongly blocked other evidence that would have demonstrated the mother-of-two's long-time hobby of mushroom foraging, they said.
The defence team also asserted that the prosecution's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was "unfair and oppressive", and that the Crown was inconsistent in its arguments about a motive.
On Friday, the appeal judges dismissed all seven grounds.
Patterson has 28 days to decide if she will seek to convince the High Court of Australia to hear another appeal over the case.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/friday.headline: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/friday.author: Libby Brooks

paragraphs.text: Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.

But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud.
As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories

• UK politics | John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.

• Patrick Stewart | The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, died at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said.
• Environment | One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.

• Europe | Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.

• US news | The Trump administration has opened a criminal investigation in California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials.
In depth: There is no evidence of election fraud

With the final results released early on Friday local time, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties won 19 seats, a record high. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.

With neither bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israeli president Isaac Herzog is expected to invite the party most likely to be able to form a government to start coalition negotiations, and has already urged politicians to have an “open mind” before talks begin. The country potentially faces weeks of rancour and uncertainty.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, told Israeli media on Thursday that he was meeting Eisenkot and others for initial talks. If the opposition can’t agree some kind of coalition, or even secure Palestinian support for a minority government, Netanyahu may have a lifeline. He is already pushing for a right-wing governing coalition, and would probably welcome new elections or a lengthy period of uncertainty during which he will stay on as caretaker prime minister.
And yet throughout the campaign, voters’ discontent with Netanyahu was evident.

That didn’t mean a shift to the left: young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations, as Emma wrote about here. The national conversation ahead of the election was dominated by security at home and abroad. Although he was in charge on 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacks resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, the prime minister tried to shift blame on to the security services.

His opponents pledged a state commission of inquiry into the events of 7 October, and spoke to voters’ concerns about the social toll of three years of multi-front wars, and anger about the draft exemption for ultra-orthodox young men when other Israelis are spending hundreds of days on reserve duty.
Netanyahu’s false narrative

Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu and his far-right allies have framed Palestinian voters – who make up about 20% of the population – as a direct threat to the state, with Netanyahu repeating the slogan “the right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.
“It’s both tragic and depressing,” Emma tells me, “attempting to paint Palestinians as untrustworthy citizens with dual loyalties, a racist trope that also appears in antisemitic attacks.”

This tactic extended to election day, when voters received a robocall purporting to come from the prime minister falsely claiming that Palestinian party leaders had been caught with envelopes full of cash. Netanyahu and his allies repeatedly made claims about high turnout in Palestinian areas, in a bid to get his own voters out.

Then on Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming, again without providing evidence, they had “stolen the election,” calling for the central elections committee and Shin Bet internal security agency to investigate foreign interference in the vote. These claims were amplified by far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who called for the arrest of Arab Israeli leaders.

He was swiftly accused of using smear tactics to cling to power. Eisenkot warned that Likud and Netanyahu “have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election”. President Herzog stepped in with a rebuke to the prime minister and said “we must avoid tarnishing an entire community”. Meanwhile, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected “ridiculous and dangerous” accusations his country had interfered in Tuesday’s election.
It bears repeating: Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud.
The Palestinian-led parties who could be kingmakers
There was a surge in support for Arab parties after Palestinian citizens came out in historic numbers to vote.

Many had boycotted previous elections “on the grounds that participating endorses a discriminatory system or because they felt their representatives had little leverage”, Emma explains. But this year, the mood changed: “They’re watching ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, a genocidal war in Gaza, and are under huge pressure inside Israel from an openly racist government, which has allowed organised crime to soar, ramped up home demolitions, and targeted political speech. They felt that, if Netanyahu managed to get another mandate with his far right allies including [extremist security minister] Ben-Gvir, this would only accelerate.”

The Joint List – which represents a number of mainly leftist Israeli Arab-led parties – is led by Yousef Jabareen. He has previously said the Joint List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s military operation in Gaza and southern Lebanon, but has left open the possibility of bolstering a minority government through confidence votes.

The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, and includes a Jewish former chief of police as number two on their slate, a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis but also their desire to tackle organised crime, which is a big issue for the Palestinian population.

Ra’am joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time a Palestinian party entered an Israeli coalition, but their pact collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.
The big dilemma
A survey taken as polls closed on Tuesday showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu.

While Eisenkot has not ruled out cooperating with Palestinians because of their race, he has effectively barred them from a future coalition by laying out conditions for any partner which are politically impossible for them to accept.

Still, Emma notes an inconsistency: Palestinian citizens play a key role in Israeli life, with outsized representation in professions from medics to security guards, including much of the team at Eisenkot’s election night HQ. “You would think some of these parties might ask, if you trust Palestinian citizens to secure your campaign events why don’t you trust them to be part of your government?”

Emma points to a rarely referenced precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict. Might such a compromise be possible now?

“This whole campaign has been based on Israeli voters urgently wanting change, because Netanyahu has led them to the brink of disaster. And now they have voted, this is an existential moment,” she said

“You have a parliamentary majority to bring about that change. Is your racism ultimately more important to you? What matters more: the desire to exclude Palestinians or the desire to get rid of Netanyahu?”
What else we’ve been reading

• Tim Burrows’ deep dive on how Romford might actually be the birthplace of jungle was surprising and gave me a sense of nostalgia for a time that I wasn’t really part of. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
• The latest instalment of our US politics film series, Anywhere but Washington, really captures the vibe in Texas where all eyes are on a hotly contested midterm Senate race. Michael
• Adrian Chiles on the cryptic sign outside his local pub was a lesson in when not to brag. I now know far more about pub tubes, mould and yeast than I ever cared to know. Poppy
• Andy Beckett’s ode to the British Library comes as some of its silent, free-to-access reading rooms face a #coworking space fate. Fun fact, I once fell asleep for a whole hour inside one … Michael
• Readers’ reactions to the budget was a real take on the different ways people in the country live. Poppy
Sport
Women’s Champion League | Paris Saint-Germain’s Tara Elimbi Gilbert had a late equaliser moments after Khadija Shaw scored a penalty as Manchester City drew their third league phase game in a row.
Cricket | England beat Sri Lanka in the One Day International by 55 runs but still do not progress to the final on Sunday.
Football | Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town.

“Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The Times leads with “Defence to benefit from off-the-book spending”, the Telegraph writes “Prepare for decade of pain, warn IFS”, and the i Paper leads on “No welfare cuts before election – as Britons face ‘worst decade’ for pay growth”, while the Mail has “Humiliation for Healey”.
The FT says “Alphabet shares battered as cash burn deepens investor fears over AI returns”. Metro writes “Manosphere ‘as bad as smoking’” and the Sun splashes “Fright of the round table”.

Shock and anger in Spain after deadly train crash

Spain has begun three days of mourning after at least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured in a crash between two high-speed trains. The town of Urda has become the site of a major operation, as emergency services continue to search through the wreckage and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. There is growing public anger over the incident, which is the second fatal train collision in Spain in less than a year. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent, Sam Jones.
Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Moving away from diesel-powered ferries to electric vessels has not been an easy task. Batteries are heavy, which means more power is needed to propel electric boats forward through significant resistance. But more companies are finding solutions to the problem and creating workable vessels that reduce emissions.

One such company is Vessev, whose electric ferries rely on underwater wings called hydrofoils that lift the boat above the water. This dramatically reduces drag by up to 66%, making their boats more energy-efficient. Swedish company Candela are designing boats, they claim, which can reduce energy use by 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.
