theguardian.com/science/2026/oct/29/jet-.headline: Why jet lag throws even foraging seabirds off course
theguardian.com/science/2026/oct/29/jet-.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say.

Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.

The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey.
But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles.

Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.

Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said.

Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time.

Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.

“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.”

Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.”
Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows.

“It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”

politico.com/news/2026/10/30/republicans.headline: ‘It could be quite a brutal evening:’ GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses
politico.com/news/2026/10/30/republicans.author: Meredith Lee Hill

paragraphs.text: Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they’re set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife’s edge.

House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they’ll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states.

“It could be quite a brutal evening,” said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them.”

Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump’s political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people.
One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters.

Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they’re facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day.
Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who’d voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war.
That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024.

At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? “I think they’re bull,” he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump.
Is he voting this time? “No,” Romero responded, adding: “I didn’t vote for this.”

New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch.
“Any Democrats telling you they aren’t winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations,” the senior Republican said.

In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee “Vivek’s [Ramaswamy’s] numbers have gone off a cliff” in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton’s stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12.

The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits.

South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans’ base.
“It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out,” said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party.

But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South.
Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes.

“The cakewalk turned into a knife fight,” said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. “If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it’ll be a long night in Monroe,” the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago.

In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump, and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson’s former pastor. Club for Growth Club poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff.

"POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre.

“While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets,” said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they’ve long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster.Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas).

The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed.

Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden’s (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina’s open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they’re still not confident they’ll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It’s become the most expensive House race in history.
The Republican in Kentucky’s 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people.

Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races.

Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district.

“We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it,” Finstad said. “From a global perspective, people were like, ‘Well, you won by 18, you’re fine.’ And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it.”

Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way.
“I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what’s going to happen, they’re full of shit,” one senior Senate Democratic operative said. “Everything is close.”
And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it’ll all soon be over.
“I can see the light at the end of the tunnel,” said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. “It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it."
Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report.
This just in, according to new poll results: Americans don’t trust polls.

Only 25% of Americans said political surveys correctly estimate votes, according to a new POLITICO Poll, conducted by PF Global. The result reveals that a significant portion of the public lacks faith in the industry as it contends with accusations of consistently failing to reach Republican voters.

It comes amid an intensely scrutinized 2026 midterm cycle, where public polling and campaigns’ internal polls have shown many races within the margin of error in key battlegrounds and in once-safe red territory.

Roughly one in four respondents say that polls showing a blue wave coming in November are wrong, and they expect Republicans to win key races. And 41% of Americans — including voters of both parties — either say polls tend to underestimate Democrats or that they tend to underestimate Republicans.

There have been some high-profile blunders: Polls have missed themark throughout the Trump era. This cycle alone, surveys in Democratic primaries incorrectly predicted that progressive Francesca Hong would win the race for Wisconsin governor and that Abdul El-Sayed — who did become Democrat’s Michigan Senate nominee — would win by a much wider margin than the 1 percentage point victory he eked out.

Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have cast doubt on the latest forecasts: The polls are “grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm around the country,” Johnson said on Fox News this week, adding that “more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys.”
President Donald Trump has called the polls “fake” and “rigged.” Vice President JD Vance said he tells people to ignore the polls because they have a “demotivating effect on our voters.”

Pollsters know their industry is facing heavy scrutiny. However: “There isn't another thing waiting in the wings to replace the full purpose of this tool,” said Charlotte Swasey, the director of analytics for the Democratic think tank Searchlight Institute, told POLITICO. “This is what we have, and it's difficult, it's increasingly difficult. But it's not dead by any sense of the word.”

Pollsters have made a number of changes over the years — like capturing respondents across all levels of education attainment or adjusting their methodologies to account for low response rates among any given group.
Still, roughly two in five Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 say political polls tend to underestimate Republicans.

Their feelings are not completely unfounded. In 2016, pollsters grossly underestimated support for then-candidate Trump, with most polls coalescing around a relatively secure victory for former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton.

Distrust is especially widespread among Trump voters who identify as “MAGA Republicans” — his most loyal base. Three in five MAGA Trump voters say the polls indicating Democrats will win key races next week are incorrect. Among non-MAGA Trump voters, just a third feel the same.

“National polls always underestimate support for Republicans,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. “Polls may suggest one thing, but the American people get the final say, and Republicans remain laser-focused on driving voters to the polls, defying history, and protecting our majorities."

“I do think that non-response among base Republican voters in some of these red states is a problem,” Christine Matthews, president of public opinion polling firm Bellwether Research, told POLITICO in a recent interview.

Republican candidates and officials are banking on the non-response caveat as Senate races in states like Kansas, Mississippi and Nebraska — and to some extent, in South Carolina and Louisiana — all tighten, with less than one week until Election Day. If polling proves true, they could experience once-unthinkable losses in deep-red territory.
But distrust is not limited to Republicans.

Many in both parties were outraged after one group — Wedgewood Polls — admitted under scrutiny from FiftyPlusOne to using fake data in its polling results in several Democratic primaries, which some believe impacted election results. Another group published fake polling data on the Los Angeles mayoral race as a test to see how the data would travel before being verified.
And just under a third of voters who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris say political polls tend to underestimate Democrats.

Part of the distrust can come down to the fact that polls are not intended to forecast outcomes. They are a snapshot of public sentiment at a given point in time — and people can change their minds. One in five Americans said in POLITICO’s survey they have filled in a poll on how they would vote differently than how they actually voted.

“Of course there are people who say something to a poll and then do something different a couple of weeks later,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at London-based PF Global, POLITICO’s polling partner. “I think it's quite possible that some of the races that were real big misses earlier this year were decided in the very last week.”

According to a recent POLITICO survey, polls — which, when conducted correctly, involve careful planning and meticulous methodology — don’t earn much more trust than prediction markets, where odds are determined simply by bets placed by the public.

Just 18% of people said they trusted poll-based forecasts over prediction markets to correctly predict the outcome of an election. That’s a marginal lead on the 12% of people who said they trust prediction markets over polls. A third said they trust neither.

Still, most voters say they do make decisions based on polling. Roughly 55% of Americans say they would “definitely” go vote if the polls showed their preferred candidate far behind. Even among Republican midterm voters who say the polls underestimate their party, roughly 75% say the same.

“There are a lot of voters that are motivated to send a message to the system,” said longtime GOP strategist Kevin Madden. “I think particularly on the [political] right, they'll be motivated to send a message, and essentially that message is ‘You're wrong, and the voters are right.’”
The big question for campaigns is “are there enough of those?” he said.

technologyreview.com/2026/10/30/1147838/.headline: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
technologyreview.com/2026/10/30/1147838/.author: Jessica Hamzelou

paragraphs.text: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.

What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.

Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.

It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.

Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.

That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).

The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.

Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.

It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?

Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.

When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.

The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.

Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.

Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.

In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.

Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.

“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.

Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/houthi.headline: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/houthi.author: Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.

Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.

The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.
With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.

Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.
“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.

His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”
Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.

He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.

People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.

Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.

Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.

Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

politico.com/news/2026/10/30/josh-shapir.headline: Josh Shapiro aims for a strong finish in a campaign with 2028 implications
politico.com/news/2026/10/30/josh-shapir.author: Adam Wren

paragraphs.text: POCONO RACEWAY, Pennsylvania — High up in the starting stand of a famed race track, Josh Shapiro waves a black-and-white checkered flag with an unmistakeable meaning: It’s over.
The metaphor isn’t entirely accurate.
“We may have a lead, but you're coming down this home stretch. People are nipping at your heels,” the Pennsylvania governor told POLITICO. “You’ve got to run hard.”
Shapiro, the potential 2028 contender and 2024 veepstakes short-lister, does have reasons to be optimistic — and careful.
He’s threatening a double-digit blowout over Stacy Garrity, a candidate backed by President Donald Trump, in the most important swing state in the nation.
He’s also putting his coattails to the test.

None of the other potential 2028 Democratic candidates has more at stake in their own backyard on Tuesday than Shapiro. He doesn’t have California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s map-breaking Proposition 50, designed to beat back the GOP redistricting, nor his platinum email list. He doesn’t have Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker’s billions or Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly’s deep bench of donors or former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg’s large map or the red-state credentials of Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.

Shapiro is on the brink of flipping four hotly contested congressional seats — and guaranteeing Democrats the House. Pennsylvania Democrats could also take control of the state Senate, including some heavily gerrymandered seats, giving the party a governing trifecta for the first time since 1992.
“I’m not thinking about this as a victory for me,” he told POLITICO during a swing through the state. “I'm thinking about this as a victory for our country.”
All of which paves the way for him to pass a $15 minimum wage and a raft of other measures that could buttress a 2028 presidential bid.

Shapiro is very much following the Ron DeSantis theory of a presidential primary campaign: demonstrate dominance at home before branching out nationally — a strategy, it should be noted, that didn’t pay off for the Florida governor.

“I think what really hurt DeSantis was that he decided he wasn't going to announce until after his legislative session, and that was May,” political strategist David Axelrod said. “Time is at a premium. If that’s his plan, that would be a miscalculation.”
Will we see him venture beyond Pennsylvania’s boundaries before the end of the year?
“I don’t know what my plans are,” Shapiro said.

The day had the feeling of both an ending of one campaign and the beginning of another. Even as he urged a midday audience of about 100 people to vote for Paige Cognetti, the Scranton mayor running against Rep. Rob Bresnahan, and Brian Wrightson, the state Senate candidate challenging Sen. Rosemary Brown, he is nationalizing his rhetoric.

“Don’t let Trump take away your hopefulness,” he told people gathered at East Stroudsburg University. “Don't let him make you feel pessimistic. Don't let him feel like change can't come or that we have to look in the rearview mirror for answers. The answers are always straight ahead.”
Then there’s his set piece about the “American dream slipping away.”
He’s broadening out his message beyond the commonwealth.

“I think the work I do here in Pennsylvania, the confidence I give them about their government here can hopefully restore some of their faith in democracy, and I want in our democracy, and I want them to feel like they've got power to be able to shape the future of that American dream,” Shapiro told us.

A few hours later, Shapiro materializes inside Salerno’s, a tavern in Old Forge known for its American cheese-topped pizza. He sets a room in which patrons already have had a few too many Rolling Rocks and pumpkin martinis.
On the televisions, his own ad for Wrightson is playing on TV. He grips and grins and backslaps his way through the room.
At the end of the bar, he picks up five pizzas for the road, ducks out the door and boards his bus for another Cognetti rally.
Shapiro’s gubernatorial reelect isn’t drawing the buzz of some of the more razor’s-edge, online Senate races in the waning days of election season. But his project is no less remarkable.

“If we can win enough seats here in Pennsylvania to change the balance of power in Washington and be a check on Donald Trump, then we can both hold the president accountable and get stuff done in Washington,” Shapiro says. “Likewise, here in Pennsylvania, if we can win a trifecta for the first time since Bill Clinton's election, I can raise wages almost immediately for tens of thousands of Pennsylvanians who are at or below minimum wage and raise wages for others. That's a concrete thing that we can accomplish.”
At the raceway, he has just finished cutting a video racing around the Pocono Raceway’s Tricky Triangle when he flashes a grin.
“I’ve got a surprise for you,” he says, inviting POLITICO to the starting stand above the storied three-turn NASCAR track in the Pocono foothills.
Up the stairs, the burnt-orange fall foliage dances on the Pennsylvania horizon. It’s a vantage point Shapiro, as a NASCAR fan, has taken in many times.
Despite the apt setting, he deflects when asked if he’s ready to announce the launch of his campaign.
“If this is a metaphor,” he says, “it's for finishing the race strong.”
There is just one wrinkle: Before he brandished the black-and-white flag, he picked up a green one, waving it vigorously.
“I think you mis-saw that,” Shapiro said with a smile. “I was waving a checkered flag to finish the governor’s race.”

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/bp-pro.headline: BP Profit Hits 18-Year High as Oil Refining Margins Surge
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/bp-pro.author: Mitchell Ferman

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- BP Plc said profit surged to the highest in 18 years as soaring refining margins boosted earnings, giving Chief Executive Officer Meg O'Neill a powerful tailwind as she seeks to turn around the beleaguered British energy major.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Adjusted net income was $8.46 billion, compared with $2.21 billion a year earlier, the London-based giant said in a statement on Friday. More than half the profit came from the unit that includes oil refining and trading. The company's net debt tumbled.

The results are O'Neill's second full quarter at the helm and offer a fresh look at the operational performance that she's identified as a priority. BP's first outsider CEO is cutting costs, selling assets and paying down debt while preparing to lay out her longer-term strategy for the firm in December.

It comes amid a refining boom that's showering Europe's oil giants with cash, spurring BP's rivals to announce jumbo payouts to investors — something the UK major is eschewing to focus on its balance sheet. Wars involving Iran and Russia have knocked out or disrupted oil refineries and trade routes, squeezing the world's capacity to turn crude into diesel, gasoline and jet fuel and handing outsized profits to plants that remain operational.

"It really was a banner quarter for the refining business," O'Neill said in an interview with Bloomberg TV. "We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market."

On Thursday, rival Shell Plc announced it was increasing its quarterly share buyback to $5 billion from $3 billion after its refining margins surged and earnings climbed to their highest since the aftermath of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. TotalEnergies SE has pledged as much as $2.5 billion of repurchases this quarter, while Repsol SA and Eni SpA have also boosted their buybacks.
By contrast, BP suspended share repurchases earlier this year to prioritize paying down debt and improving its balance sheet. BP made no new announcements about buybacks.
Net debt tumbled to $13.87 billion from $22.3 billion three months earlier, surpassing the company's target a year ahead of schedule.
The company's adjusted net income beat the $7.3 billion average analyst estimate compiled by Bloomberg. BP said oil and gas trading operations both performced strongly.
BP is benefitting from many of the same strong market conditions as its rivals. The major's refining margin indicator surged to $46.70 a barrel during the quarter from $29.60 in the previous period.
The company's Customer and Products unit, where oil trading and refining sit, made $4.8 billion in the quarter. It made $5.3 billion in all of 2025.
--With assistance from James Herron.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: A European Stock Trader’s Guide Ahead of the US Midterms
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Levin Stamm and Matt Clinch

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- European equity investors are turning their attention to next week's US midterm elections, with the outcome potentially shaping the earnings outlook for a range of industries across the continent.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Policy in areas from defense spending and tariffs to drug pricing and research funding could shift depending on whether Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Currently, polls and prediction markets indicate a high likelihood that Republicans will lose control of the House of Representatives, while the outcome for the Senate is less certain.

"Midterms do matter for Europe, as European equities have substantial US revenue exposure," said Andrea Gabellone, head of global equities at KBC Securities. "A Democratic House and Senate give them greater scope for coordinated funding negotiations, especially in healthcare, clean energy and defense."
Here's a breakdown of what to watch around the Nov. 3 vote:

While Europe has few stocks that directly benefit from the AI investment boom relative to the US or Asia, a handful could face greater earnings uncertainty if Democrats gain more influence in Congress.
"The industry is responding to a political backdrop that is increasingly scrutinizing AI and data centers," Deutsche Bank AG analysts wrote in a report.

For European firms in the "picks and shovels" part of the US data-center buildout chain, a more stringent regulatory backdrop holds the potential for delays and setbacks to the construction boom. STMicroelectronics NV, Schneider Electric SE and Nokia Oyj are among the companies in the space with the highest exposure to the US.

Still, strategists at JPMorgan Chase & Co. including Dubravko Lakos-Bujas expect AI capex momentum to remain intact after the midterms and potentially even strengthen in 2027 and 2028. Companies will seek to meet AI demand and advance investment "before political risks intensify around the next presidential cycle," the team said in a note.

Stocks to watch: ASML Holding NV, ASM International NV, BE Semiconductor Industries NV, STMicroelectronics, Infineon Technologies AG, Nordic Semiconductor ASA, Nokia, OVH Groupe SA, Schneider Electric, Aixtron SE, ABB Ltd

Pharmaceutical companies stand to be among the biggest European beneficiaries of a "blue wave" that would see Democrats take the House and the Senate. Greater Democratic control of Congress could slow the White House's push for funding cuts and tighter oversight of research grants. The same is true for university and research funding, according to Oddo BHF strategist Thomas Zlowodzki.
If Democrats "were to succeed on these points in the budget negotiations, this would primarily support the purchase of laboratory equipment, reagents and consumables," Zlowodzki wrote in a note.

That would help healthcare stocks continue their recent outperformance against other parts of the market, facilitated by investors' preference for safer stocks amid rising yields and worries about government finances.

Still, Bloomberg Intelligence's Duane Wright highlighted that "European pharma companies will still face US policy uncertainty" even if the midterms were to produce a divided government and legislative gridlock.
Stocks to watch: Merck KGaA, Tecan Group AG, Sartorius AG
Utilities and Renewables

Opposition to renewable energy could ease if Democrats gain ground, according to Amundi strategists, potentially improving the sector's competitiveness with fossil fuels. The JPMorgan strategists say their blue-wave scenario would be encouraging for clean-energy stocks through greater support on appropriations, oversight and permitting. Citigroup Inc. analyst Martin Wilkie, meanwhile, cautioned that changes to Federal policy likely wouldn't have an impact before 2028.

Oddo BHF highlights European names including Engie SA and Iberdrola SA for their renewables exposure, as well as National Grid Plc for its role in powering the AI buildout. The London-listed utility, which generates 69% of its sales in the US, has previously received a $50 million Department of Energy grant toward a $140 million smart-grid project. More recently, it invested in a US company developing a natural gas-fired power plant for Microsoft Corp. in Texas.
Stocks to watch: Iberdrola, EDP Renewables SA, RWE AG, Engie, Orsted AS, Vestas Wind Systems AS
Construction and Materials

The election outcome isn't expected to fundamentally alter construction's regulatory framework. However, a strong Democratic showing could give the party more scope to influence policy through budget negotiations. Support for construction is broadly bipartisan, with the main differences centered on how projects are funded and around energy-efficiency renovations.

Oddo's Zlowodzki highlights Cie de Saint-Gobain SA and Heidelberg Materials AG, among others, with both generating roughly 20% of sales in the US. Saint-Gobain is exposed to building and renovation through its local plasterboard business, while Heidelberg Materials is more sensitive to local construction and infrastructure spending through its cement, aggregates, concrete and asphalt operations. Saint-Gobain and Heidelberg Materials have fallen 22% and 32%, respectively, year-to-date.

Meanwhile, the JPMorgan strategists said a "red wall scenario," that sees Republicans keep both the House and the Senate, would likely favor construction and building materials stocks, offering the most supportive incremental backdrop for the AI and infrastructure buildout through policy continuity.
Stocks to watch: Saint-Gobain, Heidelberg Materials, Sika AG
Oil and Gas

The crucial question for Europe's energy stocks is how the results alter the outlook for a peace deal in Iran, and ultimately commodity prices. Regardless of the outcome, there is speculation that President Donald Trump may order fresh strikes against Iran, potentially increasing the risk of renewed escalation. Elevated oil prices would spur profits for Europe's energy companies, which have already been a major driver of earnings growth this year.

Beyond geopolitics, Oddo flagged Technip Energies NV among the companies that stand to benefit from a Democratic victory, given its exposure to decarbonization engineering contracts, which would face fewer risks to funding. In contrast, TotalEnergies SE, as one of the largest liquefied natural gas exporters to the US, and Shell Plc, with major production sites in the Gulf of Mexico, would be more vulnerable to changes in the current policy framework.
Stocks to watch: Technip Energies, TotalEnergies, Shell

Democratic gains could add another headwind for European defense stocks. The elections could reset the Pentagon's fiscal 2027 budget toward 2026 levels and flatten spending growth through 2028, BI analysts Will Lee and George Ferguson wrote in a note. Oddo's Zlowodzki, meanwhile, said the risk "primarily relates to the future growth in US orders relative to expectations, not necessarily to existing contracts."

The boom in European defense stocks in 2025 was largely driven by expectations that the industry will help the continent disentangle itself from its US security guarantees. But since European governments have drawn up unprecedented spending packages, the sector has traded sideways as investors wait for those promises to become reality.
Stocks to watch: BAE Systems Plc, Leonardo SpA, Thales SA, Kongsberg Gruppen ASA
--With assistance from Michael Msika.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.headline: Yields Too High to Ignore Lure Investors Back to Long-Dated Debt
finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.author: George Nixon and Georgia Hall

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Long-dated government bonds spent much of the year punishing anyone brave enough to own them. Now yields are high enough that investors are coming back.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Risk-free payouts near multi-decade highs are becoming difficult to resist, particularly with stocks looking expensive and volatile. Ten-year US Treasuries yields peaked at almost 5.4% this month, their highest since 2002, while those in Japan reached a 30-year high of 3.14%.

The comeback trade in long bonds has enticed portfolio managers at JPMorgan Asset Management, Aegon Asset Management, Ninety One and Allianz GI, to name just a few. Yields are now in reverse, rewarding investors with a return of 2.2% in October on a gauge of global government bonds maturing in 10 years or more, a level that's handily beaten the flat performance of sovereign debt due in one to three years — and the first month since February in which longer bonds outperformed.

Those profits have encouraged investors to overlook, for now at least, the dangers that sent yields so high in the first place. Energy-driven inflation, tighter monetary policy and deteriorating government finances haven't disappeared. The price of taking those risks has simply become more attractive.
"The long-end just got too cheap and too unanchored," said JPMorgan Asset's head of global fixed income Bob Michele. He's been buying longer-dated from Australia and Japan as well as US Treasuries.

As investors question whether tech companies have overpromised on AI, government bonds are looking like a haven again. That's borne out by movement in and out of exchange traded funds. The iShares US Treasury Bond ETF drew inflows for the second consecutive month while the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF flipped to outflows from inflows the previous month.

To be sure, policy angst — Fed, Treasury and election-related — continues to weigh on demand for longer-dated US Treasuries. They sold off in reaction to the Fed's decision to leave interest rates unchanged, which rekindled doubt that Chairman Kevin Warsh is committed to the central bank's 2% inflation target.

Longer-dated European government debt also fell Thursday after investors interpreted comments from European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde to signal the central bank wouldn't intervene to stem a selloff caused by France's political and fiscal turmoil.

"I'd call it a pause rather than a turning point, as the pressures behind this year's selloff haven't gone away," said Hilary Winn, investment director at AJ Bell. "We still lean towards quality and shorter duration, rather than chase a long-dated rally."

Next month's US midterms give even bond bulls reason for caution. A divided Congress could put a lid on fiscal expansion and help long-dated Treasuries, while a surprise Republican hold of both chambers risks reopening the spending-and-inflation debate.

At the same time, an economic slowdown and flight to safety could pull yields lower, while looser fiscal policy or an escalation of the war that fuels inflation could trigger another selloff, said Oliver Faizallah, head of fixed-income research at Raymond James Wealth Management.
The long end of the Treasury market is "hard to get a good fair value on," Faizallah said.

Still, October's retreat in yields offers some relief to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ahead of his department's quarterly refunding statement, where it lays out its borrowing plans. Speculation has grown the US may cut sales of 20- and 30-year bonds, after yields on the latter soared to the highest since 2002. The rally reduces the urgency of that discussion, though many banks still expect such changes could come in 2027.

The appeal extends beyond the US. Higher yields are drawing buyers to long-dated Japanese bonds, while German debt is benefiting from a flight to safety amid France's turmoil. In the UK, reduced long-bond sales by the Bank of England and improving sentiment toward Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government have helped long gilts outperform.

Royal London Asset Management moved to an overweight position on 30-year UK gilts over the past few months. Craig Inches, head of rates and cash, has been telling its clients it's the right time to extend duration.
"We've seen bond yields go higher, higher, higher, higher," Inches said.
--With assistance from Greg Ritchie and Ye Xie.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: Copper Declines as Tech Selloff, Oil Rally Dent Risk Appetite
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Bloomberg News

paragraphs.text: Thu, October 29, 2026 at 9:31 PM MDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Copper slipped on the London Metal Exchange as a selloff of technology stocks and higher oil prices fueled concerns about global growth.
Most Read from Bloomberg

A disappointing earnings season for tech companies has raised doubts about spending on artificial intelligence, while the risk of renewed US military action against Iran pushed Brent crude to its highest since April. The concerns prompted a retreat from risk assets at the tail end of a mildly positive week for industrial metals.

"The sharp decline in technology stocks has fueled market skepticism regarding returns on AI investments, leading to a retreat in risk appetite and putting downward pressure on copper," according to a note from Guangzhou Futures Co.

Industrial metals, especially copper, have been caught up in big swings in tech stocks this year, although other factors have also been at play, including uncertainty over US import tariffs and volatile oil prices. Crude climbed on Friday after the Wall Street Journal reported that a top US commander had briefed President Donald Trump on military options for Iran.

Copper fell 0.2% at $14,332.50 a ton by 11:30 a.m. Shanghai time. Investors are also monitoring developments at a giant Rio Tinto Group mine in Mongolia that halted underground production after a rockfall that injured three people. The metal is heading for a slight loss in October, snapping three months of gains.
Aluminum was little changed at $3,084 a ton, on track for a second monthly decline. Zinc slipped from its highest close since Sept. 25, and is set for a monthly increase.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Nvidia in Talks to Offer Credit Support for Nscale Project
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Brody Ford

paragraphs.text: Thu, October 29, 2026 at 5:59 PM MDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Nvidia Corp. is in discussions to provide credit guarantees for an Nscale data center facility that Anthropic PBC plans to use, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The credit support would help backstop the electricity and construction costs for an AI data center campus in West Virginia that will be equipped with Nvidia chips, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. Nvidia, the dominant provider of artificial intelligence processors, is already an investor in Nscale and other providers of AI computing services.

UK-based Nscale is racing to get a series of large data centers online, including this flagship site in West Virginia. It is also pursuing an initial public offering, with some investors pushing back on its $30 billion IPO target.

A representative for Nscale declined to comment, while Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The Information previously reported on Nvidia's discussions with Nscale, saying that the credit guarantees could amount to billions of dollars.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said earlier this month that he told the UK—based company to "work around the clock" to overcome challenges in bringing some of its data centers online.

The broader market for so-called neoclouds — companies like Nscale that provide AI computing power — has been in turmoil during recent weeks. Australian company Firmus Grid, another Nvidia-backed neocloud, abandoned a $30 billion IPO in Australia and South Korea's Elice had a rocky trading debut.
Bloomberg News has reported that Nscale has discussed a second $45 billion deal with Anthropic for the second building on the West Virginia campus.

theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/30/.headline: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/30/.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.

Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.

Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.

Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

wsj.com/world/uk/boe-survey-points-to-fa.headline: BOE Survey Points to Faster Price Rises, But Slowing Wage Growth

paragraphs.text: U.K. businesses polled in October expected to raise their prices at a slightly faster pace than in the previous month, but wage increases were seen slowing, according to a Bank of England survey released Friday.
Some 1,945 chief financial officers were questioned between Oct. 2 and 16, with energy prices having remained high since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran in late February.

The survey found that businesses expected the prices they charge to rise by 3.8% over the coming 12 months, an increase from the 3.7% expected in September. Businesses reported that the prices they charge increased by 3.8% in the year to October.
"Businesses therefore expect output price inflation to be unchanged over the next year, based on three-month averages," the BOE said.
The high rate of expected price rises will concern BOE policymakers, who meet next week to set policy and are expected to raise their key interest rate to 4% from 3.75%.
However, there are few signs that higher inflation is leading to a pickup in wage growth that could trigger a second round of price increases.
In the year to October, businesses reported that wages rose by 3.9%, a slowdown from the 4% reported in September. They expect wages to rise by 3.4% over the coming 12 months, a significant cooling.
"This implies that firms expect their wage growth to decline by 0.5 percentage points over the next 12 months," the BOE said.

kanebridgenews.com/the-origin-story-of-c.headline: The Origin Story of Candy Corn—and Other Halloween Mainstays
kanebridgenews.com/the-origin-story-of-c.author: Kanebridge

paragraphs.text: Candy Corn. Haunted houses. Seasonal spectacles that now seem inseparable from October.

Many of Halloween’s biggest mainstays started much more modestly—as ideas from entrepreneurs and small businesses that caught on, spread and eventually became traditions. Along the way, they helped turn Halloween into a $13.1 billion consumer business in 2025.
Here is a look at four of the most popular creations, and how they got their start.
Candy Corn
One of the most inescapable Halloween treats—Candy Corn—wasn’t marketed as a Halloween goody at first. In fact, it was marketed as a whimsical candy version of chicken feed.

It was created back in the 1880s in Philadelphia, which was then a candy-making hub. One popular trend among candy companies was nature: treats inspired by the agricultural world, like pumpkins, leaves and chestnuts.

Among those businesses was Wunderle Candy, owned by a family of German immigrants. (Milton Hershey worked there before he founded his chocolate business.) One Wunderle employee, George Renninger, came up with the idea of a candy shaped like corn kernels—but also took the innovative step of applying different layers of colors to the treats.

The process involved pouring layers of hot liquid sugar into tiny molds by hand. “It was laborious,” says Beth Kimmerle, founder and chief executive of Attribute Analytics and author of three books about candy.

The unusual color scheme gave the candy instant appeal. And, yes, it was marketed as faux chicken feed at the start: “an agricultural-themed novelty and penny candy that appeared throughout the year,” Kimmerle says.

How did the corn get associated with Halloween? At the turn of the last century, another candy company, Goelitz Confectionery, also began selling the treat. Kimmerle says it isn’t clear what kind of arrangement—if any—the two companies had about the rights to the candy. But, in the end, Goelitz usually gets the credit for scaling the candy and branding it as a Halloween product.

As for Wunderle, Kimmerle says, the business wound down in the 1980s, while Goelitz was eventually renamed Jelly Belly in 2001, and acquired by Ferrara Candy in 2023. (Another Ferrara brand, Brach’s, has also been selling candy-corn treats since the 1920s; Ferrara says that it doesn’t have information showing a licensing agreement between the companies.)

Candy Corn has not only become immensely popular in itself, but also has lent its colors and flavors to countless other products. This year, Brach’s launched a limited-edition fragrance, Ode to Candy Corn, which “smells exactly like how candy corn tastes,” according to the company.
Licensed costumes
Dressing up as your favorite fictional figure is a Halloween tradition. Entrepreneur Ben Cooper made it a lot easier for people to get into character—by making licensed costumes a big business.

In the 1930s, Cooper sold costumes for vaudeville, says Rob Caprilozzi, founder of the Horror News Network website, who recently made a documentary about Cooper. In 1937, the entrepreneur—whose company was simply called Ben Cooper Inc.—bought another company, A.S. Fishbach, which had the license to manufacture costumes of Disney characters.

Cooper added more costumes as new Disney movies came out, as well as updating the old ones, Caprilozzi says. In the 1960s, he expanded his line to superheroes—including Spider-Man and Batman—and then turned to “Sesame Street” and “Star Wars” characters in the 1970s.
“At its height, the company controlled 80% of the licensed custom characters,” says Caprilozzi.
And it wasn’t just fictional heroes, either: Cooper had a line of costumes based on U.S. presidents. (The company destroyed its JFK inventory after the assassination, says Caprilozzi.)

One of the selling points of Cooper’s costumes was simplicity. The costumes were just plastic masks and tarps costing a few dollars apiece, and you could toss them out after the big night—no need to hang onto them year-round.
The company lasted until 1992, when it filed for bankruptcy and was then acquired by competitor Rubie’s Costume. (The company, now known as Rubies, didn’t respond to requests for comment.)
Halloween pop-up shops
Joseph Marver didn’t change what we wear for Halloween, the candy we eat or the type of decorations we put up. But he revolutionized where we buy all that stuff.

Marver was running an apparel store called Spirit Women’s Discount Apparel in Castro Valley, Calif. October sales were historically slow, but he noticed sales booming at a costume shop across the street. According to media accounts, the other store changed locations, and Marver in 1983 decided to get into the Halloween business himself. He put his usual wares into storage and turned his store into an emporium for Halloween merchandise.

“I went to a trade show in Chicago, picked up everything I could that had to do with Halloween, and put it in my store, and it was amazing,” Marver told San Francisco Bay Area radio station KQED in July 2024. (He died in 2025.)
“His sales went through the roof,” says Lisa Morton, author of “Trick or Treat: A History of Halloween” and “The Halloween Encyclopedia.”

Marver doubled down on the gambit the following year—renting out a temporary space in a local mall to sell all types of Halloween products for eight to 10 weeks, from costumes to decorations to face paint. At the time, retail leases typically lasted a decade, and it was difficult for newcomers to land a lease, let alone a temporary one, says Barbara Kahn, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School.

In the interview with KQED, Marver described his initial difficulties. “Some of the people in the strip centers wanted to have the big boxes come in, but then, some of them realized it [was] not going to happen,” he said. So the malls agreed to take on the pop-ups, figuring, “‘Let’s do Halloween. Let’s get something going. Maybe it’ll bring business to the other tenants.’”

Over the next 16 years, Marver grew his business to 60 temporary retail outlets and changed its name to Spirit Halloween. His company spent the rest of the year preparing for the season, handling jobs like sourcing costumes and identifying potential real estate.
In 1999, Spencer Gifts bought the company; Marver stayed on as a consultant, then opened a hotel. Today, Spirit Halloween operates about 1,500 seasonal stores across the U.S. and Canada.
“I didn’t invent temporary sales,” Marver told the Seattle Times in October 2022, “but I feel like I invented temporary Halloween.”
Haunted houses

Walter Knott became famous as the founder of amusement park Knott’s Berry Farm, which has been in operation for about 80 years. But he and his marketing team also invented the large-scale, commercial haunted house.

People had been putting up private, informal haunted houses for years. Charitable organizations also set up the houses to raise funds, says Benjamin Gagne, president of the Haunted Attraction Association and owner of the Thirteenth Hour haunted attraction in Indianapolis.

But Knott’s Scary Farm Halloween event in 1973 was a first, a large-scale commercial setup designed to boost ticket sales during an otherwise slow season, says M. Stang, Ainsworth Visiting Scholar of American Culture at Randolph College in Lynchburg, Va.

Full-page advertisements flooded Orange County and Los Angeles County newspapers, promising entry to the “spookiest, ghouliest place in Southern California” for just $4. The print ads promised “bizarre, spooky antics,” a “fun-tingling plunge through Satan’s sawmill,” and “LIVE MONSTERS,” Stang wrote in a paper about the attraction.

The park also distinguished itself by having people in costumes provide the scares, says Gagne. Previously, amusement parks, including Disney, had what Gagne calls “dark carny rides,” where patrons rode around in carts, and mirrors and lighting created the mood.
The Scary Farm turned into an annual tradition. Knott’s is still running the Halloween attraction—which is open for 26 nights this season.

cnbc.com/2026/10/30/gen-z-diplo-run-club.headline: Gen Z is ditching bars for run clubs — and finding more than friends along the way
cnbc.com/2026/10/30/gen-z-diplo-run-club.author: Alex Harring, Brandon Gomez

paragraphs.text: QUEENS, NEW YORK — Diplo, the globally famous disc jockey, has become accustomed to performing in front of audiences wearing glitzy outfits and clutching alcoholic beverages in the dark.
Some of his recent shows have looked very different. Swap the cocktails for electrolytes, the swanky clothes for athleisure and the nightclubs for sunny public parks.

The Grammy Award-winner's team hosts five-kilometer races across the globe branded as "Diplo's Run Club." After runners cross the finish line, they enter a post-race festival that includes cold plunges, peptide product samples and a Diplo-led dance party. About 12,000 participants paid entry fees starting at around $70 — and up to about $250 for a VIP experience — for last week's race in the New York City borough of Queens.

Younger American adults are spending less at bars and staying home more than their older counterparts. That's left them with fewer close friends and, during the pandemic, led to what's being called a "loneliness epidemic" that has persisted in the years since. But one type of experience appears to be getting them out of the house and socializing: sporting leagues and organized races.
"There's a big generational shift right now, with young people realizing that they want to spend their time working on themselves and their bodies," Diplo told CNBC ahead of the New York City event.

About seven out of every 10 adults under 30 say they anticipate participating in a recreational sports league over the next six months, according to a survey from polling firm CivicScience earlier this year. Across all age groups, 37% of respondents planned on joining a league, up five percentage points from 2025.

Volo Sports, an operator of recreational leagues, is on track to have 950,000 total player registrations for sports like volleyball, kickball and soccer this year. That would be an increase of around 34% from the 710,000 registrations last year and almost 500% from the 160,000 seen in 2019.

Volo has attracted private-equity investors and gone on a buying spree to snap up smaller competitors in recent years. But Giovanni Marcantoni, Volo's founder and CEO, told CNBC that about three-fourths of its growth has come from organic expansion, rather than through acquisitions, as more Americans look for ways to build community.
"I think 'Volo,' I think 'friends,'" said Marcantoni, who met his wife through a recreational bocce league. "Both those things put a smile on your face, and that's what our goal is as a brand."
Demand from young consumers

The communal fitness fervor among young adults extends to categories like cardiovascular exercise that have historically been viewed as individual affairs, but younger runners have found a way to make it more social by joining clubs and signing up for organized races. On social media, some users joke that partaking in distance running or other endurance-based competitions is now a "quarter-life crisis."

The share of finishers of the New York City Marathon in their 20s neared 24% in 2025, up from about 15% in 2019. New York Road Runners, the nonprofit behind the marathon, told CNBC that 27% of registered runners for the 2026 race, which takes place this weekend, are twenty-somethings. Participation by runners in their 20s in the Chicago Marathon and the Boston Marathon has also been on the rise in recent years, according to the organizers of those races.

And Ironman said a quarter of total participants in its half and full-distance triathlons are under 30 years old, an increase from 13% a decade ago. This age group is Ironman's fastest-growing market in North America.

Gen Z was 39% more likely than Gen X to say they used fitness to meet people who share their interests, according to a 2025 survey from fitness tracking platform Strava. A year prior, a Strava survey found that nearly one out of every five Gen Z respondents said they went on a date with someone they met through exercise.

Hyrox, which runs fitness competitions that mix running with strength work, is leaning into its role as a potential matchmaker. It has teamed up with a dating app called Surf Dating to connect users of the platform for blind dates in its doubles competition. Participants meet for the first time just before they undergo a series of one-kilometer runs interspersed with workout stations.
Surf also hands out special wristbands to singles at Hyrox events to help them advertise their relationship status, and hosts post-race parties for them to mingle.
"Matching with someone based off a shared interest or passion is a better way to meet your person than hot-or-not swiping," said Rob Long, Surf's co-founder and CEO.

Demand from young consumers has helped power postpandemic expansions for some traditional gyms like Life Time and workout studios such as Solidcore. But not all businesses are feeling the same tailwinds. SoulCycle has shuttered studios in recent years, and Xponential Fitness divested from underperforming brands such as CycleBar, Rumble and Row House over the last few years.
'Barstools to barbells'

Spending by Gen Z and millennials on fitness-related categories rose at a sharper rate year over year in early 2026 than bars, according to a report from Bank of America released earlier this year. Gen X and older generations did the opposite, with bar spending climbing at a faster clip in the period tracked by the bank.

Said another way: Younger cohorts are shifting "from barstools to barbells," according to Joe Wadford, an economist at Bank of America. It's part of a longer-term trend of Americans drinking less and less, sending the share of people who say they consume alcohol to record lows.

Still, organizers of these athletic events aren't writing off booze entirely. Volo partners with bars to offer deals for players looking to fraternize before or after their matches. Diplo's Run Club had several bars in the post-race festival selling cocktails and beer.

"I definitely don't think there's a death to drinking," said Autumn Rossi, a 30-year-old sales analyst who came to Diplo's race from New Jersey. "I think people are just doing it in a different way, which is important."

Brody Short identifies as one of those young people shifting her time and spending toward community-based fitness. After struggling to convince people in her social circle to forgo late nights at bars for early weekend mornings spent running and at hot yoga classes, the 26-year-old founded a run club called Energy in Liberty Lake, Washington.

Beyond meeting each week for runs, Short's club organizes fundraisers for local nonprofits and cheering squads when members are partaking in organized races. Short is a bridesmaid and maid of honor in upcoming weddings of friends she met through the club.

"It's deeper than the running," Short said. "I didn't start it just so every Tuesday I could run three miles with somebody I didn't know. I did it because I wanted to meet friends. I wanted to find real people that I could integrate into my life."

When talking with older generations, Short said she typically fields questions about whether she's dating someone or hopes to have children soon. After she responds no, Short said follow-up questions focus on how she's filling her time instead.
"We're not raising kids," Short said. "What are we doing? Well, I guess we're running marathons and doing Hyrox."
And they're dancing — at least at the run clubs that Diplo is hosting.
The DJ, born Wes Pentz, says the run clubs he hosts are a blast, but he also has a more selfish motivation: As the 47-year-old ages, he can opt to work fewer late nights.
"I don't want to spend the rest of my career playing into the night until 4 in the morning," Diplo said. "I want to build this brand where I can have these parties in the daytime."

cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-us-tru.headline: Iran War Updates: Qatar pushes for U.S.-Iran deal under shadow of Trump's threats to resume attacks
cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-us-tru.author: Frank Andrews, Khaled Wassef

paragraphs.text: What to know about the Iran war today:

• Qatari mediators returned to Tehran Friday to push for a deal to end the war between Iran and the U.S., multiple news agencies reported, as President Trump acknowledges high-level contact with the regime but keeps his threat to resume major strikes on the table.

• A British navy monitor reported a tanker being struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, after Iran said four ships attempting to transit the waterway via shipping lanes promoted by the U.S. but deemed illegal by Tehran had struck sea mines.

• Iran has yet to respond to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance sent by Vice President JD Vance to senior regime figure Mohsen Rezaei, according to Iranian media. President Trump has denied that Vance's outreach is aimed at rekindling wider peace talks, telling reporters this week that it is only about getting medical aid into Iran.
Iran says 2 tankers on "unauthorized route" in Strait of Hormuz had "incidents and were brought to a halt"

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.

The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
