Qatari officials return to Iran to push for peace deal with U.S.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency, along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.

The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.

An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas, and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

U.S. military death toll since start of Iran war rises to 23, Pentagon says

The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.

Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.

Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.

The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations, which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.

Saudi coalition says Houthi drone intercepted in Mecca region
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reported.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.

Tanker struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says, as Iran claims four ships hit sea mines

A tanker was struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center reported, after Iran's navy claimed four ships had struck sea mines in the area.
UKMTO said the ship hit by a projectile was exiting the strait along the southern route, which the U.S. has encouraged international shipping companies to use, when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," UKMTO said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its military claimed in two separate announcements earlier Thursday that four tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires.

It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been struck by a projectile was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report from the maritime monitor suggested it could have been a separate incident.

Iran has not yet responded to letter from Vance, Iranian media says

Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.

Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/beijin.headline: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/beijin.author: Amy Hawkins

paragraphs.text: Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150889/up-first-.headline: Alaska's Senate race faces claims of spoiler candidate. And, Hegseth ousts Army general
npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150889/up-first-.author: Brittney Melton

paragraphs.text: Today's top stories

It is the final stretch before Election Day on Tuesday and candidates are making final campaign stops and delivering closing arguments. President Trump has been campaigning for at-risk Republicans, but he has abruptly switched to virtual rallies.

• 🎧 Trump's tour to boost voter turnout has focused largely on competitive Republican-leaning states, NPR's Saige Miller tells Up First. He's hosting 19 telerallies alongside in-person events. The shift in strategy, plus polling data, suggests that Republicans may face challenges, at least in the House, Miller says. Trump knows he's a key motivator for his party, but his strategy could also backfire by energizing Democrats.

• 🎧 Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation following a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race. The article revealed that Democratic campaign operatives were attempting to recruit a candidate, whom Republicans claim could confuse voters and siphon support from GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan. The candidate also shares the name Dan Sullivan. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, aims to flip the seat. Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin spoke with election law experts, who found no applicable laws but noted that the conduct described crosses moral and ethical lines.

• ➡️ The Department of Justice subpoenaed election workers in Los Angeles amid rising tensions with California officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on voter rolls.

• ➡️ At the start of this election cycle, Democrats appeared unlikely to gain Senate seats because many races were in red states. But the ongoing war in Iran has changed the landscape. Here are the key Senate races to watch.
• ➡️ NPR member stations are compiling essential info for voters, from guides to local races. Discover resources in your community here.

• ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who oversaw planning at the Pentagon. Sylvia was also part of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. His removal comes as the U.S. and Israel prepare for a new potential round of attacks against Iran. Although Sylvia held a senior position in strategy, planning and policy, he was not directly involved in day-to-day operations regarding the Iran conflict.

• 🎧 The Pentagon is investigating a leak but has not provided details, NPR's Greg Myre says. Hegseth has dismissed several generals and admirals, often without explanation. These firings have disrupted senior military operations, Myre says. The U.S. currently has two aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea, with a third, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, en route. According to Myre, it is unusual for the U.S. to have multiple carriers in one region. The last time it stationed three in the Middle East was during the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have faced higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, after the Trump administration shut down a key part of the VA's home loan program. Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.
Behind the story

I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs.

But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story.

I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street expects Democrats to win at least one of the houses of Congress in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, setting the stage for a potentially volatile ride in the stock and bond markets with artificial intelligence oversight, defense spending and crypto legislation on the table.
Most Read from Bloomberg

A UBS basket of stocks tied to Republicans has plunged since hitting a peak in August, badly lagging the S&P 500 Index. One major area where this could show up is in the AI trade that has been driving the stock market for the past few years, as Democrats are expected to push for stricter regulation and oversight of the technology. Meanwhile, local governments are under pressure to block data centers from being built in their communities.
If the "big political takeaway" from the election is that "data centers are bad, that would be impactful for growth," said Robert Waldner, chief investment officer at Invesco Advisers Inc.

At the same time, other industries could be in the crosshairs. If the Democrats push to rein in defense spending, military contractors would likely feel the pinch. Big banks that have been raking in profits on a flood of deals could face scrutiny. And firms tied to cryptocurrencies are likely to catch some Congressional heat simply based on the industry's close ties to the Trump family.

All of which has some Wall Street pros positioning for selling pressure in stocks and demand for safer government bonds. In addition, many traders appear to be so locked into their positions and their expectations for a closely divided Congress that they're vulnerable to volatile swings.

"Investors are heading into the election long the dollar and short duration, with little protection against volatility – particularly in equity markets," Corpay strategist Karl Schamotta said. "The consensus expects a narrow Democratic victory to produce gridlock in Congress, leaving the president to pursue his objectives through executive action, but there are significant tail risks."
Here are the markets and equity sectors worth watching with just days to go before the vote.

History suggests Congressional gridlock is good for bonds by preventing ambitious policies that increase deficits and raise yields on longer-dated Treasuries. This time, however, bond watchers say any fiscal relief will be limited and unlikely to generate a sustained rally because the deficit, at roughly 6% of the economy, has rarely been this large outside of a recession.

"We have way too much debt that will be reckoned with at some point," said Oliver Chambers, head of fixed income SMA at Clark Capital Management. "But if for the next two years, gridlock means we don't add to it at the same rate we've been adding to it, I think that's a good thing."

A particularly strong showing by Democrats could lead to lower Treasury yields if investors see it as a sign of Americans' appetite for AI regulation, which would pressure tech stocks and dent expectations for economic growth.
Like Treasuries, the dollar could get a boost from a Democratic victory based on the same anticipated stabilizing effect of a split Congress.

Some investors believe a divided government could lead President Donald Trump to lean on policies he can implement unilaterally through executive power. Any escalation with Iran, which Trump has suggested may come after the election, is expected to continue supporting the dollar by driving up energy prices and pushing the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. New tariffs could also support the US currency by stoking inflation — unless they spark a global "sell America" trade like the one that became popular last year.
Technology and AI Infrastructure

Regardless of what happens in the midterms, Trump will still be president and is likely to veto any legislation that's considered unfavorable to the technology industry. That may limit risk for chipmaker Nvidia Corp. and the major AI spenders like Alphabet Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Microsoft Corp. Still, strategists are bracing for Democratic outperformance to hurt sentiment around the AI trade.

"The midterms will be critical not for the immediate risk of federal policy restricting data centers but to lay the groundwork for potential legislation toward that end in 2029," said Ariana Salvatore, head of US public policy research at Morgan Stanley.

Data center real estate investment trusts and neocloud companies are exposed to proposals for a tax on computing power, according to Morgan Stanley analysts. On the other hand, off-the-grid power providers like Bloom Energy Corp., Cummins Inc. and GE Vernova Inc. may get a boost from more restrictive policies, the analysts wrote.

Hospitals may benefit if Democrats manage to walk back Medicaid cuts included in last year's tax bill, said Tobin Marcus, head of US policy and politics at Wolfe Research. Democrats looking for concessions in a possible debt ceiling negotiation may seek wins in healthcare, he said.

Hospital names like Acadia Healthcare Co., HCA Healthcare Inc. and Tenet Healthcare Corp. have near-term upside linked to the election, according to Jefferies analysts. Insurers Centene Corp. and Oscar Health Inc. also could catch bids on hopes that Democrats will negotiate to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of last year, though the firm considers that outcome unlikely.

Shares of defense contractors have underperformed this year amid worries that a potential Democratic sweep would lead to tighter oversight and funding delays. Drone stocks such as AeroVironment Inc. and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions Inc. have had some of the biggest declines. If the Democrats take control of one or both chambers, funding that's critical for the Pentagon's ambitious drone production plans may be in jeopardy.

If Republicans hold their ground, however, military spending could rise, according to JPMorgan, which points to L3Harris Technologies Inc., Lockheed Martin Corp. and Northrop Grumman Corp. as possible beneficiaries.
Financials and Crypto

Republicans tend to favor lighter oversight of the financial sector, so a surprise sweep by the party would favor lenders such as Bank of America Corp., Citigroup Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co., according to JPMorgan.

However, the election is unlikely to alter issues like bank stress testing, since the heads of the Fed, Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency are likely to remain in place for several years, Barclays analyst Jason Goldberg said.

In cryptocurrencies, the odds for any legislation supporting the industry may decline if Democrats take control. Democrats, along with a few Republicans, blocked the Clarity Act in September, sending stocks such as Coinbase Global Inc. and Circle Internet Group Inc. tumbling.
Potential Investigation Targets

Wall Street is bracing for Democrats to launch a range of investigations. Hearings focused on AI could create market risk, according to Evercore ISI, and companies like Nvidia and Amazon.com Inc. have already been hit with investigative inquiries from Democrats. Evercore also expects probes into industries tied to affordability issues, such as energy, healthcare, food production and agriculture.

Companies that have received equity investments from the US government, like Intel Corp., International Business Machines Corp. and rare earth producer MP Materials Corp. could also face inquiries, creating risk to their shares.

The Democrats winning one or both houses of Congress could have implications for major Republican donor Elon Musk's companies — Tesla Inc. and SpaceX — as investors are anticipating a possible merger of the two. Though Congress can't single-handedly kill a deal, empowered Democrats would be able to slow it down, according to First New York's Vikram Rai.
"Both of these stocks have major headline risk if we get a blue sweep," he said.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.headline: UK Debt Chief Sees Volatility Driving Demand for Short Gilts
finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.author: Georgia Hall and James Hirai

paragraphs.text: Georgia Hall and James Hirai
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 3:56 AM PDT 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The UK Debt Management Office is pulling back further from long-dated gilts to meet investor demand for shorter tenors that are less exposed to swings in the bond market, Chief Executive Jessica Pulay said.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The DMO raised this fiscal year's gilt sale plan by a few billion pounds on Wednesday, while crucially shifting issuance further away from longer-dated debt, revising it down by around a third to £15.5 billion ($20.8 billion) from April's figure.
Long gilts will now make up around 6% of this year's issuance, a large drop from the 30% seen five years ago.

"There is a strong demand for short-dated gilts," Pulay said in an interview. "I think that just reflects the ongoing shift in investor demand," she added, noting that this remained stronger at the shorter end relative to longer maturities. "Not least given the persistent volatility in global bond markets, which particularly affects the longer maturities."
Based on the DMO's assessment, shorter maturities are more cost-effective relative to longer maturities to fund government spending, she said.

The UK has been cutting long-dated debt issuance, helping reduce the weighted-average maturity to around 11 years from 17 about five years ago. That shift took on greater significance as the US-Iran war sent oil prices spiraling, stoked inflation fears and pushed the UK's 30-year yield to 6% — making it the first Group of Seven economy to pay a rate that high since the 2012 euro area debt crisis.

However, the gilt market has since cooled from those peaks and posted modest gains this week after the Burnham government's first budget and accompanying DMO remit broadly met expectations and reinforced the anticipated shift toward shorter-dated issuance.

The DMO cancelled three long conventional auctions for the rest of the fiscal year and set out details of a Treasury bill program due to start in January, responding to growing demand for shorter-dated maturities. There will also be a repo facility to support the new program.

"Overall, market participants are keen to see greater liquidity in Treasury bills," she said. Repo markets "have worked very efficiently over a number of years in the gilt market. So we felt it was important to try to replicate that for Treasury bills."

paragraphs.text: Chloé Meley
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 3:30 AM PDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- At first glance, the third-quarter earnings season is going great.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Overall earnings growth for the S&P 500 is tracking above pre-season estimates and 82% of companies have surpassed expectations, with over half of the benchmark's market capitalization having reported.
Energy and technology drove most of those gains, while other industries are flagging under the weight of weakening consumer confidence, rising oil prices and stubborn inflation.
Excluding energy and artificial intelligence-related companies, third-quarter earnings growth across the index halves to 14%, Bloomberg Intelligence data shows.

Though tech and oil giants are driving solid earnings growth this quarter, "the setup is becoming less forgiving as higher fuel costs pressure margins, consumers absorb persistent inflation and estimate-revision momentum slows," BI analysts Wendy Soong and Christopher Cain wrote in a note earlier this month.
That squeeze is already visible with expensive crude weighing on airlines and materials producers, while retailers face cash-strapped shoppers.
Nike Inc. set a grim tone for the consumer discretionary sector, with the stock plunging to a 13-year low on "ugly" guidance that forced the company to embark on a major overhaul.
Hoka-parent Deckers Outdoor Corp. shares also sank as weak demand hurt sales, while MGM Resorts International missed estimates as revelers spent less on the Strip.

In the materials industry, firms like retail packaging company International Paper Co and coatings manufacturer Sherwin-Williams Co are grappling with rising costs and tepid volumes across industrial, construction and consumer end markets.

"The softer-for-longer demand backdrop shows no clear sign of reversing after taking hold last year," BI analysts Sean Gilmartin and Jason F Miner wrote about Sherwin-Williams, noting inflation risks are unlikely to fade until the second half of 2027.
Against that gloomy backdrop, energy, tech and defensive stocks continue to "shine" in both the US and Europe, according to Barclays analyst Magesh Kumar.
But even for those outperformers, momentum is showing signs of a slowdown with "beats stabilizing, margins easing and EPS revisions peaking," Kumar said.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Alice Gledhill and Georgia Hall

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The rehabilitation of the UK bond market took another step forward as Prime Minister Andy Burnham's debut budget reassured investors this week, sending yields to a five-week low.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Its notable restraint hit the right notes, even as investors agreed that much-needed structural reforms had been pushed down the road for now. The 10-year gilt yield fell as low as 5.25% on Thursday and is set for the biggest monthly drop since May.

"The UK is starting to look like the adult in the room when it comes to fiscal discipline," said Chris Jeffery, chief investment strategist for Legal & General, Britain's largest asset manager. "There may be more tightening needed in future but this budget achieved its aim of maintaining credibility."

The positive market reception is a boon for the UK, which still suffers from an image problem with debt investors. That damage was mainly done by the 2016 vote to leave the European Union and former Prime Minister Liz Truss' 2022 mini-budget, which sparked a market rout the Bank of England had to step in to contain.

To be sure, the UK's public finances remain highly precarious. But the country has won plaudits from the International Monetary Fund for its efforts to correct course, an approach that sets it apart from the likes of France and the US.

The data accompanying Wednesday's budget was cautiously reassuring. Borrowing plans for the rest of the fiscal year ticked up only slightly to £250.6 billion ($334 billion), in line with expectations. And the budget deficit is projected to fall to 3.4% in 2027-2028, albeit declining at a slower pace than anticipated.

Since replacing Keir Starmer in July, Burnham has repeatedly stressed his commitment to fiscal responsibility. That contrasts with comments last year before he swept to power, when he said Britain shouldn't be "in hock" to bond markets. At the time, investors worried it might herald a pivot toward more borrowing and spending.

But capped by this week's do-no-harm budget, his message of financial rectitude has helped gilts weather the broader turbulence in global bond markets triggered by the US-Iran war. French debt in particular has been pummeled as the government tries to push its budget through a divided parliament, with elections looming next year and mounting signs of social unrest.

According to Bloomberg Economics, the UK's "credibility premium" on the 10-year benchmark bond — the extra yield the government is estimated to pay to compensate for past policy missteps, shocks and heavy spending — currently stands at around 20 basis points.
That's just a fifth of the level reached in the weeks after Truss's mini budget four years ago.

Robert Timper, chief global fixed income strategist at BCA Research, predicts the extra yield will fall with time. That's so long as the government sticks to its 2029/30 target of balancing government revenue against government spending before interest payments on the national debt, he said.
Still, there are plenty of long-term questions about Burnham's big plans for overhauling the UK economy, with more details due in the months ahead.

Core goals include eventually adjusting the state pension and using regional devolution, reindustrialization and public control of essential services to revive economic growth after years of stagnation.
With debt at 94% of gross domestic product, the most since the 1960s and costing over £110 billion to service a year, a route to reducing the burden is crucial.

"The budget will help for now, and in the short-term the UK looks like a relative safe-haven," said John Stopford, a portfolio manager at Ninety One. "Next year's spending review will ultimately be key."
--With assistance from George Nixon.

There’s a generational shift happening in the funeral industry: Over the past four decades, female enrollment in mortuary programs has increased from 5 percent to roughly 75 percent of recent graduating classes. But why? For the Los Angeles Review of Books, Andie Eisen examines this trend, speaking with three women working in the deathcare field. Some were drawn in by a fascination with death or a formative funeral experience; others by a calling to a higher purpose and a desire to bring intimacy and care to a field long seen as impersonal, commercial, and male-dominated.

When you speak with a mortician, their tone gives away the questions they’ve answered hundreds of times before. Don’t you get scared? No. Morticians are more afraid of doing a bad job. Have you seen a ghost? Sadly, no. Once, a cosmetologist thought a body was shaking, but it was just an earthquake. Do you get grossed out? Not really, but they’re only human, and the medical field can challenge the senses. The questions themselves hint at a broader problem: outside of urban legends and crime procedurals, the average American knows very little about the death industry.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/gulf-s.headline: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/gulf-s.author: Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).

Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.

The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.

Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an over-dependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.

The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown that longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression …
“If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, “from security provider to strategic liability”.

Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.

The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a live debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.

He said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but said: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.

“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘What can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
He suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

cnbc.com/2026/10/30/gamble-on-democracy-.headline: Gamble on democracy: Inside suspicious election-contracts trading on prediction markets
cnbc.com/2026/10/30/gamble-on-democracy-.author: Melissa Lee, Paige Tortorelli

paragraphs.text: Spencer Pratt appeared to be a shoo-in to win the June primary in the Los Angeles mayor's race, based on millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets aiming to call the race.

Pratt was an unlikely candidate for mayor. The former reality TV star had never held elective office, but after the Palisades fire destroyed his home, he turned his criticism of the city's response into a campaign rallying cry.

Using prediction markets including Kalshi, Polymarket U.S. and Polymarket International, speculators flocked to the race, which drew more than $47 million in trades, making it the most heavily traded mayoral contest of 2026. On the eve of the June primary, one market gave Pratt a 78% chance of advancing to the November runoff.
The prediction markets were wildly off base, and Pratt finished third.

Pratt supporters, though, used the failed speculation to cast doubt on the integrity of the election. That drew a response from the city: "Prediction markets can add to that confusion when people treat their projections as more authoritative than the actual votes being counted," Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder for the Los Angeles County Clerk's Office, said in a statement to CNBC.

Prediction markets' failure to call the election correctly also raised the possibility that markets can be manipulated to make candidates appear to have more support than they really do. Exclusive reporting from CNBC shows that this risk is real.

The dissonance between voter polling, speculation-fueled prediction markets and the actual outcome has grown in importance as election wagers become a prominent feature of elections. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Polymarket and Kalshi are the two largest prediction market platforms. They let people speculate on almost anything — from which team will be the 2027 NBA champions to whether the U.S. will confirm that aliens exist.

Already, on these platforms the amount wagered on contracts related to the 2026 congressional elections has more than tripled bets on the 2024 races, according to ACDC. And people are increasingly using the platforms as a source of information. For midterm election markets specifically, Kalshi reports that viewers outnumber actual traders by a 5-to-1 ratio.
Spotting suspicious trades

Despite the Pratt race being a heavily traded, liquid contract, Kalshi detected and reported on price spikes that occurred during trading on that race in a case study it published in July. A price spike is a temporary but large price jump that can make an outcome look more likely to happen, according to experts. Price spikes can happen for a variety of reasons, such as new information changing trader expectations or a trader buying a large number of contracts, which can drive up contract prices as cheaper ones get bought up.

On May 20, the company said, a trader on Kalshi spent $1.25 million on "Yes" contracts on Pratt becoming LA's next mayor. One of the trades caused the price of contracts on Pratt's victory to jump from 29 cents to 45 cents, suggesting that traders saw his chances of winning rise from 29% to 45%. However, according to Kalshi's case study, within nine seconds, the price reverted to earlier levels and the markets self-corrected.

"You can absolutely guarantee there are rational traders in that market willing to take those trades and bring that price right back down to where it belongs," said Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement at Kalshi, who is tasked with tracking unusual activity on the platform. "And by the end of the day, his price was lower than when it began."

But during the LA mayoral race, there were numerous price spikes across Kalshi and Polymarket International that pushed the odds in Pratt's favor, according to an analysis for CNBC by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, or ACDC, a nonprofit based in Washington, D.C. The group didn't consider trades from Polymarket U.S. in its analysis.

Data that ACDC collected confirms Kalshi's findings. In the case study, Kalshi provided insight through about 30 minutes after the large order was placed. However, the group found that if you expand the time frame to three hours after the spike, the price lands three cents higher and that level is sustained for about two hours. In the long term, the price does correct. But per ACDC's research, the longer a price increase lasts, the greater the risk of that information being interpreted as market sentiment.
And as ACDC's research suggests, election contracts are vulnerable to unusual price spikes — similar to those in the Pratt race.

The group found that of 167 congressional markets across Polymarket International and Kalshi worth more than $100,000, 38 markets — or about 23% — experienced price spikes moving the contract price 30 cents or more.

One example of such a spike was the Kalshi contract on whether Juliana Stratton would be the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Illinois. On March 3, according to ACDC, two purchases stood out as large — the median order was $12 before election day. One buyer spent $5,000 on contracts that favored the longtime public official's candidacy, taking the price from 47 cents to 79 cents. The price normalized after three seconds, going back down to 47 cents, but about one minute later, it shot back up to 99 cents after $3,000 of additional contracts were purchased. The price eventually sank back to 52 cents — 5 cents more than where it started — meaning a person or persons spent $8,000, and, in the process, drove up the price that made a Stratton victory look more likely.

Two weeks later, Stratton won the Democratic primary. Stratton declined to comment on this story, but a spokesperson from her office pointed CNBC to a poll from Public Policy Polling released on the same day as the price spike. It showed Stratton leading.
In a statement to CNBC, a spokesperson for Kalshi wrote, "As is common on Kalshi, the market corrected quickly to a price near fair value."

ACDC said it's impossible to know the motive behind these wagers. While profit could be a factor, it is an imperfect one. On prediction markets, participants can buy and sell contracts valued between $0 and $1, with the price reflecting how likely traders think an event is to happen. The more expensive a contract, the smaller the potential payout. Winning contracts settle at $1, while losing contracts become worthless. So traders buying in at 99 cents expect to earn only 1 cent if their predicted outcome happens, and transaction fees charged by prediction markets can also eat into that profit.

"If the theory is that prediction markets are accurate because of a price motive, [a lack thereof] begs the question: What type of goal does someone making a trade like that really have for themselves?" said Michelle Kendler-Kretsch, a researcher at ACDC.
Influencing election outcomes may be an answer.

Voters were between 10 and 20 percentage points more likely to believe a candidate would win if prediction markets favored the candidate, no matter what the polls reported, according to a new study funded by the Brennan Center for Justice, a New York City-based left-leaning advocacy organization. That survey, which took place in September, included the perspective of 1,994 registered voters.

Data ACDC shared with CNBC also shows shifting the odds is even easier and cheaper in markets where not many wagers are placed. Across 18,000 active congressional markets on Polymarket International, Polymarket U.S., and Kalshi, 88% could have their prices moved by 10 cents with a single wager under $1,000.
Policing market manipulation

Still, Kalshi market outcomes are often correct. "Across U.S. elections since 2024, when Kalshi's markets favored a candidate to win, that candidate went on to win roughly 9 times out of 10," the company wrote in a website post. Further, The Washington Post examined 268 candidates in this year's primaries who received a 70% to 80% chance of winning on Kalshi or Polymarket on any day in the two months before the primary election. Three-quarters of them won.

Kalshi says it's working to assuage election distortion concerns. It added new transparency-centered features to its midterm election markets earlier this month to help users understand how much confidence to place in a contract's odds, including labels for markets with little trading activity and live feeds showing individual trades. Polymarket also rolled out its own election-specific surveillance system "to detect potential attempts to manipulate election markets, distort probabilities, or manufacture apparent market consensus."

Kalshi told CNBC it uses algorithms to generate alerts based on parameters for unusual trading activity, including fishy trading times and volumes as well as price jumps. It's unclear if Kalshi's internal protocols alerted over the Pratt trades; the company didn't respond to CNBC's request for clarity.

Both Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. are governed by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, an independent federal agency whose rules are designed to prevent market manipulation and insider trading. Trading prices and activity are publicly visible, and at least in the case of Kalshi, its order book is public on derivatives exchanges and people can escalate and flag unusual trades to the exchanges. In addition, Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. collect "know your customer" information including full legal names and Social Security numbers.
The outside world, however, has no insight into who is behind each trade.

"I formerly worked at the FBI and in centralized finance off the blockchain," said Shana Bautista, the head of global intelligence and investigations at Polymarket. "If you want to get information on a case or a certain transaction, you have to serve either a subpoena or a search warrant to be able to get that information."

In April, Polymarket International announced a partnership with blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, which helps the blockchain-based platform track suspicious trading on its international platform.

Adam Hart, a senior product manager at Chainalysis, showed CNBC the data the firm collects on each Polymarket trader. Polymarket can, for example, see the number of trades being made, the total value of buys and sells, how much traders are wagering relative to their overall activity, and their total profits and losses.

Hart walked CNBC through an investigation his team conducted in collaboration with Polymarket: the case of Gannon Ken Van Dyke, a U.S. soldier charged with using classified information to bet on the removal of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and the entry of U.S. forces into Venezuela. Van Dyke pleaded not guilty.

Hart said the wallet was flagged because it made unusually profitable bets and never lost. Van Dyke was ultimately identified in part because he did little to conceal his identity: His wallets were funded through cryptocurrency exchanges that require users to verify their identities. Hart said Van Dyke also transferred his approximately $400,000 in winnings to a mainstream U.S. exchange.

Of course, trades that may look suspicious could be the wagers of a sharp speculator or an enthusiastic backer. That was the case of "Theo," the anonymous French whale who made about $85 million on contracts favoring Donald Trump in the 2024 elections. Bubblemaps, an on-chain analytics firm, was one of the platforms to trace Theo's approximately $60 million in wagers across at least 10 Polymarket accounts. Bubblemaps traced the activity to two crypto exchanges' deposit wallets owned by Theo, who said he based his wagers on his own neighbor polling and calls to battleground states.
Engineering election integrity

That internal sleuthing does little to reassure Jared DeMarinis. As the administrator of the Maryland State Board of Elections, DeMarinis is convinced that the only way to protect election integrity is an outright ban on wagering on election outcomes.

In July, he asked the office of the state prosecutor to investigate whether prediction markets violate state laws prohibiting wagering on election outcomes. A few months later, in September, he prohibited certain individuals and election staff, including election judges and members of the state board of elections, from trading in election markets.

"We employ 26,000 election judges that are poll workers," DeMarinis said. "They have access to information right before it's getting tallied officially and counted. They'll know certain things. This is all problematic because it goes to the legitimacy, integrity of the electoral process."

More than half of all states have laws making election betting illegal in all or some circumstances, according to the Pew Research Center. Prediction markets argue that the CFTC, not states, has jurisdiction over their contracts because they classify them as swaps, which fall under federal law. The CFTC has backed that argument.

But these laws may not apply to federally regulated prediction markets. New Jersey, backed by dozens of states, has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the CFTC rules go far enough to counter election concerns and whether the states themselves have additional standing.
In the meantime, the prediction markets are only ramping up their election offerings.

"We don't have a lot of information on whether prediction markets are accurate," Kendler-Kretsch said. "When [a trade] doesn't go the way of an election, instead of sowing doubt in prediction markets and their accuracy, it's sowing doubt in the election itself."
— Ananya Chetia contributed to this report.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62ydn7dj9eo.headline: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62ydn7dj9eo.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in a statement released by her legal team on social media on Friday.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-30/th.headline: ‘They come in droves’: How robotaxis are hogging EV chargers in one corner of Southern California
latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-30/th.author: Ella Chakarian

paragraphs.text: San Diego resident José Manjarrés has a robot problem in his neighborhood.

When he goes to charge his Ford Mustang Mach-E, he increasingly finds the charging stations are already occupied by robotaxis. Last month, he had to wait an hour for his turn as driverless Waymos filled up.
“It becomes really annoying when you see three Waymos in a charging station with four spots,” said Manjarrés. “It creates some kind of antagonistic posture against the product.”

Other San Diego residents have complained about sharing the city’s limited charging infrastructure with a new Waymo fleet that just launched in the region. Local politicians are calling for more regulation of the automated vehicles.
Welcome to the quiet beginning of the robot wars.

As AI-enabled bots enter everyday life, they are creating a brand new set of etiquette and legal conundrums. Do you need to be polite to chatbots? Do we have to make way on the sidewalk for food delivery bots? If a driverless car breaks the law, who is responsible?
California — home of many of the companies behind the bots as well as the locations where they are being tested — is where these new rules are being worked out.
Waymo officially launched in San Diego in September, but its vehicles started showing up months earlier as they were testing, locals say.
San Diego resident Finn Sadler, 24, said long lines formed in some places as Waymos took up limited charging stations.
“They come in droves,” he said.
He sometimes waits more than half an hour in line for his turn to plug in his Audi E-tron. It is so bad that he says if fuel prices were lower, he’d consider switching back to a gas-powered car.

The San Diego stations drivers are complaining about are privately owned. Electrify America, the Virginia-based charging company founded by Volkswagen Group of America, has 13 stations in San Diego and more than 300 charging stations in California.
The company said it has no official partnership with Waymo.

Waymos have also been spotted at an EVgo charging station in the city. The company has worked with autonomous vehicle partners since 2020 and also operates charging stations for them in Los Angeles and San Francisco. Earlier this year, EVgo had 120 stalls dedicated to AV companies.
An EVgo spokesperson said its San Diego stations are public sites available to all drivers, including robotaxis.

Waymo says it posts people at some public charging stations to help its robotaxis plug in and it tries to keep its vehicles from bunching up. That, however, can be difficult, particularly in areas where public and private fast-charging infrastructure is still being built out.

“As our operations in a city mature, we establish our own charging infrastructure and prioritize using dedicated charging,” said a Waymo spokesperson. “If a vehicle is being driven or supervised by a human specialist, they might also choose to charge on the road while taking their break.”
The frustration at the chargers has unraveled in a city where officials were skeptical of Waymo before its launch.

In January, after Waymo announced its San Diego expansion plans, a Metropolitan Transit System advisory committee chaired by Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera voted to oppose the expansion of driverless vehicles and urged state leaders to let communities decide whether they can operate.

On Sept. 14, the City Council voted unanimously for a resolution urging Gov. Gavin Newsom and other state lawmakers to give cities more control over autonomous vehicle operations. The resolution asks to give cities a say in how driverless cars are deployed and monitored. It also urges the airport authority to keep autonomous vehicles out of San Diego International Airport, and asks that charging hubs be kept away from homes, schools and public safety facilities.
Elo-Rivera said the charging issue is part of his opposition to Waymo’s rollout.
“Waymo or autonomous vehicles generally should not be displacing people,” he said.

His concern is for drivers who have built a routine around their job and family and can’t charge at home, either for logistical reasons or because they can’t yet afford to. Those drivers, he said, are now “competing with robots that can hover.”

A city spokesperson said San Diego is working to expand its public charging network. More than 50 sites will get chargers over the next 18 months, the spokesperson said, and the city has been retrofitting existing public stations and adding chargers at libraries and recreation centers.

“The current effort to expand our public EV charging stations focuses on providing additional resources for San Diego residents and visitors and is independent of any plans by private companies, such as Waymo,” the spokesperson said.
Waymos and other autonomous vehicles would not be barred from using public stations, the spokesperson said, and any that do would pay the same fees as everyone else.

San Diego is not the first place to struggle with sharing space with autonomous machines. In Santa Monica, neighbors complained about noise from Waymo’s own charging lots. Last year, its City Council ordered the company’s charging provider to stop overnight operations.

On social media, people have posted photos and videos of Waymo vehicles utilizing chargers at public stations across the country. One Reddit user posted a photo of three Waymos occupying spots at a charging station in Nashville. Another Facebook user posted an image of Waymos utilizing chargers at an Electrify America Station in St. Louis.
“There are precious few public fast chargers in St. Louis,” the user said.
In L.A. County, Commerce is also dealing with Waymo, which is currently mapping and training its vehicles in the city.

Following resident concern about the increased presence of Waymo self-driving vehicles, the City of Commerce announced in a social media post this week it would conduct additional overnight patrols and monitor and document vehicles parked in residential areas.
“While the State of California regulates Waymo and the City cannot prohibit these vehicles from operating on public streets, we are taking steps to address your concerns,” the Instagram post read.
People are still figuring out how to behave around other types of robots.

Shoppers in L.A. have worried they were being followed by grocery-store bots used to scan shelves. Delivery bots have been tagged with graffiti in Los Angeles, and there was even one botched botnapping attempt.

In Philadelphia this month, police arrested Carolyn Marvin, a 78-year-old former University of Pennsylvania professor, on a disorderly conduct charge after she refused to move out of an Uber Eats delivery robot’s path. She had spent months blocking the robots.
LAX, one of the most important destinations for taxis, isn’t sure it wants to open up to Waymo.

In a February report from Los Angeles World Airports, the governing body’s chief executive said that while they were “engaged in discussions with Waymo,” there “is currently no timeline for permitting” its cars to conduct pickups, drop-offs or any operations on LAX property.
Times staff writer Caroline Petrow-Cohen contributed to this report.

npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150902/blockchai.headline: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150902/blockchai.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.
The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zxj2e5qlxxo.headline: Spain train crash: Transport minister says he won't resign over disaster
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zxj2e5qlxxo.author: Angus Thompson

paragraphs.text: Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.

The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.

Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.

A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.

Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".

Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/north-korean-h.headline: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/north-korean-h.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance. The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.
The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.

In a post on X, Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.

The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”

It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices.

Software is generally built from many components, including open-source projects, which hackers regularly target, compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.
Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.

Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to a request for comment about the hack. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.”

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.

Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million.

The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.

longreads.com/2026/10/30/wellness-bpc-15.headline: Is There Anything BPC-157 Can’t Cure?
longreads.com/2026/10/30/wellness-bpc-15.author: Carolyn Wells

paragraphs.text: Do you know what BPC‑157 is? This cryptically named peptide is, according to its proponents, a miracle cure for all sorts of illnesses and injuries. Tom Bartlett remains firmly in the skeptical camp as he investigates exactly what research backs up the BPC‑157 claims. Almost all the studies prove to have a link to Croatian pharmacologist Predrag Sikirić—who is all too happy to meet Bartlett and exalt BPC‑157. But once you know what this is, the question remains: Would you take it?

Amid the sellers of red-light panels and blue-light glasses at Beyond, I stumbled on a company marketing a drinkable version of BPC‑157. Its giveaway sticker read We Prefer Oral Peptides, with the word peptides in much smaller letters because haha sex. The representative behind the counter referred to BPC‑157 as “the soccer mom’s peptide” and nonchalantly squirted some from what was essentially a hand-soap dispenser into a tiny plastic cup, then held it out to me. I hesitated, and the peptide hung in the air, unclaimed. “Are you afraid of it?” he asked. The not-so-subtle subtext was that I shouldn’t be, that taking BPC‑157 was equivalent to trying the dissolvable herbal-tea strips a few tables down or giving the giant quartz bowl a whirl. For the record: We were in a hotel hallway and I was being encouraged—dared, really—to try a drug that isn’t FDA-approved, is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency for athletes’ use, and allegedly works throughout the body via some mysterious mechanism that is not entirely predictable. I was being offered an unspecified dose, although I wouldn’t know what dose would be appropriate, because there are no agreed-upon dosing guidelines. I declined the peptide. The representative shrugged and drank it himself.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/doordash-said-.headline: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/doordash-said-.author: Ivan Mehta

paragraphs.text: There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.

“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.

Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.

DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched it June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.

The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.
