bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crz9824d5e88o.headline: Police deployed during stand-off over control of Poland's top court
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crz9824d5e88o.author: Adam Easton

paragraphs.text: A political stand-off over Poland's top court, the Constitutional Tribunal, has broken out after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.

Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Right-wing politicians from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw to protest against the move.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Tribunal wrote that the two men were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said his government was acting to restore the rule of law.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The Constitutional Tribunal was the spark that triggered Poland's long-running rule of law dispute after the PiS-led government took office in 2015.
The PiS majority in parliament quickly moved to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Taking office in 2023, Tusk vowed to depoliticise the judiciary - but he has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.

Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Tribunal, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.

"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Tribunal by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/cracks-are-eme.headline: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/cracks-are-eme.author: Rebecca Bellan

paragraphs.text: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.

Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.

Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.

The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, revenue grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.

Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank.

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. The Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: Hedge Funds Boost Natural Gas Short Positions to Most on Record
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Julian Hast

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 30, 2026 at 1:40 PM MST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Hedge funds this week amassed the largest-ever short position on US natural gas on expectations that an unusually warm winter will slash demand for the furnace and power-plant fuel.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Money managers boosted their short-only exposure, or bets on prices falling, across seven benchmark Henry Hub contracts to 625,150, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission data released Friday. That's the largest in data going back to May 2013, breaking the most recent short-only record which was set just a week earlier.

The net-short position on US gas rose to 223,591, the most bearish overall position since February 2020, when the outbreak of Covid-19 crushed demand for fuels and throttled markets across asset classes. The all-time largest net-short position, set in February 2020, was 266,416.

Benchmark US gas futures for delivery in December, which is currently the front-month, plummeted 18% to $2.898 per million British thermal units over the past three weeks as weather forecasts continued to shift warmer. Above-normal temperatures are now expected across the northern US for the first two weeks of November, according to the private forecaster Commodity Weather Group. The north is where most US heating demand is concentrated.

The bearish bets reflect traders' growing conviction that the so-called Super El Niño weather pattern will bring very mild weather. They also increase the risk of a short squeeze. Any sudden, severe cold snap can send gas demand surging while slashing production, lifting prices as traders scramble to rapidly close out short positions to forestall losses.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Apple Overtakes Nvidia to Become World’s Most Valuable Company
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Jeran Wittenstein and Ryan Vlastelica

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. reclaimed the title of world's most valuable company on Friday, taking the mantle from Nvidia Corp. as investors seek the perceived safety of the iPhone maker amid concerns about artificial intelligence spending.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Shares of Apple fell 1.2% on Friday, resulting in a market capitalization of $5.03 trillion, while Nvidia sank 4.2% to close with a valuation of $4.93 trillion. This is the first time Apple has overtaken Nvidia since briefly doing so in late July.

Friday's selloff came as a number of major technology companies disappointed with their results, including Intel Corp. and Amazon.com Inc., which followed similarly disappointing reports from Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc., among others. The reports renewed concerns about the outlook for AI spending, something Apple has largely foregone.

Fears that heavy spending on AI computing infrastructure won't pay off have helped make Apple, which has kept a lid on capital expenditures, by far the best performing of the Magnificent Seven tech giants this year. Its shares are up 27% in 2026, more than twice the gain of second place Nvidia, which is a key beneficiary of AI spending.

The outlays have gotten so large that companies like Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. have seen their free cash flow turn negative, forcing them to increasingly turn to debt markets for funding. Meanwhile, rising interest rates are raising the cost of borrowing.
Apple, by contrast, is projected to see its free cash flow climb 38% to $142 billion in fiscal 2026, which ended on Sept. 30.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index fell 6.7% in October, its worst month since March 2025. CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group, data center owners that offer AI computing services, have dropped more than 30% this month. With Friday's collapse, Intel lost more than 45% in October, its biggest ever one-month drop in data compiled by Bloomberg going back more than 40 years.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/intels-stock-c.headline: Intel’s stock crashes, knocking $12B from government’s stake
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/intels-stock-c.author: Julie Bort

paragraphs.text: Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.

This route reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports. The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the selloff.

Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if its dropped significantly from the sky high prices it commanded over the summer.

The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from the 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow.
The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing PC prices to rise.

“Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call.

The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. One of Intel’s new fabs in Arizona is operational but the next one isn’t expected to be online until 2028.

cnbc.com/2026/10/30/meta-outlook-to-revi.headline: Meta outlook revised to negative by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
cnbc.com/2026/10/30/meta-outlook-to-revi.author: Jonathan Vanian

paragraphs.text: Meta has been assigned a negative outlook by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" surrounding Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating has thus been reduced from AA- stable to AA- negative, the S&P Global Ratings said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.

The social media giant said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares sinking 7% following last week's earnings report despite though the company beating on revenue. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.

The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion to be raised via an at-the-market program.
Meta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/applebees-expo.headline: Applebee’s exposed customers’ personal data after leaving database password in app
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/applebees-expo.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that allowed anyone to access the personal information of its registered customers, after a researcher found a password for an internal database inside Applebee’s mobile app, TechCrunch has learned.
The popular restaurant chain confirmed on Thursday that it had taken action to address the security issue to prevent any unauthorized access to its customer database.
TechCrunch withheld publication of this story until the bug was confirmed to be fixed.

Robert Wiggins, a U.K.-based cybersecurity researcher at What Security, discovered the security lapse earlier this month. Wiggins is no stranger to discovering security issues, including exposed or sensitive information that should not be publicly accessible.

For this latest discovery, Wiggins used AI to help find the credential buried inside thousands of lines of source code in Applebee’s Android app, which has more than a million downloads on Google Play. The credential allowed access to the company’s customer database.

Storing a password or private key in software, known as hardcoding credentials, is one of the most severe types of security vulnerabilities because anyone with the app can extract the key and use it to log in to a remote system as if they were an authorized user.
Wiggins said that the hardcoded credential could have also allowed a malicious attacker to modify customer data in the database.

TechCrunch verified Wiggins’ findings by downloading and decompiling Applebee’s Android app to examine its source code and confirm that it contained the exposed credential. We also created an Applebee’s account with dummy account data, which allowed Wiggins to retrieve our information from the company’s database.

The exposed database contained customer names, email addresses (including whether or not the customer verified their email), dates of birth, phone numbers, and the ZIP codes. The data also included veteran status, the number of times customers had logged in, when their accounts were created, and the IP addresses of their most recent logins, which can be used to reveal the person’s approximate location.

Wiggins was unable to alert Applebee’s or its parent company, Dine Brands, as neither have ways to report security issues. Wiggins asked TechCrunch for help in disclosing the security issue to the company.

A spokesperson for Dine Brands, who did not provide their name, said in an emailed statement on Friday: “We appreciate TechCrunch and the security researcher for bringing this matter to our attention. Our security team promptly launched an investigation and has not currently found any evidence of unauthorized access.”
When asked by TechCrunch, the spokesperson would not say if the company has server logs that it can review to determine whether anyone accessed the database, or if it has any logs at all.
“Our investigation is ongoing, and we will take appropriate steps based on our findings,” the company added.

It’s unclear how many customers were affected by the data exposure. Wiggins said that figuring out the number of customers in the database would have required the AI model to unnecessarily access potentially every customer record.

Applebee’s had at least 8.5 million customers enrolled in its rewards program as of last year, though the company would not provide a number of how many customers had their personal information exposed by this security flaw.

TechCrunch asked the company if it would alert customers or U.S. regulators about the incident, including whether it would file a disclosure with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as publicly traded companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents. We also asked the company how long the exposed credential had been in the Applebee’s app, but we did not get a response.
We’ll update this article if the company responds.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/anthropic-expe.headline: Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, report says
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/anthropic-expe.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.

The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the investment giant and anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude-maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now, Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.

Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, wracking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors.
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vgxznlx7jzo.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vgxznlx7jzo.author: Jaroslav Lukiv

paragraphs.text: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies.
And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions.
"They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said.
Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

cnbc.com/2026/10/30/jim-cramer-week-ahea.headline: Cramer’s week ahead: Expect more volatility as tech earnings, midterms loom
cnbc.com/2026/10/30/jim-cramer-week-ahea.author: Alexa LoMonaco

paragraphs.text: CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over.

Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. The S&P 500 followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%.
"After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the "Mad Money" host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings."

"My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher."
With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.
Monday

Apple reports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said.
Cramer also expects encouraging results from Palantir when it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software.
Tuesday

The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them."

On the earnings front, Advanced Micro Devices reports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector following Intel's disappointing results. Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel.
Drugmakers Pfizer and Amgen also report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks.
Wednesday

CVS Health reports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said.
McDonald's earnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees.
Thursday

Kimberly-Clark reports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger with Kenvue. The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said.
Friday

The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields.
The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-30/bi.headline: AI stock selloffs fuel fears Big Tech’s best quarters are over
latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-30/bi.author: Queenie Wong

paragraphs.text: Many of the top technology stocks, which seemed almost unstoppable for months, got hammered this week as fears grew that massive spending on artificial intelligence won’t pay off anytime soon.

Some investors have expressed concerns that the AI rally has inflated some shares too much. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being spent on data centers and the research to build and test the powerful large language models behind AI, but it remains uncertain whether future profits will justify the investment.
Companies have yet to prove they have enough customers for the technology and, at the same time, have expressed the need to slow down the pace of development to ensure it can be safely managed.

The latest quarterly results confirmed many concerns: While high AI profits are still far off, much more spending is still required. Many investors have taken this moment to sell some of their tech shares as they wait for a clearer outlook on profits and spending.
Meanwhile, many tech companies are realizing that AI is hurting their business as their customers switch to AI options.

“The disruption caused by AI is on full display during tech earnings and the uncertainty around which names and sectors will be the disruptors vs the disrupted,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, in a note Friday.
The Nasdaq 100 index plunged roughly 4%, wiping out more than $1 trillion in value. The S&P 500 dropped more than 2% on Friday afternoon.

The market is “a lot more sensitive than it might normally be,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, adding that investors would rather sell first and ask questions later rather than get stuck nursing further losses.

Strategists from Wells Fargo to Franklin Templeton were among those in recent weeks predicting the S&P 500 corporate earnings expansion would decelerate as higher interest rates, tariff pressures and elevated oil prices weigh on results.

Roughly a third of the way through the reporting season, their forecasts have proved on point: Earnings growth has slipped to roughly 26% — still elevated compared with historical norms but below the 32% growth rate seen in the second quarter, the data show.
Tech companies are spending heavily on data centers and other infrastructure to power AI products that could change how people work and socialize.
AI assistants can help automate tasks, prompting companies to rethink the sizes of their global workforce.

Still, the latest corporate results confirmed pessimists’ concerns that the AI boom is going to continue to weigh on profits, at least during this intense building period, even as it helps decide new tech leaders and losers.

Intel had one of its worst days on the market. The Santa Clara-based chipmaker saw its stock plunge more than 30% Friday to roughly $62 per share after it reported a weaker fourth-quarter outlook and a slowdown in personal computer sales.
Intel’s Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan, who took the helm in March 2025, has faced major hurdles as he has tried to turn around the company.

On Thursday, Intel projected adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share in the fourth quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. That fell below estimates of $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings of 45 cents a share.
The weaker outlook is tied to an explosion that hit an Intel factory in Israel in October that killed two workers. Intel is expected to lose about $600 million in revenue because of that explosion.
The company and its customers are also dealing with rising chip prices, triggered, in part, by the AI spending boom.
“We expect the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize,” Tan said Thursday during a call with analysts.
Amazon, Google’s parent company Alphabet, ServiceNow and Meta all saw their share prices drop after reporting quarterly earnings.
Amazon, which released its quarterly earnings Thursday that missed Wall Street’s expectations, also reported a negative free cash flow of $42 billion as it spends heavily on AI.

Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy told analysts during its earnings call Thursday that the company expects “to spend meaningfully more in 2027 with a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns.”
Santa Clara-based ServiceNow also had a brutal week. On Thursday, its stock plunged 27% after the enterprise software company reported weaker-than-expected third-quarter results.
Microsoft, which announced voluntary buyouts this week, saw its stock jump after announcing financial results that beat Wall Street’s expectations. But by Friday, its stock closed down more than 1%.
The post-earnings plunges are reinforcing fears that the best quarters, particularly for AI-linked companies, are in the rear-view mirror.

“If you’ve got 50% of the market in those two sectors, people want extra; they want more validation that this trade is still intact,” said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services. A slowdown in growth challenges the narrative, he said.
Indeed, the tech and communications sectors are the only two in the red this month, while every other corner of the market has advanced.

Kimberly Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners, said investors are “trimming some of their excessive gains” in tech to pick up cheaper stocks elsewhere, rather than completely selling out of an equities market that is still poised to grow earnings, even if it’s at a slower rate.
To be sure, many analysts remain optimistic about technology’s future.

“This requires patience and it’s easy to sell the tech winners during these times of turmoil. Valuations across the tech franchise are not expensive with growth prospects that are likely stunning into the next few years,” Ives said in the note.
Bloomberg contributed to this report.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: France Gets Budget Warning as Fitch Turns Negative on Rating
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: William Horobin

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- France's credit score was put on a negative outlook by Fitch Ratings, in an unscheduled move that highlights the country's struggle to fix its public finances.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The change "reflects a deterioration since our August 2026 review comprising weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit," the company said in a statement late on Friday. "These worsen debt dynamics from an already weak starting point. Persistent political fragmentation and a challenging social backdrop increase the difficulty of delivering sustained fiscal consolidation."
France remains at A+ at Fitch, on par with Portugal and Belgium, and six notches above junk.
The announcement arrives on the eve of another weekend of protests in cities including Paris. Authorities are trying to contain violence after large-scale riots earlier this month.
"Fitch believes that developments in the country warrant such a deviation from the calendar," adding that its next scheduled review of France should conclude by the end of February.

The verdict is the latest indictment of France's inability to find a way to contain its swelling debt burden, which put the nation at the forefront of bond market anxiety over the past weeks. French yields have risen more than any other in the developed world this month, hitting the highest level in 24 years.
"We estimate the cumulative fiscal adjustment needed to stabilize debt has risen to around 3.5% of GDP, from 3.0% in August," Fitch said.

The country's ever-increasing debt mountain is fueled by a deficit set to blow out to 5.4% of economic output this year. Political gridlock, slumping growth and rising interest costs have derailed attempts at consolidation.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a finance bill to sharply constrain spending and raise tax revenues to meet a deficit goal of 5% next year, but the blueprint's future is uncertain as he has no majority in parliament.

Opposition groups are unwilling to compromise as they focus on presidential elections six months from now. Leading candidates from the far-left to the far-right are proposing radical changes in policy, including a lower retirement age and vast tax hikes for business.

The heightened uncertainty has caused a closely watched gauge of bond risk to rise to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis. The spread between 10-year yields in France and Germany, the region's safe asset, reached 178 basis points this month, compared to just 85 basis points at the start of September before the selloff picked up. It was around 165 on Friday.

Fitch's "assessment underlines the pressing need to pass a responsible budget before the end of the year that keeps our public finances on the path to recovery, by bringing the deficit down to 5%," French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said in a statement on Friday. "The government remains fully committed to fiscal consolidation. At a time of global uncertainty, it is vital that businesses and investors have a clear sense of direction."
--With assistance from Aline Oyamada.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Alphabet Is in Talks to Join Trump’s Golden Dome Defense Program
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Sana Pashankar and Kiel Porter

paragraphs.text: Sana Pashankar and Kiel Porter
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 4:15 PM CDT 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Alphabet Inc.'s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to work on a new data security effort underpinning the $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense program, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Pentagon is standing up a new industry group that aims to secure the data that feeds into military software being built for Golden Dome, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the matter isn't public.

The group is likely to involve multiple companies working to ensure data that flows into the new command-and-control software is resilient to attacks, such as attempts to cut access to landlines, cell towers and other critical communications infrastructure, the people said.

The talks have focused on Google's data storage, networking and cybersecurity capabilities, one of the people said. Conversations are still early and plans could change, they said. Aalyria Technologies Inc., a networking company spun out from Google, is involved in the consortium, they added.

A Pentagon official said that while the office may explore preliminary concepts, no final decision has been made regarding a new consortium or industry participants. Google and Aalyria declined to comment.
Golden Dome is President Donald Trump's marquee defense program to build a layer of defense systems from ground to space that will protect the US from foreign attack.

The Golden Dome's command-and-control layer, which is being developed by a separate group including Anduril, Palantir and SpaceX, is intended to control and connect weapons systems, radars, and other previously siloed systems across the US military.

The effort would mark Google's first publicly known involvement in the Golden Dome program and another sign of how the search engine giant is continuing to lean into national security and defense work.

Both the Pentagon's separate Golden Dome initiatives to pioneer space-based missile interceptors and its command-and-control consortium rely on numerous companies from startups to established primes, unlike past defense programs that have been more typically anchored by a single, large contractor.

Google has had a complicated history with defense work. In 2018, thousands of Google employees protested the company's involvement in a military AI program called Project Maven, citing concerns that the commercial technology would be supporting warfare. Google ultimately didn't renew the contract.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/ollie-a-privac.headline: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/ollie-a-privac.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week. Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO, took to X on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6.

“I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton. I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.”
The text-based AI assistant market has exploded over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.

Ollie, which discussed its $7.5 million seed round led from Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model. The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized. The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments. The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.

Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit. Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry. If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like Instinct have shown.

Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry had taken its toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.”
Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.

cnbc.com/2026/10/30/jim-cramer-consumer-.headline: Jim Cramer says it's time to look beyond tech. Here are 4 consumer stocks he likes
cnbc.com/2026/10/30/jim-cramer-consumer-.author: Alexa LoMonaco

paragraphs.text: Investors looking to diversify beyond the struggling artificial intelligence trade should consider consumer staples stocks, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Friday.

The Nasdaq-100, which tracks the biggest tech stocks, ended October down almost 7%. Investors rotated into other more defensive areas of the market. The S&P 500 Equal Weight gained roughly 5% for the month. (The equal weight index treats all the S&P 500 stocks the same, rather than weighting them by market cap.) The consumer staples index surged 11.4%, making it the second-best performing sector behind energy.

"You've got to take what the market is giving you, and until we sort out some of the issues for the tech sector, some other groups might be better bets for the time being," the "Mad Money" host said. "I like the idea of camping out in the staples for a bit."

Cramer highlighted four companies he finds particularly attractive in consumer staples — a group that features companies with household brand names that people tend to buy regardless of market conditions or economic environment.

• Kimberly-Clark: The maker of Kleenex tissues and Huggies diapers is one of the newest holdings in Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club. Cramer sees significant upside from its pending merger with Kenvue, which owns brands including Tylenol and Band-Aid. He expects the deal to generate efficiencies and create a consumer products powerhouse. Kimberly-Clark shares gained nearly 11% in October, but the stock still trades at less than 15 times earnings, with a 4.7% dividend yield. "I think the move is just getting started," Cramer said.

• Procter & Gamble: While the Investing Club exited its longtime P&G position in July, Cramer said the company remains an attractive defensive investment following better-than-expected quarterly results last week. He also expressed confidence in new CEO Shailesh Jejurikar. Shares of Procter & Gamble rallied 11% in October, though Cramer prefers Kimberly-Clark's lower valuation and higher dividend yield.

• Constellation Brands: The maker of Modelo and Pacifico beers is showing signs of a turnaround, with its core beer business gaining market share and its smaller wine and spirits division reporting 15% shipment growth last quarter. Shares of Constellation Brands surged 20% in October, but Cramer still sees value in the stock, which trades at roughly 11 times earnings and yields more than 3%. "It increasingly looks like the worst is behind Constellation Brands," Cramer said.

• Coca-Cola: This is the one Cramer favors among the major soda makers. Coca-Cola delivered a strong quarterly report on Tuesday driven by higher volume rather than price increases. He also praised its innovation in zero-calorie beverages and its protein options with its Fairlife milk business. Shares gained 9% in October.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-30/.headline: Video shows ICE agent pointing handgun in North Hollywood bystander's face
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-30/.author: Salvador Hernandez

paragraphs.text: A federal immigration agent pulled out their handgun and pointed it just inches from the face of a bystander during an apparent operation in North Hollywood Friday morning, according to video obtained by The Times.

The bystander was not detained or taken into custody by federal officials during the incident, but a person who appeared to be a masked federal agent shoved the man into bushes and pointed the handgun directly at his face after the bystander tossed a spray canister into the street that had been dropped by another agent, according to video and a witness.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request to comment on the incident.

The encounter occurred just before 8:30 a.m. near the intersection of Vineland Place and Otsego Street, said Damari Butler, a resident. Butler was sitting on his balcony when he said he saw a pedestrian get tackled on the sidewalk by two masked men who appeared to be U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
Butler said there seemed to be no warning before the man was tossed into nearby bushes. That’s what prompted Butler to record.
“There was no asking what his name was, no ID, nothing,” Butler said. “They just grabbed him.”
The video shows a masked ICE agent taking a pedestrian into custody on the sidewalk, as a man with two dogs on leashes stands nearby.

After a few seconds, a second masked person wearing tactical gear that says “ICE Police” across the chest runs over, telling the man with the dogs to back up while aiming what witnesses say was a can of pepper spray at him.
The man with the two dogs is then seen stepping back as the two agents handcuff the man on the sidewalk. Someone can also be heard yelling “ICE!” in the background.
As the agents carry the man by his arms, one agent is seen in the video dropping the canister. The bystander with the dogs is then seen rushing toward the can and tossing it away, toward the street.
“The guy with the dog, I guess he moved the pepper spray out of the way, and then the other ICE agent ran over,” Butler said.
The confrontation between the two lasts only a split second, because the man with the dogs steps back after tossing the canister, and the agent confronting him lets up.

But behind that agent was the other one who’d been detaining the pedestrian. That masked person pulls out their firearm with their right hand, aims it at the man with the dogs and walks toward him. He then extends his left arm and shoves the man into the bushes and leans over him, holding the gun just inches from the man’s face. The person then steps back and reholsters the gun and walks back to the SUV.
The agent yells at the unidentified bystander and leaves him on the sidewalk while another agent retrieves the can from the street.

Someone in the area can be heard using whistles, a tool that some activists have employed to alert people when ICE is in the area. Meanwhile, the detained man is seen lying on the street yelling for help in Spanish.
Eventually, more agents show up and put the detained man into the back of an SUV. As the man with dogs and a second witness look on, an agent approaches them and sprays the man with the dogs.
The bystander is seen running away.

ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials did not respond to inquiries about the man who was detained, or why he was detained. The incident occurred a day after a federal judge barred agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes, and found that immigration officials had stopped and detained people in the area because they appeared Latino.
Butler said the incident was unnerving to witness, and has left residents in the area rattled.

“It just shows you how powerless we are,” he said. “I thought that man was going to die. If someone is throwing out a gun and putting a gun to his face that close, you just expect the worst to happen at that moment.”
Since then, the video has been circulated on social media.
Ron Gochez, a leader with Union del Barrio, a community group that has been monitoring ICE activity in the area, said several videos of the North Hollywood incident have been sent to the group.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/salesforces-ma.headline: Salesforce’s M&A spree continues with a reported $375M deal for defense tech startup Rune
techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/salesforces-ma.author: Marina Temkin

paragraphs.text: Salesforce has agreed to acquire Rune Technologies, a startup that builds AI software to help the U.S. military predict supply needs and manage logistics from the field, for $375 million in cash and stock, Resilience Media reported.

The acquisition underscores Salesforce’s push into defense tech through Missionforce, its business unit serving national security and defense agencies. Since Missionforce launched last year, its business has grown 80% year over year, driven in part by a new 10-year, $5.6 billion contract with the U.S. Army, the company said in a blog post. By integrating Rune’s frontline logistics data, Missionforce will extend beyond back-office administrative planning to support battlefield operations.

Since its founding in 2024, Rune has raised a total of $30 million from investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures, and IQT, a CIA-backed non-profit venture firm formerly known as In-Q-Tel. The startup was last valued at $127 million when it raised a Series A led by Human Capital last year, according to PitchBook.

Salesforce has been on an acquisition spree this year. In addition to Rune, the CRM giant agreed to buy AI agent platform Fin (formerly Intercom) for $3.6 billion, bought Qualified for $1.2 billion, and signed an agreement to buy Listen Labs after the startup walked away from a $125 million Series C term sheet at a $1.5 billion valuation, as TechCrunch reported.
Salesforce didn’t respond to a request for comment.

cbsnews.com/live-updates/2026-midterm-el.headline: 2026 elections live updates as Trump heads to Florida for rally
cbsnews.com/live-updates/2026-midterm-el.author: Kathryn Watson, Joe Walsh

paragraphs.text: What to know as Election Day approaches for the 2026 midterms:
• With just four days to go until Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, candidates in key Senate and House elections are making their closing arguments to midterm voters.
• President Trump is heading to Florida for a rally in Daytona Beach at 7:30 p.m. ET, continuing a weekslong blitz to urge his base to turn out.

• He reversed course earlier in the day and said he will now hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday that he previously canceled. He said he heard from allies in both states who asked him to come in person, as opposed to calling in for a tele-rally.

• Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied allegations that her team helped recruit a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, amid state and federal investigations. She told supporters she's "not interested in tricking voters."
• The latest CBS News polling shows Democrats with an edge in the House — but the Senate could hinge on toss-up elections in Maine, Ohio, Texas and more.
In intra-party feud, El-Sayed says Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago"
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate, hit back at Rep. Haley Stevens, whom he defeated in the primary, after she demanded an apology for comments he made about Israel.

The dispute between the former Democratic rivals comes two days before they are expected to appear at an event in Detroit with Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina — marking one of their only joint appearances since the contentious primary.

In a statement Friday night, El-Sayed says his former rival "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago" instead of focusing on beating the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and addressing Michiganders' cost of living concerns.

Stevens said in an earlier statement Friday she planned to appear with El-Sayed on the campaign trail, but she expected him to apologize for comments about Israel and condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. She also wanted El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring Tucker Carlson.
"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," she said. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

Susan Collins says she can do more for Maine because of seniority
Speaking about her closing message to voters, GOP Sen. Susan Collins said, "My final message to the people of Maine is to think about who can do more for Maine."

"If I am fortunate enough to be reelected, I will be fifth in seniority among the 100 senators. My opponent [Democrat Troy Jackson] would be either 100 or 99," she said while campaigning in Milo, Maine.

"And the fact is that seniority, relationships, knowledge and experience all really count in the Senate. They're the key to whether or not you're effective," she continued. "It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Appropriations Committee. I feel that I've had a once-in-a-century opportunity to really deliver for Maine and for America."

Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in a blue-leaning state, has made her role atop the Senate Appropriations Committee central to her campaign, touting the federal funds that she has helped secure for projects in Maine.

Sullivan, a candidate with the same first and last name as the Republican incumbent senator, Dan Sullivan, is set to appear on the ballot Tuesday. "That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.

Speaking in the Oval Office with Stephen Hubbard, an American who was recently freed from a Russian prison, the president addressed the back and forth over whether he would hold in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa.

"I wanted to see if I could do tele-rallies, because I'm very successful with — we're batting unbelievable at tele-rallies. I do them well, and it's a great instrument and it only seems to work for me because other people call and nobody gets on the phone," Mr. Trump said.

"I got a call from both states, Kansas and Iowa. We're in good shape, I think, in a lot of states. We had a great rally yesterday, as you know, for Darlene [Graham] in South Carolina. The president said he would travel to Iowa first and then to Kansas.
"Monday is going to be exciting. But Sunday is going to be a very exciting day," he said. "And then Tuesday, we're going to see how it all works out. I think we're doing well."

Daniel J. Sullivan left his Alaska hometown earlier this week, sources say

Petersburg, Alaska — Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent candidate running for Senate in Alaska whose name is almost identical to the Republican senator running for reelection, left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, multiple sources confirmed to CBS News.

One resident and former student of Sullivan's said she saw Sullivan on a flight to Anchorage on Monday — two days before The New York Times first reported that he was recruited by operatives linked to Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign. The source added she did not know where Sullivan was headed, but another friend said he and his wife are known among friends as "world travelers."

Dozens of Petersburg residents also told CBS News they never saw or received any campaign materials like mailers, flyers, brochures or signs since the former elementary school teacher announced his candidacy last spring.
"I don't think it's a serious candidacy," said Andrew Worhatch, a Petersburg fisherman. "I haven't seen a platform."

Appeals court rejects DOJ request to have California set aside disputed ballots
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.
The panel's 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to assert control over state-run elections.

The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department's demands could disenfranchise citizens.

"As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system," the appeals court wrote.

DOJ sent letters to all 50 states telling them to preserve election records
The Justice Department said in a court filing on Friday that it sent letters to all 50 states reminding them of their obligation to preserve election records for 22 months after an election.

The disclosure came in a filing in a suit brought by Democratic groups and officials over the Trump administration's efforts to pressure states to remove alleged ineligible voters from their rolls. District Judge James Boasberg in Washington, D.C., is overseeing the case. The judge had directed the DOJ and DHS after a hearing on Thursday to identify states where federal officials had sent communications since July 1, 2026.
The administration told the judge that federal agencies contacted election officials in five states about voters they identified as potentially ineligible.

The lawsuit, filed Oct. 20, was brought by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic Governors Association, Nevada State Democratic Party, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and a California voter.

The government confirmed it sent communications to California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Washington. (DHS contacted California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, while the Justice Department contacted California and Washington.)

The government said the July 16 letters to California, Nevada and Pennsylvania did not demand that states remove voters, withhold ballots or segregate ballots, but asked state officials to work with DHS to verify whether individuals identified through a preliminary analysis were noncitizens.

Sen. Susan Collins focuses on bolstering support in rural Maine

In the final days of her campaign, incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is focusing on bolstering support in the northern, more rural part of Maine through smaller-scale stops highlighting projects and developments she helped secure for local communities.

On Friday morning in Greenville, a town of about 1,400 year-round residents on the southern tip of Moosehead Lake in Piscataquis County, Collins attended a groundbreaking ceremony for a new childcare facility at Greenville Consolidated School. The facility will accommodate more than 60 children and include a new town recreation and fitness center.
During brief remarks ahead of the groundbreaking, Collins spoke about her role in advancing the project and the impact the new facility will have on the community.

"I worked hard to secure more than $1.5 million in federal funding to advance this project because I am so confident that it will produce a great return in terms of quality of life," Collins said. "Quality child care helps children be ready for school as active and engaged learners. It promotes economic development by enabling parents to work, further their education and increase their own skills, knowing that their children are in a safe and happy environment. This supports the businesses that are already here, and it helps the region attract even more employers."
Collins did not take questions at the event.

Mamdani's political clout in Washington may expand via DSA candidates
Election Day is fast approaching, and many candidates for office are busy doing everything they can to convince any remaining undecided voters.
And then there are Democrats running in New York City Districts 7 and 13, areas so blue that candidates for Congress don't need to campaign at all.
Darializa Avila Chevalier is running in the 13th District. Claire Valdez is running in the 7th District. They're both members of Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA.
"We're still encouraging folks to go out. Early voting has already started. Election Day is Nov. 3," Avila Chevalier said.
The district she's running in covers parts of Upper Manhattan and the Bronx. Valdez's district covers parts of Brooklyn and Queens. Both are viewed by election analysts as safely Democratic.
The inevitability of their victories doesn't make them any less notable, since they're both DSA members, along with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Mamdani's endorsement of both of them was the key to their primary victories over more experienced, non-DSA opponents, according to political expert and law professor J.C. Polanco. So does that make Mamdani the most powerful politician in Washington who doesn't work out of Washington?

Peltola supporters in Alaska weigh in on ballot controversy
Supporters of Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola in Juneau, Alaska, told CBS News they still support her bid.

Peltola is facing intense criticism over a New York Times report that operatives aligned with her campaign were involved in the Dan Sullivan recruitment effort. Peltola has denied any involvement or knowledge of the scheme.
Democrat Bob Coghill said he thinks the controversy could hurt Peltola with late deciders.

"I do think it will hurt her chances," Coghill said. "I think there are people that will see this as something just a little too clever, a little too untoward, and it's going to hurt some votes of the people who — particularly the last-minute voters."
Carter Bancroft, an independent voter heading to vote early for Peltola, said he disliked the political gamesmanship, but questioned the push to prosecute Peltola.
"Seems like a mess," Bancroft said. "Seems to me possible, probable, that he is in this race to confuse things."

He added: "I don't like the shenanigans that go on on both sides, gerrymandering in a variety of ways, that it seems like politicians stump more on confusing people, in many ways, than they do on actual issues. I feel like that's possible here, and I don't like that. On the other hand, it doesn't seem — it may be tasteless if that's true, but it's not criminal."

Democrat Leah Haskell-Cummins called the allegations against Peltola "ridiculous" and "fearmongering." She said the ballot clearly distinguished between the two Dan Sullivans, making voter confusion unlikely.

Labor unions sue DOJ and DHS, accusing them of intimidating California election workers

A coalition of labor unions and civil rights organizations — including the Service Employees International Union; the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees; the NAACP; and the League of United Latin American Citizens — have sued the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security, alleging that federal officials are unlawfully intimidating California election workers and interfering with the administration of the midterm elections.

The 46-page lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Northern California on Thursday, accuses the Trump administration of using subpoenas, threats of criminal prosecution and demands involving voter eligibility to pressure state and local election officials. Plaintiffs argue that the actions exceed federal authority and threaten the lawful processing and counting of ballots.
The groups are seeking a court order barring federal officials from threatening election workers or improperly interfering with ballot processing.

President Trump will hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, reversing course on plans to cancel the events and hold tele-rallies instead.

A source familiar with the plans told CBS News the rallies "were rearranged for scheduling purposes to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies that were recently added to the President's schedule."

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election, casting mail ballot in Chicago
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pontiff, submitted a mail ballot for the midterm elections in Illinois, the Vatican said Friday.

Why Pennsylvania could be one of last states to count ballots this Election Day
With four days until Election Day, Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker and city commissioners are urging people to vote.

Officials on Thursday escorted the media through a warehouse in Northeast Philly known as Philadelphia Election Headquarters. Every ballot placed in the city, whether in person or by mail, ends up at the warehouse to be counted on Election Day.
As mail-in ballots are returned, they are first sorted by a huge machine that separates the envelopes by ward and division.
Then, they are stored securely behind locked cages and won't be touched until Tuesday.
Unlike most states, Pennsylvania doesn't allow workers to start processing mail-in ballots until Election Day.

Then, starting at 7 a.m., workers use heavy-duty machines known as extractors to open the envelopes, but a person has to physically remove the ballot. From there, election workers sit at long tables and flatten the ballots before they are scanned and counted.

nytimes.com/2026/10/30/science/space/mar.headline: A Meteorite Found in the Sahara Is a 4.1-Billion-Year-Old Piece of Mars

paragraphs.text: Reddish rocks found in the Sahara four years ago turned out to be older than almost anything on Earth. In fact, they are not of this world: They are pieces of Mars dating back 4.1 billion years.

Scientists described the meteorite fragments in a paper published on Thursday in the journal Science. Together they make up a space rock named Teghaza 001, after an ancient, abandoned salt-mining settlement in Mali close to where the fragments were found.
“It’s very rare to find something this old,” said Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California and the lead author of the Science paper.
Of the more than 400 Martian meteorites that have been found, only two, Allan Hills 84001 and Northwest Africa 7034, which is often called “Black Beauty,” rival Teghaza 001 in age.

For scientists, Teghaza 001 serves as a time machine. Its mix of igneous minerals preserves a snapshot of what Mars was like a few hundred million years after it formed. The minerals provide hints about both the mantle and the crust of early Mars.

“We really don’t have this kind of mineralogy in our Martian collection,” said Arya Udry, a professor of geoscience at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who was not involved in the research. “Any new rock that is unique from Mars is really exciting.”

An earlier paper by some of the same scientists reported that the meteorite contained evidence that abundant water flowed on Mars when the rock formed, based on water molecules bound within a mineral known as apatite. (The Martian apatite is similar to the mineral that is the main ingredient of your teeth.)
But the analysis also showed that the planet had already lost much of its water. Ultraviolet light broke apart the water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, and the hydrogen floated away into space.

The meteorite’s journey began when a meteor hit Mars, knocking the rock into space. Eventually, it crossed paths with Earth. A chunk of the rock weighing nearly two pounds survived the fiery entry through the atmosphere. It landed as a meteorite and broke into eight pieces.

When Dr. Liu first received the meteorite sample to study, she did not expect it to be very interesting. It had been initially classified as a shergottite — the most abundant type of Martian meteorite and one that is usually not that old.

But when she looked, she saw zircons, a type of crystal that is usually not found in shergottites. “It’s very unusual, and I see a lot of them in the sample,” she said. “That was a quick alarm bell going off.”
Using a dating method based on the ratio of uranium isotopes, the scientists learned that the zircons were about 4.1 billion years old. Two other dating methods confirmed the age.

“Once we recognized that this Teghaza sample was an ancient one, we immediately became interested in trying to characterize its water,” said Lee Saper, a planetary scientist working at the NASA Ames Research Center in Mountain View, Calif., and another author of the two Teghaza papers.
The water in the apatite appears to have come from two different sources. Some of the water was in the magma that rose from the Martian mantle.

Dr. Liu said the mix of elements of the mantle portion of Teghaza 001 looked significantly different from what had been measured in other Martian meteorites. “Which is suggesting it’s more primordial, not affected by later processes,” she said.

Other water molecules came from the surface and the atmosphere, percolating through the crust. The scientists could tell that much of the water on Mars had already escaped to space, because those molecules possessed a higher concentration of deuterium, the heavier version of hydrogen, which is less likely to float away.

The deuterium-to-ordinary-hydrogen ratio in Teghaza 001 is similar to what was found in Allan Hills 84001. “It’s not completely changing our view of Mars at that time, but now we have two data points instead of one, which gives us a lot more confidence,” Dr. Saper said.

It is not certain when the rock was knocked into space or when it landed in the Sahara. But by comparing the mineralogy of the meteorite with what robotic spacecraft have measured from orbit around Mars, the researchers have identified 13 locations where Teghaza 001 could have originated.
The researchers said they looked forward to additional analysis by other scientists. “We looked at a small part of it,” Dr. Saper said. “There’s a much more complex story that’s yet to be uncovered.”

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Big Tech Holds $3 Trillion in Spending Commitments for AI Boom
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Brody Ford

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The five largest players in the data center race have committed more than $3 trillion in spending over the coming years, pointing to massive ongoing investment in AI infrastructure.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Alphabet Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Oracle Corp. have each disclosed ballooning commitments on leases, buildings, energy and other equipment as they've rushed to build fleets of data centers. This is a mix of short-term spending and some pledges that are as long as decades away.

The largest chunk of these commitments comes from Google, which reported more than $1 trillion of commitments, including technical equipment, energy and leases. That figure is nearly eight times higher than it was a year earlier and includes agreements for technical equipment, energy and leases, according to the company's regulatory filing.

Meta has reported a similarly sharp ramp-up, disclosing more than $800 billion in future spending. A bit less than half of that is for data center leases that haven't yet started, and will be paid off over periods as long as 30 years. "We expect to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives," Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said during a call with analysts last week.

One of the biggest debates in business this year has been whether the hundreds of billions being spent on server farms for artificial intelligence work will really pay off. Some of the most profitable businesses in history like Alphabet and Meta have dipped into negative free cash flow, citing the need to invest in a transformative new business line.

Not all of the spending is strictly tied to data centers, and each company discloses commitments in slightly different ways, making it difficult to compare them directly. For example, Meta notes that some of its planned spending is related to consumer hardware products in the Reality Labs division. Alphabet and Amazon each note planned spending on content licenses. There are also major pools of spending — such as current leases and debt — that aren't captured by this analysis.

In all, the future lease commitments total $1.3 trillion, while other purchase commitments amount to $1.9 trillion. All of the figures come from the company's most recent financial reports, save for Microsoft, which most recently disclosed its purchase and construction orders as part of its annual report for the end of June.

Oracle was the first major company to dip into negative free cash flow due to its AI data center investments. During an investor presentation earlier this week, it charted a return to free cash flow in 2028. In part, it will achieve this by using vendor financing and customer prepayments to reduce its up-front costs.
