kanebridgenews.com/microsoft-will-offer-.headline: Microsoft Will Offer Buyouts to 60,000 Employees
kanebridgenews.com/microsoft-will-offer-.author: Kanebridge

paragraphs.text: , the company said on Monday. Around 60,000 employees are eligible for the program, according to a person familiar with the matter. K.

S. “The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s chief people officer, said in a message sent to employees. Microsoft said the program was “time-limited” and would provide eligible employees with financial support and career planning resources.

Coleman said eligible employees would receive an email link with their offer details in the next few hours. Microsoft in April announced a voluntary retirement program, which offered around 8,600 employees buyouts, the person familiar with the matter said, and more than 30% accepted the offer. The company expects a far lower percentage to accept the latest buyouts, the person said.

Microsoft employed 223,000 employees as of the end of June. The voluntary retirement program was part of a broader shift by Microsoft to alter its performance system and how it awards bonuses and stock options, according to a memo to employees from Coleman viewed by The Wall Street Journal at the time. Microsoft earlier this year announced 3,200 job cuts in its Xbox videogames division.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2818elrnzo.headline: Evacuated Ukrainians from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2818elrnzo.author: Jacob Phillips

paragraphs.text: Residents evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have arrived in Belarus and are expected back in Ukraine later on Saturday, authorities have said.
They were taken out on Friday during a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Planes carrying Oleshky residents landed in the city of Gomel on Saturday morning, according to Belarusian state media and a senior Ukrainian official.

"The last, fourth plane landed in Gomel (Belarus). In a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky, together with the Ukrainian delegation, will be on Ukrainian territory," said David Arakhamia, a key Ukrainian official.
The state-owned Belarusian news agency Belta reported a bus convoy of Oleshky residents had left Gomel airport and was heading towards the Ukrainian border.
A humanitarian ceasefire took force across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ceasefire allowed the road out of Oleshky to be demined and will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and a lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".

Ukrainian military positions lie just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky but evacuees first had to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa, where they flew to Gomel.
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.

science.org/content/article/serbia-just-.headline: Serbia just elected the world’s brainiest parliament
science.org/content/article/serbia-just-.author: Nenad Jarić Dauenhauer, Mićo Tatalović

paragraphs.text: An astrophysicist who studies galaxy evolution. An electrical engineer who has helped design robots. An organic chemist who, during the pandemic, worked on COVID-19 drugs. An education researcher, a sociologist, several political scientists, economists, physicians, and medical researchers. They have all been elected to what may well be the brainiest parliament in the world.

After a student-led opposition movement won in Serbia on 25 October, the group, named Student List – Students Are Winning, has 141 representatives in Serbia’s 250-member National Assembly. Dozens of them come from the academic world, and more than half have a Ph.D. or M.D.

Now, this group is tasked with forming a government and charting a new course for Serbia, after 13 years of populist authoritarian rule by Aleksandar Vučić, first as prime minister and later as president. Student List has promised to fight corruption and establish meritocracy, accountability, and the rule of law.

But with so many academics suddenly close to the center of power, Serbian researchers are also hoping for major changes in the country’s science and higher education landscape. During Vučić’s reign, academic freedom eroded, universities became highly politicized, and critics were sidelined. Student List has promised more academic autonomy, more stable science funding, and affordable education. It hopes to stop the country’s persistent brain drain.

“For our universities, this victory is decisive—it immediately halts the previous regime’s active dismantling of higher education,” says Sofija Stefanović, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Belgrade. “While the new government must first restore the rule of law and fight corruption, meaning the full recovery of our scientific sector will take time, change is clearly on the horizon.”
“Better times lie ahead,” adds Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade. (The office of the president and Vučić’s party did not respond to a request for comment.)

The winning political movement emerged from countrywide student protests sparked by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad train station in November 2024 that killed 16 people. Students blamed the tragedy on corruption in the public sector and demanded transparency and justice. But as their calls went unheeded, their protests grew stronger, drawing support from academics, teachers, and the wider public. By May 2025, they called for an early election and started to draft candidates.

Rather than stand themselves, the students pulled together a slate of trusted figures—not just academics, but also farmers, lawyers, artists, teachers, and a former basketball player. At the top of the numbered list of candidates is Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist, but he is not the group’s official leader and his future role in politics is unclear. Although some of the elected academics could end up as full-time politicians, many may choose to keep their academic careers going; the Serbian parliament allows its members to have other jobs if they don’t present a conflict of interest.

Many of the new representatives have zero experience in politics. But their unparalleled professional expertise should be helpful in reforming Serbia, says molecular biologist Željko Popović of the University of Novi Sad (UNS).

Scientists hope the reforms will extend to academia. Vučić’s government has been accused of pressuring universities and academics to fall in line with its policies and appointing political allies to university governing bodies. Some academics deemed disloyal have lost their jobs. “A university must be free to think, conduct research, and offer criticism, without fear of political repercussions,” says Marija Lesjak, a chemist at UNS who was just elected to parliament. One source of political pressure was a centralized financial management system that routes all transactions through the country’s treasury. That “significantly limits the ability of faculties to manage their own funds and plan for their own development,” Lesjak says.

Researchers also want to make science funding more meritocratic. Under Vučić, “Funds were frequently distributed based on political or personal connections rather than merit, which severely undermined the quality of scientific work,” says Miodrag Krmar, a physicist at UNS who was a candidate for Student List.

Student List is promising fixes. Its platform includes more predictable funding, an independent Science Fund, an end to political meddling in research funding evaluations, and support for researchers working abroad who want to return to Serbia.

Now, the movement needs to choose a prime minister. A presidential election will also be held, likely by the end of the year. Vučić, who has served two terms as president and can’t run again, resigned in September, hoping to win the parliamentary election and become prime minister instead.

Popović warns that transforming the research sector in Serbia “will not be such an easy and quick process.” But students have set an inspiring example, he says, showing academics and the rest of society that change is possible even when a national populist appears to have consolidated power.

And he hopes academics’ support for the 2-year revolt has changed the public’s view of scientists. Sometimes seen as elitist or a burden on society, university professors took to the streets alongside students, often standing as a physical barrier between them and the police, he says: “We showed that we are part of this society, with all our heart and soul, and that we are ready to do anything to defend our common values and our freedom.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/opinion/democrats.headline: Democrats Are the Populist Party Now

paragraphs.text: In the waning days of the midterm election campaign, Republicans have finally stumbled on a closing message: defending the honor of the Cheesecake Factory.

Last week, Barack Obama made a viral crack about Donald Trump’s renovations: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Conservatives feigned outrage on behalf of the humble American volk for whom the Cheesecake Factory is the height of sophistication. Fox Business interviewed the centimillionaire Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, after lunch at the restaurant; he sniffed, “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.” (His Massachusetts beach house, which he sold for a couple of million dollars in 2012, was in Provincetown.) The Wall Street Journal suggested that Democrats had shot themselves in the foot in their quest to win back “the working man in Middle America.” The White House posted a list of Trump’s “accomplishments” in the style of a Cheesecake Factory menu.

Republicans have been trying to brand Democrats as the party of out-of-touch elitists since at least the 1960s, but this time, it felt particularly forced and desperate. After all, it’s become screamingly obvious which party represents billionaires and unchecked plutocratic power.

On the stump this week, an increasingly disinhibited Trump scoffed at the idea of “suffering at the pump” while boasting that high oil prices have been a windfall for the energy industry. Elon Musk, the richest person on earth, is almost single-handedly funding the Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign. Susan Collins ran a closing ad in which a retired broadcaster seemed to mock her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, for being a logger, saying, “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here; we’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate.”

Meanwhile, Democrats all over the country are running against the ultrarich. “The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right,” the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico says on the campaign trail. “It’s top versus bottom.” In the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed is a political protégé of Bernie Sanders who accuses his opponent, Mike Rogers, of being bought by corporations. Former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, defeated with the help of crypto dollars two years ago, may regain his seat thanks in part to widespread fury at data centers and the tech billionaires behind them.

If Democrats win big on Tuesday after running such populist campaigns, it will be more than a victory over Trump. It will be an opportunity for them to once again develop an image as the champion of working people against predatory elites. That, in turn, could realign American politics. But it will happen only if Democrats can resist the entreaties of the tech donors and lobbyists who, having realized that going all in on MAGA was a bad bet, will now spend big to rebuild bridges to the center left.

For decades now, American politics has been shaped by two very different conceptions of class. Liberals tend to view class as a primarily economic distinction: a millionaire car dealer in the Midwest has a class advantage over a Brooklyn adjunct professor on food stamps. Conservatives, by contrast, are more likely to understand class as a matter of taste, culture and education. They’ve long seen America as riven between what some called a “new class” of intellectuals, professionals and bureaucrats and an alliance of capitalists and traditionalist blue-collar workers. “The simple truth is that the professional classes of our modern bureaucratized societies are engaged in a class struggle with the business community for status and power,” wrote Irving Kristol, godfather of neoconservatism, in 1972. (He very much sided with the beleaguered businessmen.)

Neoconservatism fell out of fashion, but Kristol’s ideas about class didn’t. If anything, as the two parties sorted by education, they became a kind of cultural common sense. Obama, who was still paying off student debt in his 40s, was tagged as an elitist, while Trump, who loves to brag about his wealth, was not.

The 2024 election was a triumph for the right’s conception of class politics, with Trump making gains with low-income voters while Kamala Harris won those earning over $200,000 a year. In surveys and focus groups, voters described Democrats as elitist and condescending. When the Democratic firm Navigator Research polled swing districts after the last election, 56 percent of respondents said the party didn’t look out for working people, and a majority said Democrats didn’t share their values. The road to winning back working-class voters looked difficult and uncertain.

Trump, by abandoning all restraint in his kleptocratic smash-and-grab, has made it easier. In a September poll from The New York Times and Siena University, voters identified Republicans as the “elitist” party by 10 points. The Times quoted a 40-year-old who’d voted for Trump two years earlier: “The people that are ‘in with him,’ who look or act a certain way, are the ones that are going to be given an opportunity.”

Few things have laid bare the president’s essential elitism like his alliance with America’s tech oligarchs. Trump ran against Big Tech in 2020, when he saw it as an ally of Democrats, but he was less interested in curbing the industry’s power than co-opting it. Now that he’s done that, tying Silicon Valley’s fortunes to his own, he can’t countenance criticism of it. He’s attempted, absurdly, to rebrand A.I. as “super intelligence,” and said that communities that reject data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor.”

Silicon Valley was once seen as a bastion of liberalism, but a recent Politico poll found that voters across the political spectrum now associate it with the Republican Party. At the same time, Big Tech — and particularly A.I. and data centers — has rarely been more reviled. This summer, a leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee called data centers “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle” and warned that public fury about them could cost the Republican Jon Husted his Senate seat in Ohio.

Rob Flaherty, former head of digital strategy for Joe Biden, is a founder of Tomorrow Together, a new super PAC that goes after Republicans for their ties to the A.I. industry. He shared polling his group commissioned about A.I. and data centers in several swing districts. In Pennsylvania’s Eighth District, held by a Republican, Rob Bresnahan, 51 percent of respondents feel strongly unfavorably toward data centers. Only 5 percent feel strongly favorably. Voters see A.I., Flaherty told me, as “these guys sitting in a room somewhere cooking up technology that’s going to make your life worse, making you pay for it, and buying off the government to do it.”

Now that Democrats seem likely to retake at least one house of Congress, tech companies are rushing to hire Democratic lobbyists. Given the enormous resources Silicon Valley kingpins wield, some Democrats might be tempted to seek a rapprochement with the industry. “I worry that Democrats are going to say, ‘We need to rebuild our alliances with tech,’ and miss the opportunity that’s in front of their face here,” said Flaherty. That would be a terrible mistake. The opportunity before Democrats is about more than being on the right side of a winning issue. Democrats have a unique chance, after decades of culture wars, to wrest the mantle of populism from Republicans and thus change the terrain on which American elections are fought.

“They are unanimous in their hate for me — and I welcome their hatred,” Franklin Delano Roosevelt said in 1936 about monopolists, speculators and war profiteers. Democrats should remember his words when they retake power. A good enemy is a terrible thing to waste.

My landlord’s spooky-season sidewalk tableau this year features three skeletons carrying an open casket, inside of which is yet another skeleton, as well as a disembodied hand. One morning last week, I emerged from the building to see two women with infants in strollers parked out front. It’s not unusual around Halloween to see families taking pictures of the spectacle, but I found it amusing that these people had stopped to show it to their babies. What would these tiny humans make of a surprisingly lifelike rotten-toothed crone beckoning them from the hedge? Would they recognize Halloween’s creepy cast of characters as frightening? Perhaps they were too young to even register what they were seeing. Perhaps the world in their eyes was still a series of shapes, light and color — everything new, everything still coming into focus, still taking on the valence of scary or safe.

The things that spook us as children leave their mark. We grow into adults who must disentangle real threats from perceived ones, and often discover that a present-day fear took root when we were too young to know better. Growing up, my family had a vinyl record of Boris Karloff narrating Prokofiev’s “Peter and the Wolf” that I found so frightening I could not look at the album cover. I insisted it be removed from my room and then lay awake worrying because the album was still somewhere in the house, pulsing with its fearsome power. Listening to a recording this week — No matter how hard the duck tried to run, she couldn’t escape the wolf. He was getting nearer, nearer, catching up with her — I felt a similar surge of terror as I felt as a child, combined with a pleasurable measure of gratitude that my more mature, rational brain can separate a ghost story from imminent menace.

In a recent Times article, the writer Alessandra Schade recalled that as a child she lived next door to the “Goosebumps” author R.L. Stine. She read his horror stories for kids and convinced herself that Stine’s house was haunted. Twenty years later, Schade met Stine, who told her about his career and how he came to inhabit the home from whose chimney she once was certain she saw ghosts floating. She learned that Stine and his wife, who met when they were editing magazines at Scholastic in the 1960s, had lived there, on a quiet cul-de-sac in Sag Harbor, on the eastern end of Long Island, for a quarter century. The source of her childhood anxiety turned out to be, as she put it, “a friendly octogenarian” who “goes by Bob.”

Our childhood fears resist rationalization. We can turn on the light and see that the boogeyman is just a pile of clothes, but we sleep with one eye open nonetheless. As adults, we have the tools to distinguish between real and imagined peril, but we don’t always use them. The scary album is replaced by the amorphous worry about a difficult conversation, a potential loss, things not turning out as we wish. We picture the worst-case scenario; we still see monsters where there’s just dirty laundry.
No matter how old we get, we still need to remind ourselves that what is unknown or mysterious to us isn’t necessarily dangerous.

Halloween is a laboratory for experimenting with this. All around us, bedsheet ghosts haunt the neighbor’s oak tree, spiders as big as hatchbacks climb up the side of tenements. And children, the ones most likely to shrink from this pageant of frights, walk through it delightedly, meeting witches and vampires and learning to distinguish costumes from reality.

Tomato-Parmesan soup

5 life-changing cleaning hacks
I’ve learned all kinds of useful and unconventional hacks in my many years immersed in Wirecutter’s cleaning coverage. Here are five that have totally transformed my approach:
• You can skip dry-cleaning plenty of things, even if the label insists you should.
• Hand-washing many delicates — like wool or cashmere sweaters — can actually help them last longer.
• Dish soap is an underrated cleaner, and works wonders on far more than just dishes. I use it to clean my oven, wood floors, appliances and even some laundry stains.

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/magazine/martin-m.headline: Martin McDonagh Says Art Can Change the World. Just Not as Much as Murder.

paragraphs.text: The writer-director Martin McDonagh has carved out a highly esteemed cinematic career as a chronicler of extreme, and often extremely bloody, behavior carried out on a relatively intimate scale. “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), to pick one of his films, was about two friends on a remote Irish island descending into a feud. “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” (2017), to pick another, looked at a mother’s attempt to get justice for her murdered daughter. That those movies, despite their dark setups, are often as vulgarly funny as they are emotionally affecting is evidence of McDonagh’s originality — and his skill too. (McDonagh was an enfant terrible of the British theatrical world before he turned to filmmaking.) The 56-year-old’s films have earned a cumulative 18 Academy Award nominations, and “Six Shooter” (2004) earned him an Oscar for best live-action short.

With the new “Wild Horse Nine,” his fifth feature, which is already earning major awards-season buzz, McDonagh has widened the aperture. The movie, in theaters Nov. 6, follows two C.I.A. agents, played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, who have been deployed to Chile in 1973 to destabilize the country’s nascent democracy after President Allende was elected. That setup, which pivots on a fateful trip to Easter Island, allows McDonagh to explore big ideas about political power and America’s foreign misadventures, in addition to his more typical forays into male friendship, interpersonal ethical dilemmas and gleefully crass humor. As he explained to me when we spoke in New York this fall, those elements all add up to something that for McDonagh — however counterintuitive it may seem — are expressions of hope.

“Wild Horse Nine” is coming out in the middle of a broader conversation — and argument — over America’s place in the world. That often comes down to a binary: Is America a force for good or bad? How do you see America’s place? Right now, I’m not sure. I guess we’re all a little bewildered about what it stands for. But the film explores a time when, seemingly, America’s place in the world was as the good guy, which is what most kids in the West — not just in the U.S. but in the U.K. and Ireland, Western Europe — are brought up to feel. The C.I.A. are the good guys and the K.G.B. are the bad guys; America is the good guy and Russia is the bad. But the more I read about what the C.I.A. were up to throughout the end of the last century, and particularly in Chile — to destabilize and help overthrow a democratically elected government, which ended up in fascist horrors for 15 years — it makes you think that you’re not being told the truth about the West and its moral outlook.

There’s a line in “Wild Horse Nine”: “Life is sad, everything is sad.” That line struck me as a melancholy iteration of a line from your play “The Pillowman,” which is: “The world’s a pile of [expletive].” There are moments of grace in your work, but is that your view? That’s not me. In both instances, it’s the setup to a joke, in a way. And both of those characters are quite nasty, tough cop characters. So I don’t know if that’s the way I feel about cops. I don’t think so. It’s weird because I guess my stuff comes out dark and sad in a lot of places, but I’m so the opposite. I never thought I’d be in a position to make a film, for instance. I never thought that would be open to me growing up as a working-class kid in London. So no, I definitely don’t feel that way about the world.
I do think of your work as generally pretty dark. Really?

Yeah. How could it be the case that the work doesn’t represent something about your innermost feelings about life? But questioning and disbelieving what you’re told isn’t dark, and making art is always hopeful, even if it’s dark art. I always think of Leonard Cohen and people saying that his stuff is depressing. I find it the total opposite. The tunes are beautiful. It’s poetic. I mean, I’m not disagreeing with people who say my stuff is on the dark side, but in the writing of it, I’m joyful. The performances are so wonderful, and the visual, cinematic parts of it are so wonderful, that darkness honestly doesn’t come into it from my perspective.

You said that making art is a hopeful act. Do you think the art that you make has the ability to change the people who see it? That’s a hard one. But if an audience has come out having laughed a lot and learned some stuff, particularly in this one about Chile, then that is what I’m after, and all of that is hopeful.

I used to agree with you, but now I don’t. I often think of a quote, from the British comedian Peter Cook, about the political efficacy of satire. He said, I’m paraphrasing, something like, Well, the greatest satire in the world was in Weimar Germany, and that stopped Hitler right in his tracks. [Laughs] It’s a very good line. Is hopeful work going to stop stuff? I don’t know. But is anything?
So I think of your work as —— Dark and bleak. [Laughs]
Dark and bleak, but also as the product of someone who likes to provoke a reaction, even if that’s a recoil. Um. …

Am I wrong about that? No, no. “Recoil” I might question. I often think about this. Yeah, it’s all quite provocative. It’s never intentionally offensive. It’s often outrageous. For instance, Malkovich’s character in this movie is outrageous. But I don’t think he, or even the film, or any of my stuff, is offensive. I always feel like my heart is in the right place morally. I have a predilection for being naughty. In this movie, there’s a scene about cheeses, for instance, that is quite naughty. But it never occurs to me to be offensive.

What’s the difference between being outrageous and being offensive? One is deliberately trying to hurt or attack an audience, whereas the other is to almost delight in something you haven’t heard before or you might not have thought of.
Do you want to say the thing about cheeses, or should I? You can go ahead.

So Malkovich’s character has a little disquisition about how what he calls the “gay countries” make the best cheeses. Yeah, Holland, France, the U.K. and Switzerland make great cheeses, and they are some of the “gay countries.” Russia is definitely not a gay country. I’m going to get in so much trouble.

It’s in the movie! It’s true. And Russia doesn’t have good cheese, and there’s a connection between the two, which is then connected to democracy, and democracy leads to gay, leads to good cheeses. Something I’ve thought about often and I think is true.

I’m sure there are people who will find that scene problematic or offensive. But when you’re watching it — and I’ve watched it with a whole lot of audiences, mostly pretty liberal audiences — the biggest laughs in the whole film are in that scene. And I think it’s because it’s outrageous, but there is some kind of weird something to it.

But going back 30 years, there have been people who have said your work is offensive. Do you feel as if the conversation about what causes offense — who can say what, and using what language — has evolved or changed in that time? It’s gotten worse, especially in the last 10 years. Only in the last 10 years have I been asked to change words in plays from 25, 30 years ago because of offense taken by certain words that wasn’t there 25 years ago. Those words were there to be either outrageous or to be truthful. If you’re writing a racist character, they’re going to use racist language. To try and cut those out 25 years later — for what reason? I’m never quite sure. If you don’t like that in a play, you should just not do the play. You shouldn’t try and change the play 25 years later.
Is it the N-word that people ask you to change? No, actually much softer, but words that could be seen as equally racist or offensive.

When I was preparing for this interview, I read a lot of essays about your work, and there were two that stood out to me on the topic of race. There was a piece by Hilton Als about your play “A Behanding in Spokane” where he equated a Black character in it to a Stepin Fetchit type. And my colleague at The Times, Wesley Morris, wrote a piece about “Three Billboards” where he said he thought the characters’ use of the N-word was glib. Those are two Pulitzer Prize-winning critics, both Black men, who saw something troubling in the work. Does that make you think, Maybe there is something I need to look at that I’m doing? Or do you think, No, they just don’t get it? After the play, the one that Hilton had the issue with, I did have a look back on it and wondered about the amount of offensive words. I felt my heart was in the right place when I wrote it, mostly about portraying the stupidity of the main guy who is racist. But you definitely take it on board. If you grew up completely antiracist, and that’s part of what your attempt at art is about, when that doesn’t go across to certain critics, you definitely have a think about it.

What do you think about it? Just to question the language a little bit in the next one, or maybe take a little more care about that subject. Less so about the film. I feel like the film was taken as redemption to a character that I didn’t feel was true. I don’t agree as much with that one.

Your work often generates questions about political correctness or the use of language. But there’s comparatively less writing about the violence. Why do you think one subject gets people agitated and the other — violence — seems to raise no questions for people? It’s weird, right? Well, I’d have to disagree.
You get it for violence, too? Yeah. That it’s gratuitous and always there and doesn’t need to be.

What do you make of that? I don’t think it’s always there, and I never make it gratuitous — never intentionally. Especially with the stage work, I was brought up having to watch English plays, which were, like, people drinking cups of tea for two and a half hours, and I always wanted to shoot them — onstage. [Laughs] So that naturally evolved into the plays I made. I’m being a bit glib, but I did think plays should be as exciting as the best films, and that meant you should be able to do anything onstage that you can do in a film, which led to a little violence now and then, but always with a moral dimension to it. Again, I would never want to be offensive with it. But I think they’ve been getting less and less violent. If you discount all the fingers in “Banshees,” there’s hardly any violence at all. I guess the donkey gets it, but offscreen!

“Wild Horse Nine” is a film, like “Banshees of Inisherin,” about characters who are thinking about their legacy — what they’re leaving behind and what their life will amount to. Is that a question that you think about? Oh, I knew you were going to go there. I think so. With every piece of work, you’re hoping to add to your canon of good stuff, and if you do enough of them or leave behind enough of them, that’s a route to happiness.

Why would leaving behind good work be a route to happiness? Well, you’ve got to have something. When you get a play right, it’s gone forever. It’s beautiful in the moment, but I can’t show you “The Beauty Queen of Leenane” from ’96, or “The Pillowman” from London. You put all your energy into those pieces of hopeful art and they’re gone. I think that’s probably why I’ve stuck with films lately, and why I’m happier artistically: They’re there and I can see them and I know that other people are going to be able to see them. In answer to the legacy bit of the question, it’s a pretty good thing if that’s what your role has been in the artistic world, just leaving some good films behind. I want them to be full of good acting and funny moments, and in this one a bit of truth about history that isn’t spoken about enough, and in “Banshees” a take on male friendship that’s not explored too much.

The new film is also about a male friendship. What ideas were you interested in exploring this time around? “Banshees” was the end of a loving male relationship. “Wild Horse Nine” is in the middle of a love affair, almost. I think of these two guys, Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, as this old married couple who bicker and drive each other nuts, but there’s a love that’s fundamentally there in every scene. My male friendships are quite deep and sad and open and everything that a female friendship is acknowledged to be and is seen in the culture. I like the gentleness of my male friendships, and to show a bit more of that and not just have a buddy movie is what I was trying to get at with this film.
A lot of the male friends in your work are exploring ethical dilemmas. In your own life, have you and a friend had to work through an ethical problem? I don’t think so. Have you?
Of course. I think the great ethical dilemma of my life is, if it makes sense to say, a post-mortem ethical dilemma. I’m wasting your time talking about this. I’m loving it.

My best friend from growing up died from suicide. I had no idea he was hurting that much. And then trying to think through — this was a few years ago now — What were my ethical responsibilities there? How did I fail? What was I culpable for? And then also how much blame — or not — to apportion to him for what he did. I still think about it. And do you talk about that with your male friends?
Yeah. And do they have a similar feeling?

We have pretty different feelings. One of my good friends says this was an instance of mental illness and my friend had fallen through the care cracks, as it were, and how can you blame someone for that? But probably too harshly I can think, I don’t think he was mentally ill, and my friend who died does have some responsibility for what he did. I don’t think either of us are incontrovertibly right. Yeah, but even that right there is a fascinating discussion you’ve had with your close male friends, and that’s not necessarily something you ever really see in a Hollywood movie. And that, in a very different way, is what I’ve been trying to explore from “In Bruges” (2008) up to now.

I read a collection of academic essays about your work, and at the back of one there’s a biographical timeline. It says, at age 12, “Loses his Catholic faith and begins to listen to punk rock.” What was going on when you were 12? Were those things related? They totally were. I got into the Clash particularly around that age, 12 or 13. They were such a great band to help a kid question everything. I was a working-class kid who had no future apart from a dead-end job, and I left school very young, at 16. Bands like the Clash showed you that there was another way. You didn’t have to have a life that was dictated to you. You didn’t have to work in a factory or an office. There was hope. So, yeah, I grabbed onto that with both hands at the age of 12. And the Catholic thing, I think if you’re starting to question governments and people who force you to do things against your will, which is the punk-rock ethic, naturally the Catholic Church is going to be right in the firing line.

Have you ever regained your faith? No. There are parts of it that never fully go. I’m sure my moral sense is informed by the good stuff I took from the stories of Jesus or whatever. But I’m getting more and more entrenched in some kind of antireligious feeling in general. It is one of the worst things that’s happening in the world, and it seems to be getting worse.
What aspects of your current self would the Clash-loving teenage Martin McDonagh feel most proud of? And what are the aspects that would make him think, Oh, that’s who I turned out to be? Oh, god.

If any. I don’t want to assume you’ve betrayed any youthful ideals. Weirdly, the first time I learned about Chile and Allende and Victor Jara and all the things that this film talks about was from a Clash song called “Washington Bullets” on the album “Sandinista!” And again, I was like 12 or 13 when I first heard it, didn’t know any of these people or any of those situations, and started reading up about it. Joe Strummer was a god to me, and his passion and his morality was always an inspiration, and I always wanted to do something like that. I might have done it in one or two plays, but never in the films have I had a place of anger or wanting to help, I guess. So, for the first time, Joe might be proud of this one.

And what would make the teenage version of you roll your eyes at who you’ve become? That I probably don’t do enough to help in real life. That I have made too much money from it. I don’t have too much guilt about that, because it’s not like I’m killing anyone, I’m just making a film, but that complacency in real life is not what a proper punk rocker should be.
But you can change that now. I can change that this afternoon. What should I do?

Figure out what matters to you and find out how to help. But I think that would be making another film. You can get a viewpoint across to millions of people by making a film. If that’s going to help or not, we don’t know. But I would always come back to that.

So, I think of your dialogue as being stylistically identifiable. Are there things that you know you like to do? I couldn’t put my finger on exactly what it is, but it’s always just slightly overly theatrical and heightened in some way. Pinter and Mamet had a poetic heightening of how people really speak that I thought, This is the way to go.

I can hear Pinter and Mamet in your work — the attention to rhythm, the use of vulgarity, the interplay between a sophisticated wit and low comedy. But I also see your work as coming out of Tarantino — the shocking explosions of violence. [McDonagh bristles]

Was he not an influence early on? Early on. “Pulp Fiction” was around the time I was starting to write the plays. But I don’t really see it anymore. I remember in the early interviews I did, I name-checked him a bit, but I think my stuff has changed since then. That is the only reason I bristled, because I don’t quite see it anymore. And I don’t think our approach to violence is quite the same. The coolness of cinematic violence — I’m trying to walk away from that a little bit. I don’t think Quentin might be in the same place. We talked about gratuitousness, and it’s definitely something I’m trying to stay clear of these days.

You and Phoebe Waller-Bridge have been together for a decade. You’re both private about your relationship, but I read a quote that she gave about being inspired by your play “The Pillowman.” She said: “It was the first play I saw that made me think theater can be really exciting. Sometimes you need to see something like that — a piece of work that wakes you up, that makes you go, ‘Yes, of course that can be done,’ and gives your imagination permission to go 17 million other places.” What of her work has inspired you? “Fleabag” was game-changing and eye-opening and so insightful and funny. I learned so much about that woman, and women and feminism and storytelling. And then Season 2 took it to an even more beautiful place, and I think I learned a lot about love through Season 2.
What about love? Just about how important it is, and how lovely it is when you get there.

I want to return to the punk-rock informed portion of the interview. People are talking about “Wild Horse Nine” as an awards-season contender. You’ve been fortunate enough to be in that position a couple of times in your career. What’s the punk-rock part of Martin McDonagh’s soul that’s like, “I cannot believe I’m here doing this?” What makes you blanch? I knew you were going that way with the question. I knew it! What’s a punk-rock boy like you doing at the Oscars?
No, no. It’s not that. Good for you that you’re at the Oscars. I do ask myself that question.
I’m trying to understand where that part of you manifests in the world. I can see it in the work. It’s a good question. I’m not taking the piss.

You can take the piss. I’ve done it to you. You can do it back to me. That’s true! I think the young me would never give a damn about any kind of awards-y thing because it’s all irrelevant. But once you start getting nominated, I find it fascinating. I’m always googling, “Is John Malkovich still the leading contender?” Who’s coming up? Andrew Scott’s coming up. What can we do to destroy his race? [Laughs] Not really. But because even making films is so far away from anything I’d ever thought I’d be involved in, if you double that and think that an Oscar race is something you never thought you’d be involved in, I just find it fun and enjoy it. The work is the work. I would never change what the work is to get one, or make something Oscar-baity or any of that.
I would really like to see Martin McDonagh’s version of an “Oscar bait” movie. Jesus Christ, what would that be?
“The Orphan of Inisherin.” Who’s going to play it? Timothée Chalamet!
There you go. Hang on, he doesn’t win those, though. I’ve got to get it.
By the time he does your movie, he’ll be due. It’s all about the long game. True.

But earlier when you said you should be doing more to help, you then landed on making art as what you can do. That made me think about a scene in “Wild Horse Nine” where John Malkovich’s character is talking to a young left-wing student about going on a march, and he’s so cynically sarcastic. What do you expect to accomplish going on a march? I could imagine that the Malkovich character is even more cynical about the possibility of art changing the world. In your heart, who do you think is closer to the truth, you or him? [Long pause] I think art has changed things. But I think murder has probably changed a lot more. That’s a terribly bleak answer. But I ain’t going to murder anyone, so I’ve got to keep plowing on.

I was thinking about why I feel so pessimistic about the possibilities of art and I realized that a powerful counterargument to my feelings is already in your film: Victor Jara, the Chilean activist folk singer who was targeted and killed by the Pinochet regime. If the Pinochet regime didn’t think it mattered, they probably would have left him alone. And the Pinochet regime is gone and we still have his songs, so that’s something. But in terms of art changing the world, all of the art we’ve seen or the films we’ve loved or the paintings, they have changed the world, because they’re in it. They might not have changed things politically, but this world’s better because of the poems we love and the books we love and the films that we adore. So it’s not that it’s going to affect Trump or society necessarily, but it is a new piece of beautiful art that’s out there, and I think that is always hopeful.

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/haley-stevens-.headline: Why Haley Stevens Can’t Stop Talking About Abdul El-Sayed

paragraphs.text: Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan stood up from her dining table, where the tuna fish and matzo ball soup sat half-eaten, and let loose about the moment she grew disillusioned with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed.

It happened this month, during her state’s first Senate debate between Dr. El-Sayed, who defeated her in a bitter Democratic primary in August, and former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee. Dr. El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, was asked if Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States. He dodged the question, calling it a “ridiculous hypothetical.”
This was unacceptable to Ms. Stevens.

“He’s a good speaker,” she said during the lunchtime interview on Friday at her home in Birmingham, Mich., raising her voice and rising from the table. “He’s an orator. He is gifted. Then how does that happen? Come on!”

Since the debate, Ms. Stevens has sat for a procession of cable television interviews that have been increasingly critical of Dr. El-Sayed, her endorsement of him becoming shakier by the day. Their hug at a party unity brunch in August has faded into distant memory.

On Friday, Ms. Stevens announced that she would attend a Sunday church service in Detroit with Dr. El-Sayed, a peace offering brokered by Representatives Debbie Dingell of Michigan and James E. Clyburn of South Carolina. But Ms. Stevens’s statement came with a caveat: a demand that Dr. El-Sayed publicly disavow an ad that one of his allies posted online. She called the ad antisemitic because it blamed U.S. support for Israel for high grocery prices.
On Friday, Dr. El-Sayed pushed back.
In a blistering statement, he offered a reminder that he beat her in August and an assertion that “Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
Whether their planned joint appearance on Sunday will go ahead seems up in the air.

Ms. Stevens said late Friday that she was not sure if the church event was still happening, or even if she was still invited. She said that no one from Dr. El-Sayed’s team had called her on Friday. She also said she had not retracted her endorsement of him and did not plan to.
“I haven’t had time to digest this,” she said. She added, “I don’t think this is a melodrama.”

Some other Michigan Democrats have been baffled by Ms. Stevens’s unsupportive media tour in the final days of the campaign, with Dr. El-Sayed serving as a key chess piece in the party’s push to take back the Senate. Polls show Dr. El-Sayed in a close race with Mr. Rogers. To win the chamber, Democrats need to retain Democratic-held Senate seats like Michigan’s and flip at least four states held by Republicans.

“I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who also ran for the U.S. Senate in Michigan and dropped out a month before the primary, said on CNN on Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.”
Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to discuss Ms. Stevens’s commentary.
Ms. Stevens’s growing criticism of Dr. El-Sayed serves as a stark sign of just how fiercely resistant some moderate Democrats and Jewish voters remain to his candidacy.

Several times in the interviews, she returned to her anger over the online ad, made by Rebellion PAC, a left-wing group that backed Dr. El-Sayed, and his refusal to publicly disavow it. The El-Sayed campaign has said it did not make and is not responsible for the ad.

“Maybe it’s how you fund-raise, maybe it is what you want people to believe, but the reality is that we are not going to say that the cost of groceries is because of Jews and the Jewish state,” Ms. Stevens said. “We’re not going to say we don’t have health care because of Jews and the Jewish state.”

Ms. Stevens is not Jewish but has always been a pro-Israel Democrat. She attended a Jewish sleep-away camp as a teenager and now represents suburban Oakland County, which is home to a large segment of Michigan’s Jewish population. Tensions over Israel dominated her primary with Dr. El-Sayed, when the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s main super PAC spent at least $30 million backing her campaign.
She also now has a partner who may feel even more strongly about the issue than she does.

Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, a Jewish lawyer who has raised money for both Democrats and Republicans, has gone even further than she has in criticizing Dr. El-Sayed. He publicly endorsed Mr. Rogers and appeared at a campaign event with him on Wednesday.
Ms. Stevens said that in anticipation of her wedding next summer to Mr. Turkish, she had met with a rabbi to discuss the possibility of converting to Judaism.

Over lunch and in two subsequent phone calls, including one with both her and Mr. Turkish, Ms. Stevens said she felt compelled to speak out for Jewish constituents who are scared of the prospect of Dr. El-Sayed in the Senate.

“There’s people who are hurt and worried about a bunch of different things,” she said. “They’re making sacrifices because of affordability. Someone in the Jewish community said, — six months ago, it was during the primary — safety is our affordability issue because of attacks on Jewish elected officials’ homes, attacks to their lives, attacks on the synagogues.”

Ms. Stevens repeated her assertion that she supported all Democrats running, including Dr. El-Sayed, and that she planned to vote for him. But asked if she wanted him to win, she was more circumspect.
“I think he’s going to win,” she replied.
Asked again if she wanted Dr. El-Sayed win, she dodged again.
“I don’t know why you’d ask me that,” she said.
Pressed one more time about her public criticism of Dr. El-Sayed, she offered a little more.

“I ran for a Democratic nomination, intent in understanding that I wanted a Democrat to win,” she said. “We sat down for a long period of time, Abdul and I did, in the first quarter of ’25, before we both decided to run, making that commitment to each other, so of course.”
It was not a ringing endorsement.
But while Mr. Rogers has welcomed Ms. Stevens’s supporters, she said he had not called her.
Then there is the matter of Mr. Turkish.

Even as Ms. Stevens had lunch with a New York Times reporter, Mr. Turkish was sitting for his own interview live with TMZ. He said Ms. Stevens would pull her support from Dr. El-Sayed if he did not soon disavow the grocery prices ad.
“I don’t think she’s going to be supporting Abdul El-Sayed very much longer,” Mr. Turkish told TMZ.
After his comments aired, Ms. Stevens invited the Times reporter to call her back, and this time she had Mr. Turkish on the line.
She said that her fiancé had not caused her to change her positions on Israel or Dr. El-Sayed.
“I think I’ve changed his opinion,” she said. “He goes, ‘You’re more Jewish than me.’”

In the interview, Mr. Turkish said he had expected Dr. El-Sayed to “move to the middle” on Israel after the primary. He called Dr. El-Sayed’s response to the debate question about Iran and Israel “the tipping point for me” and declared that his own safety would be in jeopardy if Dr. El-Sayed were elected to the Senate.

“I think I’d be less safe on this planet if Abdul El-Sayed is the senator, if he is insisting on sticking to the current program,” Mr. Turkish said. “He is so unwelcoming to people who have reasonable anxieties about Jews being scapegoated once again, as they have been for thousands of years, that the idea that he will steer not just U.S. policy, but foreign policy globally, it makes me extremely, extremely anxious.”
Mr. Turkish said he believed Ms. Stevens, 43, still had a bright future in politics.
“I know there’s going to be other opportunities,” he said. “I think she can run for the United States Senate again if she wants to.”
Though he is a veteran fund-raiser and an accomplished lawyer, Mr. Turkish had not been a sought-after political surrogate. His endorsement had never made news before now.

But he said he felt compelled to make a public endorsement for Mr. Rogers and appear with him at a campaign event because he did not want his public image to be a late-night TV sendup of him and Ms. Stevens.
“My friends and family members are asking me what I’m doing,” Mr. Turkish said. “I think they wanted to hear more from me than what they got off of two spoofed appearances on ‘The Tonight Show.’”

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/world/middleeast/.headline: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections

paragraphs.text: Little is clear about the power dynamics that will govern Israel and the United States in the coming months after pivotal elections in both countries. But Iran’s leaders are watching the contests closely, analysts said, and bracing for a renewed round of conflict whatever the outcome.

In Israel, this week’s national elections showed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right alliance nor the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, the country’s former top military official, won enough votes to form a government. That has set the stage for weeks of uncertainty.

In the United States, Democrats appear to be in a strong position to at least take control of the House in the midterm elections next week. But the exact size of their win, and whether they secure a majority in the Senate, will determine if they can actually put a brake on President Trump’s policies, including the war with Iran.
Tehran expects more attacks whoever takes control in Israel or of Congress, and has shown little willingness to make concessions demanded by the Trump administration to seal a peace deal.

“They have been expecting a new round of war already for a few weeks, and they’ve been preparing accordingly,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said of the Iranian government.

In Israel, Iran would welcome the removal of Mr. Netanyahu from power, said Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies in Tehran. The Israeli leader helped persuade Mr. Trump to attack Iran this year and sought to orchestrate new airstrikes on Iran ahead of the election. But Iranian leaders believe that changing prime ministers would probably have an impact only in the short term rather than leading to a fundamental shift in Israeli policy, Mr. Sedghian said.

“Iranian and Israeli policies toward each other have remained consistent regardless of which government has been in power in Israel since the 1980s,” he said. “Any changes would likely be temporary rather than strategic.”
Mr. Azizi said there were several scenarios for how the Israeli election results could unfold, but that “we should not expect a fundamental change in the hostility between Israel and Iran.”
Even if Mr. Eisenkot or another opposition leader takes power and shifts Israel back into deploying covert tactics against Iran rather than all-out war, Iran’s response could still be escalatory.

“The Islamic Republic’s strategic thinking has undergone a significant shift, involving, first and foremost, a greater willingness to take risks and a move away from its long-established policy of strategic patience,” Mr. Azizi said. “As a result, Iran could still respond to indirect Israeli operations through direct military action.”

When it comes to the United States, Iran’s leaders are keenly aware of how the costs of the war, including higher gasoline prices for Americans, have affected Mr. Trump’s popularity and the Republican Party’s prospects in the midterms. Their assessment appears to be that a deal with Iran would benefit Mr. Trump politically, giving Tehran leverage in any negotiations to end the war. Iran, on the other hand, has already borne enormous costs including spiraling inflation, without its leaders changing their stance.

Mostafa Najafi, an analyst who is said to be close to Mr. Rezaei, wrote on social media on Wednesday that the Trump administration was pursuing a deal with Iran in the days leading up to the midterms as Republicans face a difficult fight to retain control of Congress.

“They want to leverage the agreement for the elections and insist that nuclear concessions also be part of the pre-election deal, which Tehran does not accept,” Mr. Najafi wrote. “If no agreement is reached in the next two days, the atmosphere will likely shift toward confrontation in the first week after the elections.”

Last week, Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to a top Iranian official to propose a new round of comprehensive peace talks, a senior U.S. official and an Iranian official with knowledge of the communication have said. Mr. Vance bypassed Iran’s elected government and President Masoud Pezeshkian and instead addressed the letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the top national security adviser and the former longtime commander of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. The outreach to Mr. Rezaei reflected the Trump administration’s view that it needs to deal directly with an Iranian official with influence over hard-liners, who have opposed agreeing to a deal.
On Friday, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran for talks, Iran’s state news outlet reported. Qatar has been mediating discussions between Iran and the United States.

The burst of recent diplomacy comes at a significant moment. Mr. Trump has been weighing whether to renew attacks on Iran, potentially after the midterms, and the United States and Israel have drawn up specific plans for new strikes, U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations have said. But there are major obstacles that would need to be overcome for the United States and Iran to reach a final agreement.

“The two sides remain far apart on several critical issues, including the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief, oversight by the International Atomic Energy Agency and the scope of Iran’s nuclear commitments,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, an Iran expert at Missouri University of Science and Technology. “My sense is that Tehran will pursue a dual-track strategy, engaging in intermittent diplomatic negotiations while simultaneously preparing, to the best of its ability, for a possible resumption of hostilities.”

Mr. Najafi, in his social media post on Wednesday, said that Iran “insists on the fulfillment of its seven conditions” before agreeing to any interim deal. Iranian officials have referred frequently to the conditions in the past month without fully explaining what they are, and framed them as a prerequisite for new talks or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping waterway on Iran’s southern coast.

Mr. Najafi said in a voice message to The New York Times that the conditions included lifting the U.S. naval blockade on Iran and sanctions on Iran’s oil sales; ending the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group; releasing frozen Iranian assets; and accepting Iran’s management of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Iran has put forth these to the American side as preconditions for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Mr. Najafi said. “The American side must first fulfill these preconditions, and then the negotiations will enter the main phase.”
Mr. Najafi also expressed deep pessimism about the prospects of a lasting agreement between the two sides, saying that Iranian officials have no trust in American intentions or promises.

“Here, the messages exchanged with the United States are viewed with profound skepticism,” he said. “The issue of Iran-U.S. relations has become so complex that even if Iran were to agree to nuclear negotiations and make concessions, it is highly unlikely that this tangled web of conflict between the two nations will reach a meaningful resolution or result in a lasting agreement.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/talar.headline: Talarico Makes Final Election Pitch to Texans: ‘You Are My Slingshot’

paragraphs.text: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, invoked the mythological grandness of his native state when he told a crowd in El Paso this week, “Our musicians are so iconic, they only need one name: Willie. Beyoncé. Selena.”
Improbable as it might seem, the once-obscure 37-year-old state representative and former middle-school teacher with the choirboy face has entered an elite pantheon himself.

A little more than a year after Mr. Talarico began his candidacy, he has become a marquee political persona, and not just in Texas. His race, which could become the most expensive in the history of nonpresidential campaigns, may well decide which party controls the Senate.

The Democratic candidate’s celebrity has thrown Republicans into a panic, prompting the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to donate an unheard-of $158 million to groups that support Mr. Talarico’s G.O.P. opponent and the state attorney general, Ken Paxton.

A smooth orator and prolific fund-raiser, Mr. Talarico has cast his upstart campaign in biblical terms. He is David, the corrupt political system exemplified by Mr. Paxton is Goliath and in whatever city he happens to be in, he declares, “You are my slingshot.” He has run a largely mistake-free campaign, although the flu took him off the trail for nine days.

He has consistently drawn overflow crowds, many of whom wear T-shirts declaring themselves to be “Talafreakos,” first deployed by Mr. Paxton as a term of derision. Last Tuesday, an estimated 4,000 people turned out in Lubbock — an extraordinary number for a Democrat in the ruby-red city — while Mr. Paxton was campaigning with President Trump less than three miles down the road.
In Texas, these count as remarkable feats for a Democrat. But because it is Texas, such accomplishments may still not be enough for victory.

“I think James has at most a 50 percent chance of winning,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party. “Which, look, in Texas, that’s phenomenal. If you told me a year ago a Democrat would have a coin-flip chance of winning, I’d be doing backflips.”

People close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign privately echoed Mr. Warford’s assessment of the race. A New York Times/Siena University poll in September and a CNN/SSRS poll conducted Oct. 20 to 27 showed Mr. Talarico ahead by 6 percentage points, but other recent public surveys show him either tied with Mr. Paxton or within the margin of error with a 2-point lead. The candidate’s internal polls match those tighter surveys, people close to Mr. Talarico said, and may not be fully capturing the sentiments of rural conservative voters who support Mr. Trump.

There is plentiful evidence the race could go either way. During the homestretch of Mr. Talarico’s campaign, from deep-blue regions (San Antonio, Laredo, the Rio Grande Valley and El Paso) to steadfastly Republican terrain (Midland and Lubbock), Mr. Talarico’s bursting-to-capacity crowds made it possible to imagine that he could flip a statewide race for the first time in decades. Just as ubiquitous were signs his efforts could fall short.

A major obstacle facing Mr. Talarico is the avalanche of attack ads funded by Mr. Musk, in which the candidate is portrayed as a far-left extremist. At a stop one afternoon at the Bexar County Democratic Party headquarters in San Antonio, Mr. Talarico assured volunteers that their door-knocking work would surmount Mr. Musk’s efforts, saying, “The political science is very clear: TV ads don’t make much of a difference.”

But three days later, one of Mr. Talarico’s supporters who attended the Lubbock event, Rebecca Murrow, begged to differ when a reporter asked whether the attack ads were having an impact among people she knew. “Oh, you better believe they are,” she said.
A friend standing next to her, Luke Anderson, concurred, citing his mother as one example of a person who could not bring herself to support Mr. Talarico after viewing the ads.
Still, Ms. Morrow added, “It makes me proud to be supporting someone who’s trying to change their minds, no matter how hard it is.”
‘One of Y’all’

Mr. Talarico’s barnstorming tour, “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts,” is named after part of the motto of the film and TV series “Friday Night Lights,” about Texas high school football. The candidate frequently recites the lyrics of Lyle Lovett, the Texas singer-songwriter. His omnipresent footwear is not-too-shiny Lucchese cowboy boots, primarily made in El Paso. In short, Mr. Talarico has made one thing abundantly clear in every campaign appearance: He really wants you to know that he’s a Texan.

Flashing his Lone Star credentials as an eighth-generation native son is a tacit acknowledgment that the pale and slightly built pastor-in-training does not personify the Texas swagger the way the state’s political titans of yesteryear did, among them former Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson and George W. Bush and former Govs. Ann Richards and Rick Perry. (As it happens, Mr. Paxton was born in North Dakota and spent some of his youth in California, though his party does not seem to hold that against him.)

The “I’m one of y’all” references also constitute a self-normalizing effort to make up for what Mr. Talarico now terms “cringey” remarks he uttered several years ago about God being “nonbinary” and his belief that there are six biological sexes.

While those earlier statements live on in attack ads, Mr. Talarico has provided little in the way of new material for his opponent’s ad makers. He is self-disciplined, stays on script and comes off as more the seminary student he once was than the kind of fire-breathing populist fashionable in the Trump era. He wears the same youthful, Texas business casual uniform every day: a tailored blazer, a crisp white dress shirt, jeans and those cowboy boots.

Although he talks to the local media, of late he has declined all interviews with the national press, including The New York Times, on the grounds that those engagements are less likely to win votes. He travels aboard his “Talarico for Texas” R.V. with a small inner circle of young aides rather than outside political consultants. At events, his volunteers distribute signs that have his name on one side and “Love Thy Neighbor” on the other.

Projecting himself as a conciliator has helped win support from more than two dozen current or former state Republican officeholders, not to mention two relatives of Mr. Bush: his brother Neil and his daughter Barbara. A source close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign confirmed that members of the family had reached out and that the candidate has been in touch with them. That said, the Bush name no longer means what it used to in Texas, and it remains to be seen if Mr. Talarico’s throwback appeal for a kinder, gentler political culture can prevail amid a pugilistic zeitgeist.
In Hostile Territory

Mr. Talarico’s trip to Lubbock pointed to the subtext of his campaign. No matter what the polls say, in Texas the underdog is by nature the Democrat. Mr. Talarico does not have the luxury of focusing his efforts on the deep-blue urban areas of the state. He is obliged to find votes everywhere he can, even in hostile territory.

In both Midland and Lubbock, Mr. Talarico’s advance staff had to scramble to find bigger places that would accommodate his crowds, then made sure to post those images on social media. Talafreakos living outside Texas contrasted what they saw with Mr. Paxton’s lackluster gatherings and asked the inevitable question: With these crowds, how can we possibly lose?

Few if any of the roughly 600 Midland Democrats standing in line for Mr. Talarico’s event suffered any such illusions. “Our Talarico lawn sign is the only one for blocks around,” said Linda Jordan, 78, a Democrat. “The neighbors don’t talk to us much.”

Tamara, a 43-year-old Midland Democrat who declined to give her last name, said of her neighbors that “there’s no changing their minds” and that her energies were instead focused on persuading her husband to vote for Mr. Talarico. She suspected, she said, that he had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, though “he still won’t tell me.”

Mr. Talarico’s allies acknowledge that for him to win, he will need to maximize turnout in Latino-heavy communities. But Democratic Party officials said in interviews that while knocking on doors in both San Antonio and El Paso, they encountered abiding loyalty to Mr. Trump and an aversion to Mr. Talarico, particularly among Latino men. In downtown Lubbock this week, a long line of the president’s supporters waiting to get into a Trump rally included numerous Latino men, many of them wearing “Make America Great Again” caps.
Mr. Talarico’s surrogates are now couching their sense of urgency about the Latino vote in comic appeals.

In San Antonio, the actress Eva Longoria exclaimed: “Tell everyone! Tell your ex-boyfriend!” In El Paso, the city’s congresswoman, Veronica Escobar, beseeched a group of volunteer canvassers, “By all means, harass your family and your friends.”

In the end, people close to Mr. Talarico acknowledge that though Mr. Trump’s popularity has waned in Texas over the past two years, enough of his supporters remain to determine the outcome in Mr. Paxton’s favor, assuming they choose to back him.

In a last-ditch effort to split Republican loyalties, the Talarico campaign recently authorized the state party to send out mailers featuring a quote from a Texas woman: “I voted for Trump, but I cannot vote for Ken Paxton.”

Standing in line while awaiting Mr. Talarico’s arrival in Midland, Javier Soto, 59, said his father was among the many Texans who had supported Mr. Trump throughout the years. “But he says it’s time for a change,” Mr. Soto said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/trump.headline: Trump and GOP Close Midterms With Ugly Personal Attacks

paragraphs.text: In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a vulnerable Republican, baselessly said his Democratic opponent “probably is grooming” children.

In Texas, Republicans have cast James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, as a “freak” and insinuated he is gay, secretly a vegan, and obsessed with transgender children because he made statements supporting them in the past.
And in Michigan, Republicans have targeted the Democratic Senate nominee, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, with Islamophobic attacks. Mr. Trump has described Dr. El-Sayed as a “vicious, violent jihadist.”

Facing a backlash over rising prices and working to overcome the president’s deep unpopularity, Republicans across the country have tarred their opponents with false, inflammatory and deeply personal attacks in the final stretch of the midterm election.

In many cases, they are following the lead of a president who has repeatedly rewritten the rules of acceptable discourse in American politics. Many of the attacks have drawn little pushback from within the party, but some Republicans say they are concerned by the trend.

“It’s awful,” said former Senator Jeff Flake, an Arizona Republican and critic of Mr. Trump. Mr. Flake, who is backing candidates in both parties in the midterms, said Republicans had gone down a darker road in their messaging: “We’ve gotten progressively more crass and crude and vulgar. But this seems to be a new level.”

The strategy risks turning off some moderate voters who see the rhetoric as over-the-top or offensive, political observers said. But it could be effective at energizing the Republican base. Democrats, who have widely condemned the Republicans’ attacks, worry the lines will land with some voters.

Democrats themselves have at times used strikingly personal attacks, often accusing Republicans of corruption. And some Democrats have imitated the president’s crude approach: Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, for example, made social-media posts this year suggesting that various conservatives were gay.
But in the midterms the Republican attacks stand out for their viciousness.

American political campaigns have long been awash in negative and dubious attacks by both parties — in debate lines, TV commercials and stump speeches — but this bitter, hard-fought cycle may set a new standard. Some political scientists said this election season had devolved into the most negative, dark campaign in modern American history.

“I think it’s the worst,” said Christina Greer, a political science professor at Fordham University. She attributed the tone to candidates’ desire to package their message for social media, and to Republicans’ mirroring of Mr. Trump: “He’s opened a portal to the degradation of our electoral system.”

In Texas, Vice President JD Vance suggested at a rally that Mr. Talarico was gay, drawing gasps from the crowd. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Mr. Vance added, referring to Mr. Talarico’s past statements in support of transgender youth.
Mr. Talarico has a girlfriend. The attack was part of a broad effort by Republicans to portray Mr. Talarico as extreme. Mr. Trump has taken to referring to Mr. Talarico as “Talafreako.”

A spokeswoman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee suggested that Democrats had brought the attacks upon themselves. In a statement, the spokeswoman, Bernadette Breslin, claimed that Dr. El-Sayed had “pledged support” for a terrorist regime and said that “if Talarico didn’t want to be called anti-meat, he shouldn’t have announced his campaign would go vegan.”
Dr. El-Sayed has said he is loyal to the U.S. Constitution. Mr. Talarico has said he is not a vegan and that his campaign “basically” runs on barbecue.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Flake said the coarseness of some Republican attacks stemmed from a mix of desperation in the party and a mimicking of Mr. Trump. But he said he found a “silver lining” in the backlash some of Mr. Trump’s “imitators” had experienced — including in Republican criticism of a headline-grabbing attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race.

That ad came from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor. The commercial featured the mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, who says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling,” even as Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance defended it.
Former President Barack Obama, appearing at a rally in Ohio this month, said he was baffled that “the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a Republican who built a brand on civility, denounced a radio ad from the top super PAC for Senate Republicans that cast her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, as a “freak” for having two children with his second cousin. Ms. Collins called for the ad to be taken down.

But Ms. Collins, who has deplored Mr. Jackson’s efforts to cast her as corrupt, herself commented on Mr. Jackson’s family in the summer, telling Politico: “I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin.”

Other Republican attacks have gone largely unchallenged inside the party. After Mr. Marshall suggested his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, was a “groomer” of children, there was no significant Republican criticism. And there was no Republican uproar after Mr. Trump used an anti-trans slur to refer to the Democratic Senate nominee in South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews, calling her “Tranny Annie.” (Dr. Andrews is not transgender.)

A spokesman for Mr. Hamilton, Tyson Brody, said in a statement that Mr. Marshall was “resorting to increasingly unhinged and inexplicable smears.” Dr. Andrews released an ad this month in which she said she did not support transgender women playing in women’s sports or gender transition surgeries for minors. (In 2022 she had spoken out against a trans sports ban in South Carolina.)
On the campaign trail in Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate, has often brought supporters who have questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to America.

At a Rogers rally in Plainwell, Mich., on Thursday, Senator Tim Sheehy, Republican of Montana, told the crowd, “You better be afraid,” suggesting that supporting Dr. El-Sayed would be a step toward Shariah law in Michigan. “We have a radical Islamist on the other side of this ticket who hates this country.”
Asked later about Mr. Sheehy’s comments, Mr. Rogers told reporters, “You haven’t heard me say any of those things.”
Dr. El-Sayed said at a rally on Sunday that Mr. Rogers’s “whole campaign is to point at me and my name and my faith.”
“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Islamophobic attacks have long been a feature of American politics. But in the past, candidates in both parties sought to push back. In 2008, the Republican nominee for president, Senator John McCain, defended his opponent, Barack Obama, when a woman at a rally said she did not trust him because “he’s an Arab.” Mr. McCain replied, “No, ma’am, he’s a decent family man.”
This year, Democrats say they fear that Islamophobic attacks on Dr. El-Sayed have resonated with some voters and are hurting his chances in a race that is critical in the battle for Senate control.

“I won’t say it’s the worst and most horrific ever,” Mike McGuinness, the Democratic mayor of Pontiac, Mich., said of the Republican attacks on Dr. El-Sayed’s faith and background. “But it is definitely a Hall of Fame contender.”
The Rev. Horace Sheffield III of New Destiny Christian Fellowship in Detroit said the rhetoric in the campaign felt to him as if it came from long ago in American history.

“This tenor and tone that we find ourselves in now is very dangerous,” said Mr. Sheffield, who supports Dr. El-Sayed and whose daughter is Mayor Mary Sheffield of Detroit. “And it’s all based on prejudice.”

Cayce Myers, a professor of political communication at Virginia Tech who studies negative ads, said the race in Michigan was a “test case” for how inflammatory a message could be and still help, rather than hurt, a candidate in 2026.

Negative ads typically are the most motivating, he said, and Republicans in Michigan and elsewhere appeared to be betting that their approach would help activate base voters more than it would alienate voters in the middle.
But, Professor Myers added, Republicans are “pushing up against the limit of what voters and the electorate have an appetite for.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/business/beef-pri.headline: Pick Another Protein? Americans Still Want Beef, Despite the Price.
