parameter.ai/labs/we-found-a-gap-at-open.headline: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
parameter.ai/labs/we-found-a-gap-at-open.author: Mukul Goyal

paragraphs.text: In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.
The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.
OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.
The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.
Technical walkthrough
It started with a graph and a Preview
The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.
At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.
That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.
The message that should not have worked
The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.
This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run.
The next step was an iframe using srcdoc, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.
Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:
The response began like this:

Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.
Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.
We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.
The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:
• A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page.
• A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.

The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.
An alert was not enough

At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:
GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2

This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.
Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.
What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed
The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.
Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:
• MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
• The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
• That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity.

The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.
The defensive lessons are fairly simple:
• A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission.
• Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML.
• Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame.
• CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.

This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.
Timeline
Technical notes
The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.
The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:
Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:

createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

The parser and CSP transition. The innerHTML operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed srcdoc caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted www.youtube.com in script-src-elem.

The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with ;void consumed the error object appended by the endpoint.

For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with toString(), double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. URLSearchParams then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside <script src>, and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's srcdoc attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters.

The authenticated read. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers:
Authorization: Bearer <victim token> ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account> Accept: application/json
The primary requests were:

GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true

Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers.
Key takeaways
• Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender.
• postMessage receivers must authenticate both event.origin and event.source before accepting state-changing instructions.

• HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe.

• The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as chatgpt.com, it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert.
• Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone.

The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/berkshire-ekes-out-s.headline: Berkshire ekes out some new highs, but October rally stalls
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/berkshire-ekes-out-s.author: Alex Crippen

paragraphs.text: (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire ekes out some new highs, but October rally stalls
Berkshire Hathaway shares managed to set a few more all-time highs in an otherwise lackluster week of trading.
The Class A stock closed Monday at a record high $821,931 but ended the week up just 0.3% at $815,600.

It spiked at Friday's open to almost $822,929, but that wasn't enough to top its record intraday high of $824,765 set on Thursday of last week as Berkshire entirely erased what turned into a 15% pullback after Warren Buffett announced last year that he would step down as the company's CEO.
The more widely held Class B shares also set a new record high close on Monday, finishing that day at $548.56.
But their high during Friday's session of $550.47 is enough for a new all-time intraday record, edging out last Thursday's $549.96.
For the week, however, they inched less than 0.1% higher.
Despite losing some steam this week, Berkshire shares are ending October with strong gains, especially when compared to the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite.
The latter index lost 2.9% Friday, its worst one-day drop since June, as money moves away from high-flying AI and tech stocks over spending concerns.
Berkshire appears to be benefiting from the back-to-basics rotation.
It's closing out the month with an 8.9% gain, as the S&P fell 0.9% and the Nasdaq dropped 5.3%.
BRK.B trimmed its year-to-date deficit against the benchmark S&P from 3.5 percentage points last week to 2.8 percentage points this week.
As shown in the "Berkshire Stock Watch" chart below, it's ahead of the S&P over the past 12 calendar months by more than two percentage points.
AI jitters cut Berkshire's bet on Alphabet by billions
While Berkshire's stock is benefiting from Wall Street's move away from AI stocks, one big holding in its equity portfolio is taking a substantial hit.
Google parent Alphabet's market value fell by around $500 billion Thursday as the stock plunged almost 13%, its worst day since going public in 2004.

The company's third quarter earnings report late Wednesday included negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, more than triple the $2.7 billion analysts had expected, raising concerns among investors about the enormous cost of building out AI infrastructure.
At the same time, revenue from web searches missed estimates for the second straight quarter, in what CNBC.com is calling the "first real sign AI is taking a bite" out of Alphabet's core business.
Berkshire's enormous Alphabet stake, initiated by Buffett last year and boosted by a $10 billion private placement during this year's second quarter, hit a Q3 high of $40 billion in early August.
Since then, it's lost a quarter of its value, falling to $29.6 billion Friday, making it Berkshire's fourth largest equity holding.
(That's based on the number of shares held as of June 30. The values in October may change based on Berkshire's September 30 portfolio snapshot that will be released in two weeks.)
Coca-Cola has moved decisively into third place, with the position increasing by almost 16% from a low of $32.5 billion in late July to $37.6 billion now.
Barron's estimates Berkshire likely paid more than $300 a share for Alphabet, and "perhaps close to $320," putting it in the red for the investment, at least so far.
DaVita holding trimmed again under deal to keep percentage stake steady
In an SEC disclosure this week, Berkshire said it sold $69 million of DaVita shares on Tuesday.
The remaining 28.3 million shares of the dialysis provider in its portfolio are worth $5.3 billion.
Don't interpret the reduction as sign Berkshire has changed its view of the company.
This is the latest in a series of quarterly share reductions under a 2024 agreement with DaVita in which Berkshire agreed to keep its stake in the company at 45% or lower.
As DaVita reduces its outstanding shares through buybacks, Berkshire needs to also cut its holdings to keep the ratio intact.
DaVita shares are up 65% year-to-date despite a one-week drop of more than 23% in August when the company released disappointing earnings just days before Berkshire's previous trim under the pact.
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
• Business Wire news release: Berkshire Hathaway completes further $330 million investment in Bending Spoons (The planned investment was initially announced last week)
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Robinhood takes advantage of 'gambling instincts' (2021)
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the popular Robinhood trading app, accusing it of encouraging its customers to make short-term bets on stocks and options. Munger calls it "deeply wrong."
BECKY QUICK: This question comes from Robert Miles in Nebraska.
"The trading apps. What do you think about Robinhood and other trading apps, or fintech companies, enabling all ages and experience to participate in the stock market?"
WARREN BUFFETT: (Laughs) Well, I'm looking forward to reading the S-1 on Robin — that's the big thing you file with the SEC when you're going to be offering securities, and —
It's — you know, it's become a very significant part of the casino aspect — of the casino group — that has joined into the stock market in the last year or year and a half.

And I do want to say I'm concerned of how they handle the source of income when they say they don't charge the customer anything. I mean, you know, I'm — it'll just be interesting to watch how they describe it. I mean, but —
But they — they have attracted — maybe set out to attract — but they have attracted, I think I read where 12 or 13% of their casino participants were dealing in (option) puts and calls.

I looked up on Apple, you know, the number of seven-day calls and 14-day calls outstanding. And I'm sure a lot of that is coming through Robinhood. And that's a bunch of people writing — they're gambling on the price of Apple over the next seven days or 14.
There's nothing, you know — there's nothing illegal about it. There's nothing immoral.

But — I don't think you'd build a society around people doing it. I mean, if a group of — a group of us landed on a desert island, and we knew we would never be rescued, and I was one of the group, and I said, well, I'll set up the exchange over here. (Laughs) And I'll trade our corn futures and everything around —

I think — I think the degree to which a very rich society can reward people who know how to take advantage, essentially, of the gambling instincts of the — not only the American public — worldwide public — it's, you know, it's not the most admirable part of the accomplishment.
But I think what America's accomplished is pretty admirable overall. (Laughs)
And I think actually, you know, American corporations have turned out to be a wonderful place for people to put their money and save. But they also make terrific gambling chips.

And if you cater to those gambling chips when people have money in their pocket for the first time, and you tell them they can make 30 or 40 or 50 trades a day, and you're not charging them any commission, but you're selling your order flow or whatever, it —
I hope we don't have more of it, I'll put it that way. And I will be interested in reading the prospectus.
Charlie?
CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, that is really waving the red flag at the bull. (Laughter)
I think it's just God-awful that something like that would draw investment from civilized men and decent citizens. It's deeply wrong.
We don't want to make our money selling things that are bad for people.
WARREN BUFFETT: But we've got the states doing it with the lottery, you know.
CHARLIE MUNGER: No, but that's bad, too.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, I know. I understand, but I'm saying —
CHARLIE MUNGER: That's very bad. That's very bad —
WARREN BUFFETT: Once you —
CHARLIE MUNGER: That's one of the things that's wrong with it. It's getting respectable to do these things.
The states are just as bad as Robinhood.
WARREN BUFFETT: Well, in a sense they're worse. I mean, they're really taxing the —
CHARLIE MUNGER: I know it's — I know, I know.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. They're taxing hope.
CHARLIE MUNGER: Not only that —
WARREN BUFFETT: And they don't get much in the way of taxes from me and Charlie than they do —
CHARLIE MUNGER: The states in America replaced the Mafia as the proprietor of the numbers game. That's what happened.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yep.
CHARLIE MUNGER: They pushed the Mafia aside and said that's our business, not yours. Doesn't make me proud of my government.
WARREN BUFFETT: When I was a kid, my dad (Howard Buffett) was in Congress. They had a numbers runner in the House office building (laughs), actually.

thebignewsletter.com/p/why-anthropics-fi.headline: Why Anthropic’s Filing Crushed Tech Stocks
thebignewsletter.com/p/why-anthropics-fi.author: Matt Stoller

paragraphs.text: The past month has seen some signs in the financial markets that the AI bubble is beginning to deflate. First it was the neoclouds, which are off-balance sheet entities for large tech and chip companies, getting crushed. Then on Monday, AI giant Anthropic made public its initial draft S-1 filing, the form it has to submit before it sells shares on the stock market. Then, a few days later, Google and Amazon released their earnings, disappointing investors with misses in revenue targets and higher than expected negative free cash flow. Google stock alone fell by 12% on Thursday, a half a trillion dollar collapse. The next day, the whole tech sector got crushed, and it now down 10% from its high.
Wall Street, it seems, is worried.

Whatever one might say about AI, whether it’s a bubble or not, right now, the traditionally profitable big tech firms are consuming large quantities of capital from investors. Last year, for instance, Anthropic lost $80 billion, and Amazon had negative $42 billion free cash flow. The entire big tech complex, it seems, has moved from minting cash to burning it. And investors are, well, not panicking exactly, but wondering if the bubble is ending.

I’ve spent some time going over it, and while the document is suspiciously missing key financial details, there’s enough there to understand a lot about this company and this industry. There’s something unusual about Anthropic’s filing, and big tech earnings in general, that has important policy implications. Unlike nearly any other initial public offering I can think of, large chunks of Anthropic are owned or controlled by its rivals or suppliers: Amazon, Google, Broadcom, and Microsoft. Indeed, I have read a bunch of S-1’s, I have never seen one discuss how dependent the company doing an IPO is on other large firms. These dependencies explain why the entire tech complex is now rising and falling together, as if it’s one interconnected entity. Because in some ways, it now is.

Anthropic itself notes this dynamic under one of the risks listed in the IPO about managing conflicts of interest. Anthropic’s relationships with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, it says, “create potential conflicts of interest that are difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate.” These “strategic partners,” the company notes, serve as “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors,” while chipmaker Broadcom “simultaneously serves as a supplier and lessor.” In essence, Anthropic looks less like a stand-alone business and more like four monopolies in a trench coat.

One way to visualize the dynamic is to look at how many third party companies are noted in the S-1. In a normal S-1, no other company would get more than a dozen mentions, if that. An IPO document would discuss the bankers for the deal, competitors, comparable firms, major creditors or partners, and the companies for which the executives used to work. An individual company that isn’t the company going public might be discussed a few times, if it is the main competitor.

But Anthropic’s document is just different. I created a table that lists how many times Anthropic mentions third party firms. Amazon has more than one hundred and fifty citations, and Google has over a hundred. Broadcom and Microsoft also have more than a dozen. All are trillion dollar plus firms, and all have deep relationships with this trillion dollar plus Anthropic IPO.

I wanted to see a contrast, so I looked at comparable S-1 documents for Google in 2004 and Amazon in 1995. They are nothing like Anthropic’s, they are much simpler and describe a comprehensible stand-alone business. The top mention for Google for instance, was Silicon Graphics, at just sixteen times. Why? The two had a technology licensing agreement. Yahoo got thirteen mentions, and Microsoft had twelve, all of which were in the context of them having rival search products. Similarly, Amazon in its 1995 S-1 mentioned Coast Wide Supply, a company from whom it leased warehouses, twenty eight times. These are simple relationships.

Why does Anthropic discuss other companies so much in its S-1? Maybe it’s nothing. Mentions in the IPO don’t necessarily prove anything. But as I noted, that was just one way to visualize the dynamic. The reason these companies are mentioned many times is because the relationships are complex. Consider:
• Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are the main distributors for Anthropic, selling roughly 50% of the company’s products, including Claude for Microsoft 365 and Claude in Chrome.

• Amazon, Google, and Microsoft own large chunks of the company and are significant lenders to it. Google has around 15% of the stock, Amazon has between 10-12%, and Microsoft has an undisclosed if smaller amount.

• Google and Amazon are also significant lenders, with Amazon offering tens of billions of dollars to the company in a complex convertible debt offering, which is unlocked through purchases of AWS cloud computing services. Broadcom is also a massive lender, guaranteeing $42 billion in borrowing, and a significant supplier of essential computing resources.
• Anthropic is reliant on Amazon, Google, and Microsoft for “many of the internal tools [Anthropic] uses to operate [its] business.” These three companies also use Claude as customers.
• Anthropic is buying hundreds of billions of dollars of non-cancellable computing resources from Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.

These relationships have implications for the other companies, too. On Wednesday, Google released its earnings, and so I took a look at its financial documents. Its share of Anthropic is worth a significant amount. Under the baroque heading “gross unrealized gain on non-marketable equity securities,” the number equals $117 billion.

That’s a lot of money, even for Google. How much of that is Anthropic? Well, a few lines up it says “our investments in non-marketable securities accounted for under the measurement alternative primarily consist of our investment in one private company.” (I bolded it for emphasis.)

And that’s before Anthropic goes public, and it’s at a valuation that Google chooses. So there’s another hundred billion of gains to go. That is, as they say, a lot of money in the banana stand. And you can be sure that there’s something similar on Amazon’s balance sheet, and Microsoft’s. There’s also convertible debt, and cash owed back and forth, and promises in compute and non-cancellable data center leasing, and infrastructure tools, these companies using each other products, and so on and so forth.

Since Anthropic will be a multi-trillion dollar initial public offering, this dynamic suggests something systemic about big tech. Google and Amazon both emphasized on their earnings calls the growth in cloud computing, with Google’s revenue jumping 103% to $30 billion a quarter, and Amazon’s up 39% to $46 billion a quarter. Who are they selling to? Well, Anthropic is a major customer. And it turns out the other multi-trillion dollar IPO of the year - SpaceX - has as its largest customer none other than Anthropic. Big tech and AI is now one big complex whose valuation rises or falls together.
That didn’t use to be the case.

When BIG started, in 2019, the five large big tech firms (Microsoft, Apple, Google, Meta, Amazon) dominated individual lines of business. They were distinct, and did not really compete with each other, except in narrow ways. There were alliances, such as Google and Apple in search on the iPhone, but they were stand-alone businesses.

In 2024, however, it became clear something was changing, as these companies each used the margins from their monopolies for capital investment in AI, and cross-investment in third party firms and adjacent off-balance sheet entities like neoclouds. Policymakers saw what was happening, the blurring of these lines, and did start acting. Lina Khan’s FTC opened an investigation into AI investment overlaps. And the Biden Antitrust Division, during the remedy phase of the Google antitrust suit, filed to prevent Google from investing in Anthropic, asking for a divestment of the search giant’s existing stake.

But Trump had a different philosophy of governance, encouraging these cross-ownership investments. He focused his economic policy framework on building more data centers, and encouraging investment and cross-investment from and into ten different firms, as well as their satellites: SpaceX, Oracle, Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, Broadcom, Meta, Amazon, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Khan’s successor didn’t follow up on her investigation into overlaps, and the Trump Antitrust Division quickly rolled back its demand for Google to divest its Anthropic stake.

And these conflicts could explain Google’s lack of positioning at the frontier of AI models, which is otherwise a bit puzzling. It is a key player here, since it has a product, Gemini, as well as the capital and ability to build comparable tools to Claude, as well as chips, data centers, and unique data sets. It also can underprice Anthropic, which it does to rivals when it wants to monopolize. Google scientists even created the fundamental architecture of LLMs!

But the byzantine relationship introduces something odd. If it did compete, vigorously, as it ordinarily might, well that “non-marketable securities” line would drop from $117 billion to $10 billion, instead of increasing to whatever it will after the IPO. That’s not a good incentive. Similarly, its amazing cloud computing growth would slow, upsetting investors. The same is true for Amazon, which just got rid of its division trying to catch up on frontier models. Why compete on price, if these companies already own a large chunk of Anthropic and undermining Anthropic’s enterprise value hurts them? And it’s not as if Anthropic’s rival, OpenAI, isn’t tied into this structure; Microsoft owns a quarter of OpenAI.

There’s also the question of power. Anthropic and OpenAI both rely on the infrastructure of Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, on their financing, their tools, their chips, and data centers. Anthropic and OpenAI may be able to take share from Google, but would they really try to do that? Maybe, but the incentives are certainly not clear. Throw in Broadcom and SpaceX, and you have an extremely opaque system. The motivations here are byzantine, and suggest that what’s really happening is every insider wants to see every company in this world maximize its market value, regardless of underlying intrinsic cash flow or competitive dynamics.

Big tech has become jammed together into one giant quasi-holding company, with interlocking business relationships, cross-shareholdings, and long-term cooperation. As a result, we have a situation where Anthropic is going public, with a massive chunk owned by an ostensible set of rivals. There are a few other important dynamics. Here are the other parts of the patronage network, listed on the S-1.

It’s not just these “rivals” to Anthropic who want to see the IPO succeed. Much of Wall Street, many insiders in Silicon Valley, and a large number of hedge funds, own Anthropic stock or are otherwise tied to the company’s fortune. If Anthropic is able to sell at a high valuation, then everyone in that ecosystem, as well as all of the associated chip, neocloud, and AI firms, will see a boost. If it can’t, look out below. In other words, anyone who might be able to compete with Anthropic still has an incentive to see the company do well.

Now, none of this corporate engineering would matter if big tech were still the capital light money machines of the 2010s or early 2020s. Sure stocks might take a hit, but it doesn’t matter when your free cash flow is in the tens of billions, and you don’t need to invest. Moreover, it wouldn’t really matter that much to anyone but that particular industry if a big tech stock got hit. In 2022, the Nasdaq drew down by a third, it did not matter much on a macro level.

But now, it does. These companies are no longer capital light, they are investing hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and infrastructure. And it’s not coming out of profits; Google, Meta, and Amazon are all cash flow negative, while even Microsoft is dipping into the debt markets. The chipmakers, like Nvidia and Broadcom, are cash-rich, but that’s because the big tech firms are paying them. Indeed, the AI system is one giant tech stack, chips, data, power, software, et al, costing trillions every year, with every insider hoping that enough money is pouring in from corporate America (and the rest of the world) to make it worth it, or at least to ensure that someone else is holding the bag.
If the AI bubble pops, we’re in recession.

The final piece is that the politics and legal problem has changed. It’s clear the monopolization crusade against big tech didn’t break up their concentrated power. Instead, Trump took over, and big tech mutated into something different, something more dangerous and weirder. The legal risk isn’t so much antitrust and privacy, it’s more normal forms of liability, but also, securities law. The analogy here is now much less Standard Oil and much more Enron. It’s not that antitrust has no relevance; Section 8 of the Clayton Act bans interlocking directorates, which is clearly a precedent for what we’re dealing with. It’s just that big tech is no longer micro, it’s a macro-economic phenomenon. The Fed is concerned about AI.

The shift in politics is even starker. In the 2010s and early 2020s, big tech was well-liked by most people. But AI is absolutely loathed by the public. These companies have never faced real public dissatisfaction, they all imagine themselves to be the good guys, with the credibility of having created magical search engines and smartphones. But that era is gone. They are now akin to the bankers on Wall Street in 2008, and politicians are winning elections by saying they hate AI as much as the voters do.

To most economists and Silicon Valley insiders, this Anthropic IPO is good, and represents a healthy tech ecosystem. Selling shares is a standard commercial practice, used to finance economic activity. And AI promises productivity, profits, and industrial transformation, in just a few years. But to many, this IPO, and the SpaceX IPO a few months ago, looks a conspiracy of vastly wealthy men doing whatever they want, in collusion with an unaccountable White House. They are simply minting more billionaires with political power, and this time, there may not even be the cash flow to justify it.

Thanks for reading! My name is Lee Hepner, I’m a guest-writer for BIG while Matt is out on paternity leave. Your tips make this newsletter what it is, so please send tips on weird monopolies, stories I’ve missed, or other thoughts. And if you liked this issue of BIG, you can sign up here for more issues, a newsletter on how to restore fair commerce, innovation, and democracy. Consider becoming a paying subscriber to support this work, or if you are a paying subscriber, giving a gift subscription to a friend, colleague, or family member.

npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-6015466/perspec.headline: Perspective: Forget the ballroom, we're headed to Cheesecake Factory!
npr.org/2026/10/31/nx-s1-6015466/perspec.author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: Food fight!
This week, the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain unexpectedly found itself in the political discourse.

During a campaign event in Ohio, former President Obama criticized President Trump's affection for gold decor, saying, "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent retaliated by having a French Dip Cheeseburger for lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House, telling reporters, "I had a great meal, always have a great meal. I would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try."

But this latest partisan debate made me wonder. Why spend $600 million or more to build a new White House ballroom to host state dinners? Why not just host those esteemed events instead at the Cheesecake Factory?
Come to a state dinner, I've been told, and you kind of have to gulp down whatever yellow squash velouté or fricassée of fava beans a server slides under your chin.
But isn't America all about freedom, choice and options galore?
Cheesecake Factory restaurants have more than 250 items on their menus. Now that's America! Chicken and Waffle Skewers! Tex-Mex Eggrolls! Pickle Fries!

What says America more? The Dover Sole Meunière, served with Potato Pavé, Spring Ramps, Snow Peas, and Parsley Oil served to King Charles III at a state dinner this spring? Or the Cheesecake Factory's Buffalo Blasts: chicken, cheese and hot sauce stuffed into a spicy wrapper, deep-fried, and served with celery sticks and blue cheese dressing?
"I'm absolutely stuffed," I imagine His Majesty saying. "British troops in 1814 would never have burned down a Cheesecake Factory!"

When French President Emmanuel Macron received a state dinner at the White House in 2018, it opened with a Goat Cheese Gateau. I'd bet that wherever French officials travel, hosts push a Goat Cheese Gateau in front of them, saying, "You'll love it! So French!"
So I can imagine a French president saying, "Forget the gateau! I want Asian Chicken Nachos! Wonton chips, peanut sauce and fromage fondu? Le yum!"
Move state dinners to a Cheesecake Factory, and foreign heads of state might even say, "Give me that plate of Fried Macaroni and Cheese balls, and I'll sign any tariff agreement you want!"

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/ai-agents-humans-daz.headline: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/ai-agents-humans-daz.author: Jonathan Vanian

paragraphs.text: The next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software.

That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI, still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade.

"We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors.

Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes.

Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill.

For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers.
"We work on a model that is not dissimilar from Uber, where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked.

Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably.
"And then we track what happens," Joyce said.
Confused agents

Mayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop.
But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window."
The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete.
"Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution."
Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and even CAPTCHA tests intended to fend off bots from sites.
"I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks.
Chatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works.

Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test using human contractors to handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process."
Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests.

Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies.
Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant.

"We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them."

Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people.
"We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/2026-midterm-electio.headline: ‘Pop-up’ super PACs pour $637 million into 2026 midterm races
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/2026-midterm-electio.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: A super PAC called Our Heritage Matters registered with the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 15.

Five days later, it began spending to boost third-party candidates and attack Republicans. By Oct. 29, the group had spent about $1.2 million across 10 House and Senate races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
What voters still cannot see is who supplied the money.
Because Our Heritage Matters formed after a key campaign finance reporting deadline on Oct. 15, its first regular report identifying its donors is not due until Dec. 3, a month after Election Day.

The group is an extreme example of a broader surge reshaping the midterm election: late-forming super PACs, including the latest-forming "pop-up PACs," pouring money into races before voters know where it came from.

Federal law requires super PACs and political committees to report large independent expenditures within 24 or 48 hours depending on how close to Election Day the spending occurs, showing how much they spent and which candidates they supported or opposed. Their donors, however, are disclosed less frequently through periodic campaign finance reports.

And in 2026, the practice of creating new, last-minute PACs has exploded. Both parties are using the tactic, with Republican-linked PACs spending about twice what those connected with Democrats have disbursed.

Twenty-two super PACs that registered with the FEC during the final 10 weeks before Election Day have each spent at least $1 million on congressional races, according to CNBC's analysis. Together, they had reported roughly $637 million in independent expenditures by Oct. 29 — about one-sixth of all independent spending reported in House and Senate races this election cycle.
The number of million-dollar late-forming super PACs has more than quadrupled since 2022, while their spending has grown nearly 35-fold.

At the same point in the 2022 midterms, just five comparable groups had spent about $18 million combined, according to CNBC's analysis. In 2018, three had spent about $12 million. The total has even eclipsed the past two presidential elections, when comparable late-forming super PACs spent less than $50 million combined on congressional races in both 2020 and 2024, according to CNBC's analysis.

"The reason for this is almost entirely to avoid disclosure, even if just temporarily," said Michael Kang, a Northwestern Pritzker School of Law professor who studies campaign finance. "Many times, if the donors were known, then it would undercut their cause."

CNBC's analysis includes super PACs formed in the final 10 weeks before Election Day that spent at least $1 million on House or Senate races by Oct. 29. Spending includes regular FEC filings and 24- and 48-hour reports, with duplicates removed.
From zero to millions in late-forming PAC spending
One of the defining features of late-forming super PACs is speed.

Among the 22 groups in CNBC's analysis, 18 began spending within 30 days of launching, and almost all started spending before filing their first regular campaign finance report showing where their money came from.

“It’s happening more often, and they’re spending more money doing it because it works, and they’re getting away with it,” said Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the Campaign Legal Center. The group is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by a former Republican FEC chairman.

Despite their late start, the groups accounted for more than 22% of independent expenditures in congressional races during CNBC's 2026 window, up from less than 2% at the same point in each of the previous two midterms.
Many are new only on paper. CNBC found financial or organizational ties between nine of the 22 groups and established political networks.

Lower Costs Now, for example, formed on Sept. 10 and disclosed an affiliation with the Future Forward PAC, the main outside group that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign. Nineteen days later, Lower Costs Now began spending in Senate races.

But voters did not get a fuller picture of its financing until Oct. 15, when its first regular financial report showed that Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect Senate Democrats, had given the group $23 million, according to FEC filings.
By Thursday, Lower Costs Now had reported about $75.5 million in independent expenditures across eight Senate contests, including Iowa, Texas, Kansas and Ohio, according to CNBC's analysis.
Republicans have used the same playbook.

No Going Back PAC formed Sept. 1 and began spending three days later. Public reporting soon linked it to MAGA Inc., President Donald Trump's marquee super PAC. But its formal financial report did not arrive until Oct. 20 — more than six weeks after the spending began.

By then, No Going Back had already spent roughly $187.8 million, according to FEC filings, which revealed that MAGA Inc. had supplied the group with $200 million. By Thursday, the super PAC had spent roughly $242.2 million, according to FEC filings.
“They are a vehicle designed to emerge from nowhere and spend a bunch of money on an election” before voters can learn “who’s supplying that money and what their motivations might be,” Ghosh said.
PACs built for one race
Many of the new groups are also narrowly targeted.
Fourteen of the 22 million-dollar super PACs identified by CNBC spent all of their money in a single congressional contest.

Take The Maine Standard. It formed Sept. 11 and began spending five days later. Since then, it has spent $8.2 million, all of it opposing Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, according to FEC filings.

The Cornhusker Majority followed almost the same pattern. It formed Sept. 10, began spending Sept. 16 and has spent about $7.1 million in Nebraska's Senate race, almost all of it opposing independent Dan Osborn, according to FEC filings. Osborn is running against Republican incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts in a tight race.
The connection between the two groups did not appear in their regular financial reports until Oct. 15: Both were financed by Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC.

On the Democratic side, Texas Forever launched Sept. 24 and began spending five days later, according to FEC filings. By Thursday, it had spent about $27.5 million to help Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, according to the FEC. Unlike some other pop-up groups, however, its initial FEC filing identified the Senate Majority PAC as an affiliate.

"A locally branded PAC doesn't necessarily hide where the money comes from, but it fragments the picture. Instead of seeing one national organization spending tens of millions of dollars across the country, voters see a series of different groups operating race by race," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks such spending.
But even identifying the national group behind a pop-up PAC can still leave another layer of the money trail hidden.

Texas PAC formed Aug. 28 and soon began spending to help Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race. The money flowed through the SLF, but Elon Musk's role was not public until Oct. 12, more than a month after the spending began.
On Oct. 15, FEC filings showed Musk had given the SLF $158 million in two contributions, with the group transferring matching amounts to Texas PAC the day after each donation.
By Oct. 29, Texas PAC had spent about $181.6 million in the race, according to FEC filings, making it one of the largest late-forming super PACs CNBC identified.

Together, Texas PAC and No Going Back accounted for roughly two-thirds of all spending by the 22 million-dollar groups. But the surge was much broader than those two giants: Even excluding them, the remaining groups spent nearly 12 times as much as comparable late-forming super PACs did at the same point in 2022.

"The growth is huge this year," Kang said. "Maybe you don’t want to be known this election, or want to hide away for a period while you might be unpopular, like AI is right now, but you kind of want to build a reputation for the players inside the system."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: OpenAI Funding Target Cut by $10 Billion as AI Slumps, FT Says
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Yoolim Lee

paragraphs.text: Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:09 AM CDT 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10 billion as an AI stock selloff and rival Anthropic PBC's impending public listing complicate its efforts to secure investor commitments, the Financial Times reported.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, down from $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation last month, the FT said, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

Some investors have reduced their commitments to OpenAI's funding round, according to the report. The scaled-back ambitions reflect growing investor unease over the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence. The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5% on Friday.
Bloomberg News reported last week that OpenAI was seeking to raise capital at a $1.25 trillion valuation during the final stages of negotiations.

A group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, including state-backed MGX, is expected to be the largest participant in the round, the FT said. SoftBank Group Corp. and venture capital firms including Sequoia Capital, Coatue Management, Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz also plan to participate, according to the report.

OpenAI, Sequoia, Founders Fund and SoftBank declined to comment, the report said. MGX, Coatue and Andreessen Horowitz did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to the Financial Times.

The fundraising effort faces additional competition from Anthropic, which is preparing to go public next month at a valuation of at least $1.5 trillion, the newspaper said. OpenAI, which raised $122 billion in March, is seeking fresh capital to finance its vast computing ambitions as it prepares for a potential IPO of its own next year, according to the report.

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/business/dealbook.headline: The New Hot Job in Law Doesn’t Require a J.D.

paragraphs.text: In 2018, when Daniel Himmel first moved from practicing law to a job that today might be called legal engineering, it felt like a big career risk.
“I was nervous,” he said. “I thought, what is my career going to look like? Where do I go from here?”

He doesn’t feel that way anymore. As the head of legal engineering for North America at the legal tech company Legora, Himmel has hired about 70 people over the past year. They’re part of a global team of about 200 legal engineers the company has built since 2024. “We’re hiring hundreds, and competitors are hiring them, and our clients are hiring them,” he said. “It’s a true profession.”

And it’s one of the hottest jobs in the rapidly changing world of law. As artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of legal work, technology vendors like Legora, law firms, and in-house legal teams are all looking for people who understand both law and technology well enough to rewrite work flows and teach others how to use A.I. tools.
Often, they’re called “legal engineers.” But they are also sometimes described as “knowledge and innovation counsels,” “innovation attorneys,” or “legal applications engineers.”

Exactly what the job entails varies from company to company, as does the salary: The law firm Latham & Watkins is hiring “legal engineering attorneys” in at least five cities, with a salary range of $220,000 to $250,000. An “A.I. innovation adviser” at Kirkland & Ellis can make between $153,000 and $220,000 a year, according to the company’s job listing, while Gibson Dunn is advertising a salary for a “legal technology & AI Attorney” between $250,000 to $300,000.

In-house legal teams have posted similar jobs. The chip maker Nvidia is hiring a “legal operations engineer” for $124,00 to $195,500 a year, and Microsoft wants a “principal legal engineer” at a salary between $147,000 and $278,900, according to job postings.
A.I. companies that make tools for law firms, including OpenAI, Thomson Reuters, and Google, are also hiring legal engineers.

Parameters of the job, which has expanded in both prevalence and scope in recent years, are still being defined. “If you were to just put it into an equation, it’s law plus technology plus business process,” said Irene Liu, the executive director of the A.I. initiative at Stanford Law School, which in September began promoting a two-week in-residence executive program called Legal Engineering Academy.

The program isn’t accepting applications yet, but about 1,400 senior leaders have signed up to be notified when it is — about half are part of in-house legal teams, and about 20 percent are law firm partners and senior attorneys, according to the school.

In the first six months of this year, almost 50 lawyers left the 200 largest law firms in the United States to move to A.I. companies, including 15 who moved into jobs with legal engineering titles, according to Firm Prospects, a platform for legal recruiters. (The collapse of the venerable law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges this week was another sign of the change sweeping through the industry.)

At A.I. companies, legal engineers sometimes help build tech for lawyers, but more typically help clients integrate the product into work flows, run trials and onboard employees. The legal A.I. giant Harvey has about 180 legal engineers who do this type of work (it advertises a salary range of $220,000 to $320,000 a year), all of whom are former practicing lawyers.
Legal engineers employed by law firms often do similar work-flow design and educational work, but with a wider focus.

Ropes & Gray hired the first of its five legal engineers, whom it calls practice innovation attorneys, at the end of last year. “In the old days, there was technology and there was law. And as long as my email worked, I didn’t have to talk to people who dealt with the technology,” said Howard Glazer, a longtime partner at the firm who became its head of practice A.I. about a year ago. “But now we actually provide our service and provide our product using the tools.”
“‘Legal engineer’ kind of makes it sound like someone made it up,” he added. “But it’s not. It’s a role which the current environment just screams for.”

The law firm Latham & Watkins now has more than 100 people dedicated to its A.I. initiatives, it confirmed to DealBook. Some of them work on building proprietary technology, while others focus on A.I.-enabled work flows, encouraging lawyers to adopt them and other areas.

Virtually no schools offer formal training programs for legal engineers, though some have added classes. Many legal engineers are former practicing lawyers who taught themselves A.I. skills or learned on the job. Some have backgrounds in legal operations, paralegal work or consulting. Fewer are former software engineers who then went to law school — “the unicorn,” one hiring manager said.

Ankita Puri became a senior legal engineer at Legora after working in commercial litigation at a law firm, and then as the chief legal officer of a financial institution. She said she appreciates the greater diversity of work and more frequent interaction with clients that has come with the transition.
“It’s not so much going from actively practicing law to not,” she said. “I think it’s more embracing this generational shift in the legal industry.”

Mary O’Carroll, the C.E.O. of LegalEng Consulting Group, which works with in-house legal teams, has been an executive in legal operations for more than 20 years, including for 13 years at Google. She, too, sees the rise of legal engineers as part of a shift in the industry.

“You don’t necessarily need a giant pyramid of lawyers anymore,” she said. “People who have this kind of skill set don’t have to have a J.D., and they don’t have to be software engineers, but there’s business process re-engineering, or this M.B.A. type skill, that I think is really necessary.”

The position fits into what some see as a category of job becoming more essential in the A.I. era: Those that use specific expertise to design A.I. systems. LinkedIn job postings for “marketing engineer,” for example, increased 29 percent from 2024 to 2025 after relatively little growth in prior years, according to the company.

“What’s notable is that these titles are showing up well beyond traditional engineering. We are seeing them across functions like operations, product, business development, and even design,” Kory Kantenga, the head of economics at LinkedIn, said in a statement.

The lingering question is whether this type of job stays in hot demand. “It’s absolutely growing,” said Glazer of Ropes & Gray. “The question in my mind is going to be, you know, how long will it last? Is it a transition position?”
O’Carroll said she didn’t see the pace of change easing up, and that legal engineers will be needed to maintain systems and adapt to shifting technology and work.

Byong Kim, who became chief data & A.I. officer at the law firm Seyfarth Shaw last year after working in technology there for 13 years, said he thinks every law firm and every law department is looking to understand how to use A.I. more effectively right now.

“Long-term wise, I think we’re still trying to play out how this is all going to work out as technology gets better,” he said. “It’s still too early to say what the actual answer is, but I will say it’s a very interesting time for me. I don’t think I’ve ever been as busy.”
IN CASE YOU MISSED IT

Binance suspended withdrawals after a massive hack. The crypto exchange said on Thursday that the hackers stole more than $6 billion in digital coins and that it would cover all losses. The attack appears to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist ever, and prominent crypto stocks and the price of Bitcoin slumped on Friday.

A prominent law firm plans to wind down. Weil, Gotshal & Manges has struggled amid an exodus of high-profile lawyers, a scuttled deal to merge with Willkie Farr & Gallagher, and a botched succession plan in which Ramona Nee, who had been expected to take over as the leader of the firm, turned down the top role. The firm said its senior leadership had recommended to dissolve the firm and would vote on the matter in the coming days.

Investors questioned the A.I. spending spree. The S&P 500 index fell more than 1 percent and the Nasdaq index fell more than 2 percent on Friday amid a bruising tech sell-off. Over the past two weeks, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta said they were on track to spend more than $720 billion this year on data centers and other capital expenses.

More big deals: Anthropic filed its S-1. DoorDash will buy Instacart for $17 billion. Kalshi landed a $40 billion valuation. And Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve’s chairman, said the central bank would alter its rate-setting meeting schedule next year.
The billionaire tax and the future of tech money in politics

It feels as if billionaires and Big Tech are on the ballot this election season. That’s especially true in California, where voters will decide on Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on the state’s ultrawealthy that supporters say is needed to offset federal health care budget cuts. Polling suggests the “billionaire tax” could go down in defeat on Tuesday.

The journalist Jonathan Weber has chronicled the rise of tech and its influence on politics, economics and culture for decades, including in his new book, “City on the Edge: Technology, Politics, and the Fight for the Soul of San Francisco.” He spoke with DealBook’s Bernhard Warner about the fight over the proposed tax, Big Tech money in politics, and the national significance of tech titans. The interview has been edited and condensed.

The Times recently reported that tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen, had become the biggest force in political giving, vastly outspending major donors Charles Koch and Ken Griffin. Did you see this coming?
The short answer is no. But it makes sense that the world’s largest industry — one with a lot at stake when it comes to regulation — would produce the biggest political donors.

Though how the money will be deployed is not as obvious. Once Trump is gone there’s likely to be a fracturing of the political right, and it’s unclear where people like Musk and Andreessen will come out on that.

There are still mainstream liberals in the industry, like investors Reid Hoffman and crypto mogul Chris Larsen. And, assuming there isn’t a big crash in the near future, we’re going to have a whole new generation of very young, very wealthy A.I. executives and investors whose political views are pretty unformed.
If Prop 40 fares well in California, similar measures could pop up across the country. What would its passage mean for California and the tech sector?

The main argument against the billionaire tax is that the wealthy would simply leave the state to avoid it, and thereby destroy Silicon Valley as we know it. Google’s Sergey Brin, who’s leading the charge against it, has already moved.

But I’m skeptical: Republicans have long argued that high taxes would drive businesses and wealthy people out of the state. While many companies have left, plenty have come in behind them. No other place has a tech ecosystem like California’s.
Brin and others are spending huge sums to defeat the tax. Can their money, influence and connections help defeat the ballot measure on Tuesday?

Opponents of the tax are pouring money into Prop 42, which would nullify the billionaire levy if it gets more votes. It’s telling that the tax’s opponents, including Governor Newsom, aren’t confident they can defeat it outright, even with a war chest of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s C.E.O., has gone a different route. He negotiated a deal with Meta’s board to create a new class of shares that ultimately will keep him in the state. What does that tell you about tech leaders’ response to this new tax threat?
I think this kind of maneuver will be more common than people actually moving to Texas or Florida.
Frankly, if the tax passes and people do start relocating, that’s likely to prompt more tax-the-rich efforts in the destination states.
Scary prices
This question comes from a story in The Times. Click an answer to see if you’re right. (The link is free.)

Halloween candy is getting more expensive. That’s not exactly a surprise given the impact of inflation at the grocery store. The cost of vegetables has jumped by 6 percent from last year, and beef is up by about 9 percent. How much has the price of Halloween candy risen since last year’s trick-or-treating?
Thanks for reading! We’ll see you Monday.
