cnbc.com/2026/10/31/401k-cash-outs-autom.headline: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/401k-cash-outs-autom.author: Sarah Agostino

paragraphs.text: Leaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under $1,000 or move slightly larger balances into an IRA. Taking the money in cash and moving on can feel like the simplest option, but it can have short- and long-term financial consequences.

A system backed by major 401(k) administrators aims to make it easier for those savings to follow workers to their next job. New research from one of those companies, Vanguard, shows it's helping fewer people cash out — although most of the money has yet to reach workers' new retirement plans.

Among workers with less than $1,000 in their 401(k), the share who cashed out within 10 months of leaving their job fell to about 9% from roughly 50% after their employers began participating in a new system called the Portability Services Network, according to the Vanguard research. Among those with balances of between $1,000 and $7,000, the share cashing out fell to 31% from 39%.

Portability Services Network is a coalition of large 401(k) administrators — including Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and Alight Solutions, among others — in conjunction with Retirement Clearinghouse and has been in operation since late 2023.

How it works: When a worker with a small 401(k) balance leaves an employer that participates in the network, the money is generally automatically rolled into a safe harbor IRA, where it remains until the network matches it with the worker's new employer plan. The balance then gets rolled into the new 401(k) from that interim IRA. The catch, however, is that the receiving employer must also participate in the network for the money to move to the next employer's plan.

In Vanguard's research, just 6% of accounts that have been transferred into IRAs as part of this automatic portability network successfully made it to a new employer's plan as of early 2026, largely because few employers have opted in. The rest generally remained in those interim IRAs, waiting to be matched with another employer plan that participates in the network. While workers can always roll over the money into their new 401(k) themselves, the point of the network is for it to happen automatically.

Of the roughly 220,000 outbound rollovers involving Vanguard participants analyzed, the median balance was just $200, and nearly three-quarters involved less than $1,000. The typical saver affected was 31 years old, earned about $20,000 annually and had worked for their employer for roughly six months, according to the research.
The cash-out analysis is based on workers at 83 employer-sponsored retirement plans administered by Vanguard that have adopted the automatic portability.
Financial consequences of cashing out

Typically, when you part ways with an employer, you can leave your money in its 401(k) plan if the account value is above $7,000. Balances under $1,000 usually result in the plan cashing you out and mailing you a check. For amounts between $1,000 and $7,000, most plans roll the balance over to an IRA if the former employee takes no action to move it themselves.

Cashing out a 401(k) when leaving a job, whether done by an employer or the employee, can have lasting financial consequences. Workers who withdraw their savings can owe income taxes on the money and may face a 10% early withdrawal penalty if they're younger than 59½. They also lose the opportunity for that money to grow over time.

Most workers — 84% — have changed employers at least once during their careers, while 53% have switched three or more times and 27% have made at least five moves, according to a new study from Empower, a 401(k) recordkeeper and a founding partner of the portability network. The report is based on an online survey of 2,005 adults.

Additionally, 50% of Generation Z respondents and 45% of millennials said they may have retirement savings from a previous employer that they've lost track of, the survey found. That compares with 30% of Gen X and 14% of baby boomers.
$71.3 million in assets have made it to new plans

Since the Portability Services Network's launch in November 2023, there have been 53,118 completed transactions, totaling $71.3 million in assets transferred from a previous employer plan to a new employer plan via automatic portability, according to Steve Holman, senior vice president of Portability Services Network strategy and development at Retirement Clearinghouse.

There are 23,787 plans that have adopted automatic portability, representing 7.73 million participants, Holman said. The overall estimate of participants in 401(k)s and similar workplace plans is about 96 million, he said.
There are 1.22 million eligible participants waiting to be matched with a new employer, up more than 25% since the beginning of 2026, Holman said.
Snags remain with the automatic portability process

Keeping the money in a safe harbor IRA can be better for investors financially than cashing out — but management fees may take a toll on small balances, especially when the money is in an interest-bearing cash account or other conservative investment.

"For many of these small accounts, earnings on the conservative default investment may not be sufficient to offset recurring account-level fees while the account remains unmatched, leaving the balance vulnerable to gradual erosion," the Vanguard study said.

Workers with Roth savings face another complication. If retirement savings are in a traditional 401(k) — funded with pretax contributions and taxed when withdrawn in retirement — it goes into a traditional IRA. Likewise, Roth 401(k)s, funded with after-tax contributions and withdrawn tax-free down the road, go into Roth IRAs.
However, IRS rules don't allow for a Roth IRA to be rolled into a new employer's 401(k), even a Roth 401(k).
"We are advocating for future legislation to allow for Roth dollars to be eligible for auto-portability — our technology can support it today," Holman said.

theguardian.com/politics/2026/oct/31/kei.headline: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
theguardian.com/politics/2026/oct/31/kei.author: Kevin Rawlinson

paragraphs.text: The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.

The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.

“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.

“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”

Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.

He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.

“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”

His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.

Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.

Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.

“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.

“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

livescience.com/archaeology/ghostly-stat.headline: Ghostly statue of 'shrine maiden' discovered at 1,500-year-old burial mound in Japan
livescience.com/archaeology/ghostly-stat.author: Kristina Killgrove

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.
Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.
The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/.headline: L.A. County sheriff's race is a grudge rematch, Luna vs. Villanueva
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/.author: Connor Sheets

paragraphs.text: Four years ago, Robert Luna went from being a little-known retired lawman to an unlikely political force — pushing Los Angeles County Sheriff Alex Villanueva into a runoff in the June 2022 primary.

Luna went on to beat Villanueva in the general election. He’s now seeking a second term running the nation’s largest sheriff’s department. But the tables have turned. This year, it was Villanueva who forced Luna into a runoff, and he’s angling to take back his old job in Tuesday’s election.

Whoever wins will be charged with a long list of priorities, including navigating tensions with the federal government over immigration enforcement and helping keep millions of people safe during the 2028 Olympic Games.

This time, Luna has a record to champion — and defend. After four years in the Hall of Justice, he is pitching himself as a steady hand working to restore the relationships and respect that he says Villanueva had tarnished, leaving a hobbled and atrophied department in his wake.
Villanueva, on the other hand, depicts the department’s Luna era as a sweeping failure that has left morale low, deputy jobs unfilled and criminals unpunished.
It’s a stark clash between two very different personalities and platforms.
On the campaign trail
Villanueva showed up early at the Burbank Realtors Assn.’s event space on Magnolia Boulevard, with a stack of campaign signs under the arm of his brass-buttoned navy sports coat.

The former sheriff stood on a low stage and presented a vision of an L.A. County that was thriving when he left office nearly four years ago, but has since gone to the dogs on the back of ineffectual leadership and poor decisions.

After years of fiery appearances on Fox News and a sharp rightward turn that alienated some of his core Democratic supporters, Villanueva’s demeanor with voters that September afternoon was disarmingly warm and casual. But his rhetoric hasn’t softened. If anything, he has sharpened his message since the primary, escalating his claims about the chaos that will reign if Luna wins a second term.

Villanueva railed against Luna’s homeless policies and disaster management capabilities. The former sheriff criticized his successor for presiding over a significant uptick in both overtime spending and sworn vacancies since 2022.

“The department is in free fall. My motto is ‘Help is on the way,’” Villanueva said, prompting nods of affirmation from the three dozen or so professionals in attendance. “The department will not survive four more years at the current rate it’s going.”
Then he fielded questions from members of the audience, who raised concerns about tenant evictions and taxes in between trips to the buffet.

Tony Rodriguez, a Republican state Senate candidate in the San Fernando Valley’s 20th District and U.S. Army veteran, said he saw the former sheriff as a stronger leader than Luna, and one who inspired more confidence in the deputies under his command.

“Leadership starts up here, but that leadership trickles down to the troops on the ground,” Rodriguez said. “Nobody wants to go to war with a general that is going to sit in the rear … I want one that’ll go into war with me.”

Minerva and Jose Corral of Corral Investments & Realty said they preferred most of Villanueva’s policies over those of Luna, particularly around the sheriff’s department’s handling of evictions. Villanueva said he would work to streamline the process and beef up what he described as the “skeleton crew” dedicated to evictions.
But the Corrals also said they weren’t convinced that returning the former sheriff to office was the solution.
“You remember when he was sheriff last time?” Minerva Corral said. “It was very combative. They were, like, brawling at Tuesday meetings.”
Jose quoted an old song by The Who to sum up his feelings about the race.
“Meet the new boss, same as the old boss,” he said.

Villanueva had intended to participate in a planned tour of homeless encampments in downtown L.A. later in the day. But the air conditioning in his BMW had gone out on the way to Burbank, so the former sheriff decided to instead attempt what he called the “Hail Mary” feat of driving himself and his wife, Vivian, a retired Sheriff’s Department veteran herself, home without temperature control.
‘You have to have relationships’
From Luna’s perspective, the Sheriff’s Department under his predecessor was marked by turmoil within and without.

Whether mending broken ties with county supervisors or striving to avoid antagonizing government agencies, journalists and accountability bodies, Luna says he has spent much of his tenure rebuilding trust and connections.

“In order to be effective in local government, you have to have relationships,” he said in a recent interview, noting that the Board of Supervisors “controls my budget” so it’s imperative that he plays nice with them. Villanueva, according to Luna, is “100% ineffective in that arena.”

Both men led the county through historic calamities. Villanueva was sheriff when COVID-19 brought L.A. County to its knees in 2020; Luna held the role last year when the Eaton and Palisades fires ravaged vast swaths of the county, including unincorporated Altadena and Malibu — both patrolled by his department. Experienced politicians with thousands of hours of shaking hands and speaking at community functions under their belts, they each have a distinctive approach to the job.

A law-and-order firebrand who once defied subpoenas to address concerns about deputy gangs within the Sheriff’s Department, Villanueva can come off as less focused on his relationships within government and with the public, and more interested in cultivating competence and camaraderie within the department.

It’s a characterization he’s encouraged over years of clashes with officials and detractors and his repeated claims that the department has been crippled under Luna by staffing shortfalls, budgetary mismanagement and lack of confidence.
Luna remains further above the political fray, favoring plain-spoken assertions about his commitment to the rights and safety of county residents, deputies and inmates alike.
Tacos in East L.A.
On Oct. 23, Luna stepped out of a large black SUV with tinted windows in the parking lot of King Taco in East Los Angeles.

He ordered a burrito before telling a story from his elementary school days, when he moved to a house a couple of blocks away from the legendary taqueria, which at the time was still just a taco truck.

Luna’s late mother, whom he described as “hardcore Mexican, best cook in the world,” wouldn’t let him join the long lines the truck drew, telling him it was a waste of money when you can make tacos at home.
“So this was, like, off limits,” he said. “But I was always curious.”

Now, Luna can’t seem to go anywhere in this neighborhood without being recognized. As he waited for his food, several people asked to take pictures with him and shared their thoughts about his performance as sheriff.

Rafael Nolasco grew up in East Los Angeles, graduated from East Los Angeles College and still lives in the area. As a first-generation Mexican American and accountant from the same part of town as the sheriff, he’s a bread-and-butter Luna supporter. So is Mike Aguilar, who also grew up in East Los Angeles and sports a Raiders tattoo on his forearm.
Both men see Luna as a role model for making so much of his humble beginnings, and also because of what he’s done in office.
“He’s trying to make a difference,” Aguilar said. “Nothing’s done 100% perfect,” he added, “but you know he is trying, and that’s what we need. The streets are a lot safer, I believe.”

Yet some of Luna’s strongest critics — including Villanueva, but also members of county oversight bodies and organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California — argue that his tenure as sheriff has been less even-keeled than the version the sitting sheriff and some of his supporters describe.

Luna, his department and the county are involved in a bitter legal battle over access to records related to three use-of-force incidents. The Civilian Oversight Commission subpoenaed the unredacted documents in February 2025, but the Sheriff’s Department has yet to hand them over, even after a new state law expanded oversight bodies’ access to confidential records.

Villanueva claimed that his opponent was purposely delaying the records’ release until after the election. Luna, citing the position of the county counsel, said his hands are tied while a “meet and confer” process plays out between Sheriff’s Department unions and the county.
While Luna has at times locked horns with the Inspector General’s office, the oversight commission and criminal justice reform groups, his tenure has been far less tumultuous than his predecessor’s.

Villanueva initiated a criminal investigation of a Los Angeles Times reporter before walking it back amid widespread condemnation. He still defends the public corruption unit he created within the Sheriff’s Department, despite concerns among government watchdogs that its actions — including an early morning raid in 2022 of the home of then-Supervisor Sheila Kuehl, a vocal critic of Villanueva — were politically motivated.

“We created a public corruption unit, and we did the very first investigation on what was nonprofit fraud, and that was the tip of the iceberg,” Villanueva said after his September campaign event in Burbank.
Luna, who quickly disbanded the controversial unit after he took office, said he is “more apt” to refer public corruption cases to the California Department of Justice or the FBI.
“I don’t believe that we should handle that in house because the appearance of either being biased, politically motivated is too high,” he explained.

Luna has a decisive fundraising lead, bringing in about $729,000 in campaign contributions between Jan. 1 and Oct. 17, versus $242,000 for Villanueva. And Luna captured 44.2% of the vote in June’s primary, more than double Villanueva’s 21.7%.

Unlike 2022, there have been no televised debates. The two finalists are the same as four years ago, and their core messages haven’t changed much. On Tuesday, the electoral results will reveal which one L.A. County voters prefer.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/31/weil-wind-do.headline: In the wake of Weil, a legal recruiter's advice for surviving a company wind-down
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/31/weil-wind-do.author: Danielle Thompson

paragraphs.text: It's hard to believe a corporate giant like Weil, Gotshal & Manges — a top 20 U.S. law firm that reportedly had over $2 billion in revenue in 2025 — could move toward ceasing operations just like that. But occasionally a Weil-like wind-down — or even a collapse like Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank or FTX — is bound to occur.
And here we are, seeing a major law firm move toward shutting down in real time.

The firm's management committee recommended that its partners prepare to close its doors after more than 90 years in business, Weil, Gotshal & Manges said on Wednesday. "Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm's Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down," the firm said in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday. "The partners are expected to vote in the coming days."

As a legal recruiter and former big law associate, I'm here to provide practical insights to the employees, lawyers and non-lawyers alike, who've just learned they're about to be out of a job — and those who are scared their company might be next.

First, let's be clear: From where I stand, Weil is an anomaly. But when a company does make headlines for winding down, or failing and shutting down, it's rarely the employees whose plight is highlighted: the people whose careers have been destabilized, whose anxiety shoots through the roof and who become the collateral damage of business decisions they had no idea were being made until far too late.

Here are my top tips, for both lawyers and non-lawyers, for when your company announces or is headed toward dissolution. In the case of Weil, it's advice I hope the firm's roughly 1,200 lawyers plus staff take to heart in the next 90 days.
1. Don't wait for the dust to settle
Yes, you can worry. Yes, you can grieve. But you should also mobilize quickly.

A lot of Weil associates are in a holding pattern right now: either waiting to see where their favorite partners are going and hoping they offer to bring them along, or thinking 90 days of pay, as reported by Reuters, means they have 90 days in which to start looking.

While many associates will eventually follow their partners, I suggest looking for a new job on your own while you wait. The market is absolutely inundated with Weil associates right now, on top of everyone else whose firm isn't dissolving but was already looking to make a lateral move. You don't want to be late to the party and find all your peers are ahead of you in line.

Partners are also under no obligation to bring you with them, and you have no say in where they choose to go. There's no guarantee it would be a good fit for you. It's best to have options and it's comforting to feel like you have some control over those options, especially in such uncertain times.

I'd give similar advice to non-lawyers. Don't wait too long. Options are always good. Be proactive. The people who tend to come out of these situations the least scathed are the ones who start looking before any announcement is made, in cases where the writing's on the wall and everyone else is still hoping for a last-minute save.
2. Don't act from a place of fear
Even as you move fast, try to be cautious. You don't want to be taken advantage of.

Just this week, I've counseled about a dozen Weil associates to do their homework, however quickly, before blasting their resume to every firm and recruiter on the block. Some recruiters — especially in the legal industry — will take you sending your resume as blanket consent to submit you anywhere they like.

But from what I've seen working in legal recruiting, if more than one recruiter sends your materials to the same firm, you're very unlikely to ever hear from that firm again. They see it as sloppy, bad form and too much of a headache to manage the inevitable fight over who's entitled to the hypothetical fee for your placement.

So keep a firm grasp on where your resume is at all times. You should know exactly which companies have it and who they got it from. If you plan to use a recruiter, pick a reputable and trusted one. Don't race to the first recruiter who cold calls you or the last recruiter in your inbox. Instead, get referrals from friends, set up intro calls with multiple recruiters to get a vibe check, pick one and only send that one your resume.

For non-legal folks, recruiting may not be so cutthroat. But I still recommend caution regarding how and where you share your information. Focus on trusted connections, including verifiable HR professionals at your target companies, friend and colleague referrals, your college career services office and known job boards. Be wary of answering outreach from questionable sources.
3. Don't worry so much about resume gaps or job hops right now
A short unemployment stint won't kill your career, and neither will multiple moves in quick succession.

When the unexpected occurs and the resulting job market frenzy ensues, sometimes, even when you mobilize early and wisely, you won't land a new job right away. Perhaps the only upside to the mass publicity of these surprise dissolutions is that every prospective employer is going to take one look at your resume and understand why you're out of work. They won't wonder what you did wrong, whether you got fired or if you're qualified.

But those favorable assumptions don't last forever. I'd give it one to six months. That's another plug for not waiting until a dissolution date to start your search, especially in the current job market, where as of September 27.1% of those who are unemployed have been searching for over six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Keep in mind too that job decisions made in haste or with your back against a wall are much more likely to end in a mismatch. Most people will take the first offer they get. Some will accept an unsustainable commute or a tyrant of a boss for short-term job security. And if it's your only option, that might be the right decision for you — we all have bills to pay and mouths to feed.

If that's the case, know it's also okay to move on quickly. I don't begrudge anyone who makes a job decision out of necessity and then course corrects when they're out of survival mode. And from my experience as a recruiter, neither will most future employers.
4. Be kind to yourself and others

None of this is your fault and all of it is horribly unfair. It's okay if you're feeling angry, terrified, overwhelmed, frozen, devastated or even a little relieved. Whatever you're feeling, both in the immediate aftermath and in the weeks and months after, is completely valid. Give yourself ample space and grace for whatever comes up and seek help and support.

On the flip side, lend a helping hand wherever you can, especially once you find a job, which I believe you will. Pay it forward by helping others who are still looking or looking again. Share a good resource, refer them to a trusted recruiter and connect them to any job opportunities you've passed up or heard about.
Corporations don't have feelings or loyalty to any given employee. But people do. We are nothing without our empathy and our communities. Hard times are when we need both the most.

Danielle Thompson is a legal recruiter and former big law employment lawyer based in the Bay Area. A managing director at Damato Search Group, she holds a J.D. from Columbia Law School and a B.A., magna cum laude, from UC Santa Barbara.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/.headline: Two competitive L.A. City Council seats are on the Nov. 3 ballot
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/.author: Melissa Gomez, Itzel Luna

paragraphs.text: Voters will elect two new Los Angeles City Council members on Tuesday, one representing the San Fernando Valley, the other South Los Angeles.

In the 3rd District, businessman Tim Gaspar and longtime local government employee Barri Worth Girvan are vying to replace Bob Blumenfield, who is termed out. The district includes Canoga Park, Reseda, Tarzana, Winnetka, and Woodland Hills.
In Council District 9, residents are preparing for a historic shift: No matter who wins, the district will elect a Latino council member for the first time since 1963.

The South L.A. district has long been represented by a Black council member, but over the last few decades it has undergone a demographic shift and today is about 80% Latino. Councilmember Curren Price also has termed out. Estuardo Mazariegos, co-director of the L.A. chapter of Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment, and Jose Ugarte, who previously served as a deputy chief of staff to Price, are vying for the seat.
District 3

Gaspar led the June primary with 46.1% of the vote compared to Worth Girvan, who secured 42.5%. Both candidates have spent the last few weeks of the campaign knocking on doors and making their case to voters, saying major issues like public safety and cleanliness are common concerns.

Gaspar, who founded an insurance agency in the Valley that he sold in 2021, would bring a pro-business perspective to City Hall, and among his top priorities would be eliminating “red tape” to stimulate small businesses in the region.
“We need somebody who’s going to come to the table with different ideas,” Gaspar said. “If we keep doing the same thing as before, we’re going to keep getting the same results.”
Worth Girvan, who worked as L.A. County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath’s district director for three years before running, would use her experience in the public sector to advocate for the West Valley.
“I am fortunate to have experience at every level of government,” she said. “That’s going to allow me to leverage relationships and know how to work together across jurisdictions to get things done.”

The race has been filled with accusations. Two weeks ago, Worth Girvan’s campaign published an ad featuring Christina Rackohn, a former employee whose family company merged with Gaspar’s insurance company, who alleged he created a hostile work environment.

Worth Girvan also filed an ethics complaint against Gaspar with the City Ethics Commission in October, alleging he failed to report more than $150,000 in personal and business expenditures related to his campaign and violated the city’s matching fund rules.

Gaspar called the allegations about creating a hostile working environment and violating campaign finance violations “lies.” He said he is focused on campaigning in the final week before the election.
Gaspar said Worth Girvan is a career politician who will only maintain the status quo.
“If she ends up getting elected, she’s going to have the same ideas and the same ways of addressing these issues as what got us into this mess in the first place,” he said.

On homelessness, Gaspar has criticized the city’s Inside Safe program and said a housing-first approach doesn’t work. He praised the anticamping zone law but believes the city should be tougher against encampments.

Worth Girvan supports Inside Safe but wants more permanent housing built instead of relying on interim housing. She would expand the city’s CIRCLE program, which provides 24/7 unarmed mobile response for nonviolent calls involving homeless individuals, to the West Valley.
In fundraising, Gaspar reported bringing in nearly $600,000 during the runoff campaign including matching funds, compared with about $287,000 for Worth Girvan.
District 9

Both Mazariegos and Ugarte share many similarities, including having arrived to the U.S. from Latin America as children and growing up undocumented. Both spent years working as community organizers, but now they diverge on issues such as policing and homeless policies.

Mazariegos and Ugarte were nearly evenly matched in fundraising, with both raising about $350,000 for the runoff in contributions and matching funds. Ugarte placed first in the June primary in a crowded field against five others, winning 39% of the vote. Mazariegos, who has been endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America‘s L.A. chapter, came in second with about 26%.

Ugarte’s campaign has received more than $1 million in support from independent expenditures, committees that can receive unlimited donations but cannot coordinate with a candidate’s campaign. Airbnb, Uber and the California Apartment Assn. are among the groups supporting Ugarte.
Mazariegos has criticized the companies supporting Ugarte’s candidacy, accusing them of attempting to displace low-income residents by pouring money into the election.

“They’re trying to displace our community. That’s what this fight is all about,” Mazariegos said. “I know this is a righteous campaign and a righteous cause with the people, alongside the people. Solo el pueblo salva al pueblo.” Only the people can save the people.
Ugarte said he has never met with Airbnb officials but would take a call from any group to figure out what is going to best benefit South L.A., including prioritizing protecting renters.
“I’d open my eyes and see what’s going to benefit South L.A.,” he said. “I want to focus on making South Central clean, safe and affordable.”

While both would defend immigrants, they diverge on issues such as the police budget. Ugarte supports Mayor Karen Bass’ goal of restoring the L.A. Police Department to 9,500 officers, while Mazariegos supports increasing oversight of the department’s budget and reducing its budget to fund other departments, including Recreation and Parks and the Bureau of Street Services.

Ugarte supports enforcing Municipal Ordinance 41.18, which prohibits camps near schools, daycare centers and other “sensitive” areas as a tool to clear homeless encampments. Mazariegos has said all the ordinance does is shuffle people around, and instead the focus should be on addressing addiction and mental health issues.
Mazariegos has been endorsed by Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez, City Controller Kenneth Mejia, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), United Teachers Los Angeles, L.A. Forward and several labor unions.
Ugarte has been endorsed by the L.A. County Democratic Party, Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights Action Fund, Rep. Sydney Kamlager Dove, the late Dolores Huerta and Councilmember Tim McOsker.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/31/set-active-l.headline: 35-year-old took on $20K in debt to launch a business from her dining room—now it brings in 8 figures a year
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/31/set-active-l.author: Megan Sauer

paragraphs.text: Set Active CEO Lindsey Carter used to lose sleep, cry to her friends and struggle to be present in her personal life after a rough day at work.

It's not that she expected entrepreneurship to be easy. Carter took on $20,000 in personal credit card debt and filled her Los Angeles home with inventory when she started the athleisure company in May 2018, she says. Yet years of obstacles — familiar to many an entrepreneur — followed as she tried to break Set Active into a crowded activewear industry. It took her time to figure out how to separate her professional stress from her personal life.

"I started understanding that struggle wasn't necessarily a sign that something was going wrong. Sometimes it's just the reality of building something ambitious," says Carter, 35. "And if I was going to let every setback rob me of my happiness, I'm going to be spending a very long time being unhappy."

Set Active is no industry giant, but it brought in eight figures in 2025 net sales and is profitable, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. That comes as growth in the broader activewear market has slowed: Women's activewear spending in the U.S. increased 2% between October 2025 and September 2026, down from 7% over the preceding 12 months, according to data from market research firm Circana.

Activewear still makes up 30% of U.S. apparel spending, says Circana apparel industry analyst Kristen Classi-Zummo. Shoppers these days particularly gravitate toward casual outfits and loungewear, like sweatpants and sweatshirts, over more active items like leggings and sports bras, Classi-Zummo says. That's good news for Carter, who sells color- and pattern-filled clothing sets that aren't solely intended for workouts. Set Active's Instagram posts feature women sitting on pickleball courts or the banks of the Seine in Paris.

Before launching Set Active, Carter ran her own social media company. While shopping around Los Angeles, she struggled to find matching sets of workout clothes she could wear while running errands, meeting a friend for coffee or working from home. "Everything was like yoga poses and upside-down headstands, and I was just like, 'That's not me,'" she says.

Her business idea became more real when an associate connected her with a production professional, she says. She decided to order some samples, collected feedback from friends and drew directly on the products with a permanent marker at her dining room table before sending them back to the manufacturer's designers, she says.

Going into debt to officially launch the business was just the first among many obstacles while growing Set Active. Some were personal: Carter had two children after starting the company and has never taken maternity leave. She now calls that decision "probably one of the biggest mistakes I've ever made."

She experienced what she describes as symptoms of postpartum depression in 2023, and felt like "a horrible version of myself" while simultaneously running the startup. "I let people down. I let friends down. I let employees down and I just wasn't my best self."

Other challenges have been professional. In 2026, Set Active has struggled to consistently deliver orders to customers on time, says Carter. The reasons are varied, she says, declining to go into detail, and the stakes are high approaching the holiday shopping season.

On Oct. 19, Carter wrote on Instagram that Set Active would cancel its Black Friday and Cyber Monday product launches until further notice. The company won't "drop" any clothes until the products arrive in the company's Los Angeles warehouse, putting a projected $10-plus million in sales during the most popular shopping days of the year at risk, she wrote.

"I'm walking away from a hefty revenue number," Carter now says, adding: "But at the end of the day, I built this brand on transparency and community, and the customer comes first to me always. And I'd rather make it right with the customer than hit a revenue goal."

A hard workday can still make her toss and turn at night, but she's learned how to return home to her family feeling grateful, she says. She gets satisfaction from solving problems and doing a job she believes in, she adds.

"I just take things day by day with the mindset that challenges are opportunities, and I don't really see them as the enemy," says Carter. "I think that when you sign up to be an entrepreneur, you're signing up for what that journey is going to bring."
