cnbc.com/2026/10/31/crypto-industry-spen.headline: Crypto industry pours more than $200 million into 2026 midterms to pressure Congress on favorable rules
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/crypto-industry-spen.author: Talia Kaplan

paragraphs.text: The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country.

Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen. Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle.
The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress.

Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities.

The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada.
Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global.

Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets. That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023.
Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC.
"The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC.

"In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said.

The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures.
Shifting voter priorities

The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread.

Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July.
"Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million.
Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty.

"It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods."
A test of influence
November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington.

The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown, a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat.

Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown.
A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%.
"A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023.
This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate.
Lynaugh told CNBC one of the reasons the group endorses candidates is because of their legislative record.

"We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added.
Money well-spent?

Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets, and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake.

Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return."

Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States.

Alderoty noted that the industry has gotten clearer rules from both the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures and Trading Commission. He also pointed to advancements for the industry from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, noting that Ripple received final OCC approval this week to charter Ripple National Trust Bank, a federally supervised national trust bank.
But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing.
Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January.

"You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said.
Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence.
"Every stakeholder needs to stay at the table and to continue to make the case why legislation is needed," he said.

If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation.
"Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC.

"It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added.
— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/how-to-invest-in-art.headline: How to start an art collection on any budget
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/how-to-invest-in-art.author: Trevor Laurence Jockims

paragraphs.text: The decision to invest in any collectibles market should start with curiosity and love, and buying art is no exception. While the rarest works of art in the world have sold for hundreds of millions of dollars, for most collectors, art is unlikely to match the returns offered by traditional investment markets.

A recent analysis of 10-year annualized returns including data through 2024 showed that the stock market vastly outperformed art. True, it has been an incredibly strong bull market on a historical basis, but the performance from the art market over the same time period produced some of the worst 10-year returns in seven decades.

As with any asset class experiencing a downturn, some experts see the recent weakness as a buying opportunity. The 2025 market did see some improvement, and 2026 has been an ever better year to date, with younger buyers showing up in a big way. But experts also stress that the art world is the least transparent market imaginable, with significant "insider information" involved in anticipating big jumps and the next major wave of hype.

"What I tell people is that there is so much inside information in the art world — for instance, who has bought a particular artist or who is getting a museum show in two years — that if you are an outsider, you have little hope" of catching the next big wave early, said Canice Prendergast, economics professor at the University of Chicago, who also oversees that Chicago Booth School of Business Harper Center's contemporary art collection, which houses more than 650 artworks.
It is important to understand that generating a repeatable investment strategy can be difficult — if not impossible.

"Most art is not a good investment," said Magnus Resch, who teaches art economics at Yale University and is widely recognized as a leading art market expert. "If you're buying on a limited budget, you're unlikely to see a financial return," he said.

Still, despite the complexities and opacities associated with art, experts advise that for anyone wishing to enter the market there are some basics to understand — from how to research art, to the various mediums, to what to buy at various budgets, and where to buy — before getting started.
Learn about galleries, auctions, and how artist values rise

Prendergast said a fundamental understanding of the market begins with knowing it is divided in two. The primary art market consists of galleries and the secondary market is typically auctions. And significant increases in value typically occur as art moves from one level of gallery to another and finally to auction.

"It's in anticipating moves between levels that most of the action is," Prendergast said. "There are many collectors trying to work out who is going to turn into a star [and] the key intermediaries here are galleries," he added.

Buying in the primary market first requires the squishy "knowing something about art," he said, but also understanding the hierarchy of galleries. The big moves happen as relatively undiscovered talents appear in galleries that have a history of discovering and elevating artists. Inside such jumps — from a lower tier gallery to a mid-tier one — there can be big, embedded returns.

Prendergast gave as one recent example mid-tier gallery David Fierman in New York City that showed artist Louis Fratino several years ago. Fratino's work jumped to New York-based mega-gallery David Zwirner, and is currently featured in a London show. Along with that jump came a 20x increase in the price of Fratino's paintings. Such moves, Prendergast said, are precisely the type of play investors dream about, but the reality is that they take a long time to unfold and are exceedingly hard to predict.

"The thing that people overlook is actually mid-career artists," Prendergast said. "My advice would be to go to a major art fair – at every art fair, the galleries they put in the corners are the up-and-comers," he said.
Keep it local as a beginning collector

Resch says that the difficulties in the art market should not necessarily discourage new collectors. Rather, they need to enter the market with clarity of purpose, as well as realistic expectations and aims. "Buy art you love from local galleries, artists you discover on Instagram, or art fairs where artists exhibit directly," he said. The limited possibilities for investment success can actually emphasize other, more essential advantages to the endeavor: "Assume you'll never see your money again. You're not investing for financial returns. You're investing in yourself, the artist, and the gallery," he added.

Roman Kräussl, professor of finance at the Bayes Business School in London who specializes in art as an alternative asset class, says that when it comes to art, the greater opportunity is to engage with culture than to beat the market.

Kräussl's research-based conclusion is that for the most actively engaged investors, art will provide a lower risk-adjusted return than financial market investments, but it can still be a positive return, and it can serve as a hedge against financial market risk. But when considering all the costs and fees associated with buying art, he says picking "winners" is critical.
Buyer's premiums, shipping, insurance, framing, storage if necessary, and resale fees, all factor in the overall return on investment.

This offers another reason to stick to the galleries and fairs over auction houses, since the atmosphere involves more opportunities for social interaction with other collectors and even the artists themselves. "Art is the most illiquid, nontransparent, opaque investment you can engage with. But it is also tons of fun," Kräussl said.
The enrichment is more likely to be to yourself as a person, not to your bank account, with the big payoffs coming from "intellectual, cultural, and human-relevant perspectives."

"You will meet the most interesting people of your life," Kräussl said. "Do not 'Spotify' art," he said. "Go to small events. See the artists. Experience. And if you like, go for it. If not, search further. But do not wait for someone to tell you what to buy. Develop your own taste," he said, "and then trust it."
How to invest on a $5,000, $10,000 and $100,000 budget
Traditional mediums still dominate in the art market.

Painting remains the most popular medium for collectors, according to the 2026 Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting, which focuses on the high-net-worth end of the market, surveying 3,100 collectors across 10 markets. That is measured by both participation (76% of buyers) and value (31% of total fine art expenditure). Sculpture was the second-largest area of spending (15%), followed by works on paper (10%) and digital art (9%).

But that may not necessarily be the best place to start for everyone, and one point emphasized by multiple experts is that the smarter plays happen in the less-hyped areas. Hype can drive extreme pricing disparity and inflation, and it is often evidence that there has already been movement behind the scenes that preceded all of the hype. In other words, hype may indicate already being too late to the table.

Another way to approach the art market, according to Resch, is through a focus on prints and editions — multiple, authorized copies of an artwork from an original source — which he says are often overlooked. "They offer access to blue-chip artists at a fraction of the price," he said.

That contrasts with investments in emerging artists, which can be riskier. "An artist can sell out every gallery exhibition and still have virtually no resale market," he said, "so don't believe in popularity. Instead, check if an artist has an auction market."
Resch says for any individual "willing to gamble at $5,000," he would look for prints or works on paper by blue-chip artists, ideally at auction.
At $10,000, he says original works in contemporary art day sales at major auction houses are an option, though works of art on auction at these events can start at much higher prices.

At $100,000, Resch says the focus can turn to artists represented by leading galleries who have exhibited at major museums. "I'd rather buy one exceptional work for $100,000 than five mediocre ones for $20,000 each," he said. But no purchase should be made without doing considerable homework: "Visit galleries, research artists, and compare gallery and auction prices. People compare prices when buying a $500 television. Why wouldn't they do the same when buying a $50,000 painting?"

Georgina Adam, editor at large for The Art Newspaper and a lecturer at Sotheby's and Christie's in London, said liking a piece remains an essential criterion, especially at lower price points and in areas of the art market that aren't particularly strong. That can lead to buying prices that are lower, but the ability to resell will also be very difficult, she said, adding that many pieces in 19th-century painting, as well as antiques, silver, and porcelain, feature these dynamics. "While it is a sum, $10,000 is not life changing if you lose it, but from the higher price points up, then readers will at least want the art to hold its value."
Higher price points are also more typically associated with the benefit of auction records and clearer research to track pricing, provenance, and resales, according to Adam.
How to research the art market and choose advice sources
Whatever you buy, "Don't buy on a whim," Adam said. "Study the artist first."
Such study can occur with the assistance of a trusted advisor, but even taking on an advisor takes research, Adam said, who is herself a member of the Association of Professional Art Advisors.
She also cautioned that while specialists at auction houses and dealers will be knowledgeable, they all have "skin in the game."

"Look for dealers who have a proven track record, and belong to a professional association with a code of ethics. Inclusion in a well-known fair (Frieze, Armory, et cetera) is a sign of seriousness," she said. "Fairs enable the buyer to look around in a less pressured environment and get prices. Galleries will generally be happy to talk about their artists," she said.

One platform she strictly advises serious collectors to avoid is eBay. "Don't buy art from eBay, unless you just want a poster that goes with your décor. There are plenty of bad actors out there. Remember that fakes can be accompanied by fake certificates of authenticity," Adam said.

Christoph Noe, the co-founder of Larry's List, which covers the current art collectors market, said direct relationships with artists, studio visits, making collections public, and openly rejecting hype and FOMO (fear of missing out) buying are all important practices for collectors. "Notably, not one collector in our listing mentioned TikTok, YouTube or LinkedIn as relevant to their collecting practice/research," he said.

According to the Art Basel/UBS report, most collectors did their own research before buying, with 72% undertaking moderate or significant research, and that figure rising to 80% among Gen Z collectors. The most commonly used external sources of advice were auction house experts (31%), art advisors (30%), artists (29%), and dealers (27%).

Digital research is being used more often, according to the Art Basel/UBS data, with 58% of respondents using digital resources for advice, led by online publications and press (27%) and apps or AI tools (22%, up from just 4% in 2024). And despite Noe's comments, social media is becoming more influential: 32% of collectors cited either Instagram or X/Twitter as sources of advice, according to the Art Basel/UBS report.

While most experts emphasize in-person research and interaction as critical to the collecting process, collectors surveyed in the Art Basel/UBS report were broadly positive about AI's role in finding and buying art, with 67% saying AI made a positive impact on artist and artwork discoverability; 66% citing it for personalized advice and recommendations; 65% on provenance and authenticity verification; and 64% on pricing and valuation analysis.

"The biggest mistake investor collectors make," according to Prendergast, "is their belief that 'I just know this is great art.' You don't. You cannot evaluate a piece of art without knowing what came before. The art market is also very professionalized in that a good MFA can often copy pretty much anything. So just because something looks nice does not mean it's of much monetary value," he said.
When it comes to properly researching art, there is no replacement for getting out into the world.

"Get a double espresso in a nice gallery, stay for a glass of red wine, meet the artists, participate," Kräussl said. "Buy your first piece, risk it, and you will have something interesting to say at the next dinner."

Kräussl says he concludes all of his art-finance presentations and seminars with the same piece of advice that he would give to a dinner party guest: "'Buy what you like!' After all, they may have to live with it for the rest of their life," he said.

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/trump-gas-diesel-pri.headline: Trump promised to slash energy costs — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/trump-gas-diesel-pri.author: Spencer Kimball

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office.
"My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign.
"Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon."

But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
"Prices have never been this high this late in the year," De Haan said.

Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year. The price of diesel, critical to transportation and agriculture, has surged about 70% over the past year, to $6.32 a gallon.
During the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, the year that Russia invaded Ukraine and triggered an energy crisis, retail gas prices stood at $3.80, according to AAA data.
Own goal

"Trump got in his own way," De Haan said. "Back in December, we predicted that 2026 was going to be the cheapest year for gas since 2020. That required no effort. And obviously, it hasn't gone that way."

Fuel prices have spiked since Trump decided to attack Iran in a joint attack with Israel on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with a wave of strikes on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, severely depressing oil flows through the vital shipping route.
Trump told voters at a rally in Michigan last Sunday that rising fuel prices are a "small price to pay" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The White House said gas prices when adjusted for inflation have been higher around previous election days.

Exports through Hormuz have rebounded since the summer as the U.S. military helped ships through the strait. But the Middle East disruption has been compounded by Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi Arabian refineries, and Ukraine's strikes on refineries in Russia. Trump had promised to end that war in the first week of his second term, but the conflict is stuck in an intractable stalemate.

"Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth," ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday after the nation's largest oil company posted huge profits thanks to the disruptions.
Airlines have hiked their fares to cover high costs from jet fuel, their biggest expense other than labor, hurting the fight to contain inflation.
Political pressure

Trump came under political pressure from Republicans to take action on fuel prices ahead of Tuesday's election. The cost of diesel is hurting big farm states like Iowa that have overwhelmingly backed Trump in his presidential campaigns. The senate race in the Hawkeye State has become competitive.

Trump briefly contemplated a diesel export ban as Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) lobbied to help the state's farmers. The president decided against it because it might also have raised gasoline prices.
Instead, Trump issued an executive order to allow truckers to use tax-exempt, offroad diesel on U.S. highways, and announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Trump later struck a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to export about 6 million barrels of diesel into the global market through November.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and even some Republican senators slammed the agreement as rewarding Russian aggression. Energy analysts said the diesel volumes in the Russia deal are small compared to global demand and won't have a meaningful impact on prices.

More recently, crude oil prices have rallied ahead of the election. Trump has said he will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterms. But the market is pricing in the risk of another round of fighting after voting ends on Tuesday. International Brent crude oil prices are up more than 13% in October and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 15%.

"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," De Haan said, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."

cnbc.com/2026/10/31/binance-hack-crypto-.headline: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety
cnbc.com/2026/10/31/binance-hack-crypto-.author: Davis Giangiulio

paragraphs.text: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange.
A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents.
Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens.
Questions over the safety of users' funds

"I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place."
For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure.
There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore.

Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan, CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.

"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this."
Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
Vulnerabilities on offshore platforms

A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.

In a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note.

"They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today."

Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X.
"Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach, though the company didn't specify what they were.
A unique target in a changing landscape

Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack.

Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents.

However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach.

It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure.
"I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said.

"Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added.

Inside a podcast studio at Turning Point USA’s headquarters last month, a former witch sat in a pink velvet armchair, telling Alex Clark about the demon that stalked her house. Even though this self-described witch, known on TikTok as @yourspiritualbigsis, had only ever used her powers for good, she believed that practicing sorcery had made her vulnerable to satanic forces. The demon—10, maybe 15 feet tall, whose face had “divots” for eyes—had tormented her, she said, until she spoke the name “Jesus” out loud and became a Christian.

Clark, whose Culture Apothecary is one of America’s top wellness podcasts, told her guest that she was going to ask “counter questions,” as she does with everyone she interviews. In this case: If the spells she was doing were technically producing good—helping people make money, get pregnant, pass a test—why is that evil? How can Christians tell whether someone has the spiritual gift of prophecy or they’re harnessing dark power? Clark wasn’t concerned about whether sorcery was real—“It is real,” she said—but when her guest brought up the occult sacrifice of babies procured through a sex-trafficking network supported by the government and Hollywood, Clark had no further questions.

This was just another day in the studio. Since 2024, when she launched her podcast with a mission to “heal a sick culture” and to do so “physically, emotionally, and spiritually,” Clark has welcomed a wild array of guests, united only by their willingness to contradict conventional wisdom and generally accepted facts. Listening to Culture Apothecary, you might hear a regenerative farmer recommend the subcutaneous fat of a “healthy, happy pig” as a miracle skin-care ingredient, a chiropractor talk about testing muscle strength using “homeopathically charged frequencies,” the self-described Christian nationalist Doug Wilson suggest spanking as a form of biblical discipline for children, or leaders in the “Make America Healthy Again” movement disavow vaccines and industrial agriculture.

On the podcast, Clark positions herself not as an expert but as a question-asking woman of the people. Depending on who you talk with—and I spoke with Clark’s colleagues, her critics, her close friends, her mom—she’s either a powerful force connecting everyday women to the GOP or an agent of chaos. She has been the Republican commentator posting bikini photos while her peers post pictures in cardigans and the single 33-year-old podcasting about child-rearing. By her own account, she is also the contributor at TPUSA, the late Charlie Kirk’s conservative organization, who causes the nonprofit the most trouble with the Trump administration.

Clark grew up in an evangelical, conservative home in southern Indiana. After high school, she worked at Sephora and took classes at a community college, and planned to transfer to a four-year school for fashion merchandising and journalism. But then she started an internship at a Louisville, Kentucky, radio station, which led to a full-time job as an anchor and the unofficial Millennial-woman correspondent for a morning show. She had always loved pop culture and politics, and came to TPUSA in 2019 so that she could air her conservative views while discussing Dancing With the Stars. Even before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Donald Trump teamed up, she pivoted to podcasting about wellness because she thought that talking about organic food, herbal medicine, and suspicions about vaccines could bring more women into the GOP. When the MAHA movement came to Washington, Clark’s own profile rose, and soon she had the attention of some of the most powerful men in the country.

But recently, MAHA and MAGA have started to drift apart. MAHA is failing to draw hordes of voters to Republicans; the Trump administration has failed MAHA on many of the issues Clark cares about. As the rift widens, Clark is stretching to keep a foot on each side and figuring out, if she does have to choose one, how to take her audience of MAHA moms and conservative young women along with her.

Between tapings, Clark ate takeout from a seed-oil-free restaurant as she reviewed podcast transcripts and a spreadsheet of upcoming episodes, reacting to them with facial expressions worthy of a mime. Her team member took notes while she dictated episode titles (“He Was Gay, Then Everything Changed” and “Acetaminophen Before Age 4: What Parents Should Know”). The whole time, she exuded the energy of someone who had incredible gossip to share. The minute I stepped away to check out a rack of Culture Apothecary sweatshirts (Trust Farms, Not Pharma), Clark shrieked. “We’re all peeing our pants, screaming, crying, throwing up,” she said, her eyes wide and made even more dramatic by false lashes. Taylor Swift had just announced a new single. She looked for clues in Swift’s post and predicted that the music video would debut later that week at the MTV Video Music Awards. (She was right.)

Like many 30-something women, she is devoted to Taylor Swift, and, however unfiltered Clark can sometimes seem, like Swift, she aims to make every detail of her world matter. Her studio’s forest-green wallpaper includes illustrations of her preferred remedies for America’s ailing culture: raw milk, steak, butter, wildflowers, hair bows, the Bible. Her podcast-planning spreadsheet is in that same bespoke shade of green, which she developed with graphic designers. (She calls it “Forks, Washington,” after the town made famous in Twilight.) Even her off-the-cuff X posts can be seen as part of her brand—a girl speaking her mind, even if that includes insinuating that Candace Owens performed oral sex on Vladimir Putin. The ads she writes for the show might seem borderline nonsensical—in one ad for a clean-beauty company, for reasons that I do not understand, she includes a monologue about a taxidermied possum who wears a cheerleading uniform and is named Gerald—but according to Clark, that strategy tends to bring high returns for her sponsors. What listener is going to want to skip those?

Not the “Cuteservatives,” as Clark calls her fandom. They keep tabs on her personal life, too, and at the TPUSA Women’s Leadership Summit in June, she orchestrated an announcement for them. “There’s one thing I haven’t told you guys,” she said. The stage lights went out, and when they came back on, she was standing beside Vance Voetberg, the bespectacled author of the MAHA fitness Substack Running on Butter. On her finger was a diamond ring. “I’m engaged!” The crowd screamed. Later, on Instagram, she described him as her “‘BUTTER’ half.” She has since released a steady stream of content about their small summer wedding at his family home in rural Washington State: a recipe for the prosciutto butter they served, details about the outfits she picked for Voetberg and her maid of honor, and a two-hour interview with her new husband, in which she revealed that she walked down the aisle to Swift’s “You Are In Love” and gifted all of her guests a Jaspr, perhaps the most aesthetically pleasing air purifier in existence.

Clark is also, like Swift, a woman of distinct eras. For most of her life, she was focused not on health but pop culture. MTV was banned in her childhood home, but when she saw Britney Spears’s “I’m a Slave 4 U” music video at a sleepover, “I was absolutely mesmerized,” she said. She idolized Spears, Christina Aguilera, and Jessica Simpson. She was also so conservative “that she’d make Rush Limbaugh look like a liberal,” her high-school radio and TV teacher, Timothy Dench, told me.

She knew even then that she wanted an audience made up of young women. She dreamed about being a fashion writer at Teen Vogue or Seventeen, but got the job on a local radio show. Listeners knew her as a fast-food connoisseur and the “Chicken Nugget Princess”—she ate nuggets at least once a day and would peel off the skin, eat that, then turn to the meat. By 2019, she was co-hosting an Indianapolis morning show, but her superiors were telling her to stop bringing up politics on air and on Twitter. She imagined a show that would combine her passions for the GOP and for pop culture—“TMZ and Fox News if they had a baby,” she told me—and pitched it to Charlie Kirk at TPUSA as a way to show women that Republicans could be cool. POPlitics became TPUSA’s first show.

Clark’s wellness era started around 2020. She was skeptical of the COVID shot and never got it, and, after watching the Hulu series Dopesick, became convinced that Big Pharma’s misdeeds were the greatest true-crime story ever told. Practically overnight, she emptied out her fridge and began her transformation into someone who keeps a tiny vial of unrefined sea salt in her purse, sits in front of red light every day, and makes a morning smoothie with six different types of powder, glyphosate-free oats, aloe-vera juice, Cowboy Colostrum, collagen, creatine, strawberries, cherries, pineapple, peaches, and an entire avocado.

And she noticed that her audience was moving toward wellness with her. Whenever she had a guest on to talk about why, say, women should be suspicious of the pill, viewership spiked, so she met with Kirk about rebranding her show around health. “If we are the ones championing these issues, we will grab all the female voters,” she remembers telling him in July 2024. Two weeks before Culture Apothecary was scheduled to debut, she watched RFK Jr. endorse Trump live at a rally in Glendale, Arizona. The crowd was so electric it reminded her of Swift’s Eras Tour.

A month later, Clark got a standing ovation at the Capitol. Her speech at a Senate roundtable, on behalf of Millennial mothers outraged by food and pharmaceutical corporations harming their children, cemented her as MAHA’s big sister. Sponsors and listeners flocked to Culture Apothecary, and Clark, who now had the attention of both stay-at-home moms and powerful politicians, became the person most visibly fusing MAHA and MAGA for women.

Over the past year, that union has gotten shakier. Trump’s accord with MAHA—his promise to let RFK Jr. “run wild” on health and food—has been one defining force in his second administration, and the health secretary has managed to remake federal vaccine policy, change the food pyramid, and extract some voluntary commitments from companies about food dye. But many MAHA supporters feel like they were owed more—especially when it came to regulating food and pesticides. The disillusionment has gotten bad enough that one of MAHA’s top leaders, Calley Means, resigned from the Trump administration less than two weeks before the midterms, reportedly out of frustration that the government wasn’t advancing MAHA’s food policy.

Clark, meanwhile, keeps getting angrier. In January, she and other MAHA activists were abruptly disinvited from an event at the Department of Health and Human Services—which they believe was because MAHA had recently launched a petition to fire the head of the EPA. Someone later sent Clark a picture of the check-in table: On the front page of the “Not Permitted List” was her photograph. (In response to a request for comment, HHS referred me to the White House, which did not comment on the disinvitation; a spokesperson told me, “The MAHA coalition has never been stronger or more empowered.”) After the White House and the Supreme Court both came down in favor of the weed killer glyphosate, the chemical that MAHA hates most, Clark headlined a rally outside the Supreme Court Building, wearing a camo jacket that read: I TURN INTO ERIN BROCKOVICH WHEN I’M ANGRY.

Clark thinks that Trump is a true MAHA believer (despite his love of McDonald’s) and that he’s getting hemmed in by those around him. Before the April rally, Trump met with her and other MAHA leaders, and he kept talking about making an executive order about vaccines. According to Clark, what he described was so extreme that if she shared the details, they would “make him look bad right before midterms.” She believes that his advisers steered him away from it. (Trump did later issue an executive order reducing the number of diseases included in the childhood-vaccination schedule. The White House spokesperson wrote in an email that “President Trump wants to execute on ideas that are durable, long-lasting, and hold up in court to ensure the permanence” of the MAHA movement.) Clark still loves the president, but “I have zero stomach for conservative commentators that all they do is blow the Trump admin,” she said. “Sorry to be crass.” As a Republican, she’d be sad if the GOP loses this cycle, but as a MAHA leader, “then I’d kind of get to flex an ‘I told you so’” about the party needing her audience’s vote.

Clark’s own career doesn’t necessarily hinge on the White House’s approval or MAHA’s political viability. Her wellness episodes were doing well before the MAHA label existed, and she’s proved that she has an instinct for where the conservative movement is going and how to get American women—even those who don’t think of themselves as political—to follow it. Maybe this election will mark the end of an era for MAHA. But Clark is already entering a new one herself.

After a day of taping, Clark took me back to her apartment in Scottsdale, Arizona, where she now lives with her butter half. It still looked like a Millennial girl’s Barbie Dreamhouse: maximalist floral wallpaper, a brocade velvet shower curtain, black-and-white striped accent chairs. A Jaspr air purifier hummed in the corner, and on the floor, her Pekingese, Mochi, ate raw rabbit and organic pumpkin puree from his dog bowl and drank glass-bottled, micro-plastic-tested Loonen water.

Voetberg had homemade cookies and raw milk waiting for us. He is a national-champion fiddle player and competitive runner, who grew up homeschooled and one of 10 kids. He’d been a fan of Clark’s podcast for years, and after lobbying mutual friends to set them up, he and Clark had their first date last fall, got engaged over Memorial Day weekend, and got married at the end of August. They’d just returned from their Bora-Bora honeymoon. “We have sex now!” She laughed and leaned over their glasses of raw milk to kiss him.

Clark’s primary goal in life was always to get married and have a family. When, at 23, she appeared on the Fox dating show Coupled, she was so earnest about looking for a husband that the producers told her she needed to relax, she said. Over the years, being single became an occupational hazard. Groypers, the followers of the alt-right leader Nick Fuentes, would DM her pictures of empty egg cartons and tell her that she was useless because she wasn’t married with kids; feminists criticized her for being an unmarried career woman who told other women to focus on their families.

Now that she’s married, she told me, she will not be a tradwife who embodies a pioneer-esque domestic crunchiness: A nail artist comes to her house every two weeks, and she “wouldn’t last five seconds living more than 10 minutes away from a Sephora.” Nor does she plan to adhere to strict domestic gender roles. Voetberg told me that he takes the lead on household chores; he made those cookies and stepped in to cook chili for dinner while Clark was busy talking with me. She has said she will put family first, but she also wants a career. Between that and her choice to continue using the last name Clark professionally, some people on the right call her a closet feminist. She is not, she told me, and believes that feminism has been a “net negative.” Voetberg chimed in to say that he could see how people might think that she has benefited from the movement. But Clark kept returning to the idea that, overall, feminism had badly served women by pushing them to prioritize their careers over motherhood.

Her latest Culture Apothecary series—“Wife School”—certainly has gone well beyond any feminist’s comfort zone. In these interviews, she asked married Christian women about how to be a good biblical wife. Guests had tips on household organization but also on giving one’s husband input while still allowing him to be the family’s final decision maker. In one particularly controversial episode, the Christian writer Tilly Dillehay said that, for the health of a marriage, women should have sex with their husbands even when they do not want to.

If part of MAHA’s success was that it could speak to people across the political spectrum, the issues Clark is now exploring almost certainly don’t. Over chili, Voetberg said that he thought aspects of first-wave feminism had been good. Like the right to vote, I suggested.
“Don’t get her started on that,” Voetberg said.

“I’m not gonna advocate to repeal the Nineteenth!” Clark replied, although some people in the MAGAverse insist that the Nineteenth Amendment was a mistake that should, like Roe, be corrected. I asked whether they’d vote as a family, and they started talking about landownership, which was once attached to suffrage, and how the question of who should vote in America was a “giant, giant topic,” as Voetberg put it. Clark joked—maybe?—that she’d love it if she needed her husband’s permission to open a bank account, as American women once did. (Later, she wrote in an email that she and Voetberg had not consciously adopted household voting as a practice—“We just automatically vote the same.”)

When she has kids—and she wants to be pregnant before January—she said that she may look at her newborn and decide to never do another interview again. But her current plan is to keep working. Her audience loved “Wife School,” she said, and she is sensing another groundswell like the one she saw toward health—this one toward human connection, in community and family. Championing those issues could be another way to grab female voters: Moms of all political persuasions can probably agree that, as a recent Culture Apothecary episode argued, “babies don’t need all that STUFF!”—even if many of them are not quite ready to give their husbands the final say on their family decisions, finances, or sex lives.

Knowing how seriously to take Clark’s more provocative stances can be difficult. If Taylor Swift is one of Clark’s idols, so is 1980s and ’90s Howard Stern: He was clever and funny, and wasn’t afraid to be shocking. (“I’m not saying, as a Christian, that I agree with the type of content he was doing,” she said.) For similar reasons, she admires the early days of the sex-and-dating podcast Call Her Daddy, when the hosts graphically detailed their own exploits. “I don’t ever want people to feel comfortable,” Clark said—and her more MAHA-leaning listeners might not be, if she doubles down on a conservative vision of family and femininity. But, she told me, “I love controversy.” It keeps people listening. “Whether you listen to me because you love me, or listen to me because you hate me,” she said, “you’re still a fan either way.”

techcrunch.com/2026/10/31/i-took-two-iph.headline: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
techcrunch.com/2026/10/31/i-took-two-iph.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: “I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”

I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh!), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.

When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.

As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases. I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.

As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.

There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”

As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)

I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.

Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.

Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.

This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)

In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.

For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.

Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.

I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.
However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.
This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.

It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.

Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.

There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.

Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID.)

Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.
Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.

For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

Below are a few photos shot with the Duo versus others shot with the 17 Pro Max. None of the photos are using any special settings or filters; they are intentionally just average, non-professional point-and-shoot shots. Among my complaints are that the Duo’s image processing can, at times, make fine details, like the leaves on trees, look overprocessed. Meanwhile, distant landscapes can appear flatter or smoothed over — though, to be fair, the Blue Ridge Mountains are naturally hazy, so it’s hard to say how much of that is the camera. (Shots from the mountaintop were in low-light conditions — it was getting dark out.)
DUO PHOTOS:
PRO MAX PHOTOS:

As for why to get the phone? This one’s easy; it’s a foldable. From Apple. First, foldables are whimsical in a way that slab phones will never be. They are toys for grown-ups! Developers are also clearly having fun building for the new format, so there are lots of new apps to play with. Plus, it’s a great way to watch movies, particularly with that Duo Folio case with a kickstand.

Second, it’s a foldable from Apple. The company has taken its time to get it right, which comes through in the details, from the barely visible crease to the consistent aspect ratio between screens, allowing content to scale proportionally. It’s also a foldable in Apple’s software ecosystem, which matters for those who move between Apple devices and services and who use and pay for apps that are designed for iOS specifically.
But here’s a small confession: in day-to-day life, I didn’t unfold the Duo as much as I thought I would. (To be clear: I absolutely did unfold it! I just thought I would do it more!)

There are two reasons for this. One: unfolding the device in public invites conversation, and it feels sort of like a flex; I’m not always in a place where I have time to chat. I expect this problem to diminish in time as the novelty wears off.

That said, I still had roughly half a dozen conversations with strangers while I was on vacation, from fellow shoppers to servers to business owners. I even handed them the device at times (when they couldn’t easily run off with it!) and let them fold and unfold it. One person wanted to see the Kid Cue feature in particular, which displays playful Snoopy animations on the phone’s outer display to get children to look toward the camera when you take their picture. They were genuinely delighted by this.

Anecdotally, the consensus was that the unfolded screen was something of a marvel to most: “You can’t see the hinge!” “Is that a screen protector or is it just like that?” (The inner screen has a matte, nano-texture finish, reducing glare. Once explained, it was also praised as “pretty cool.” )

“What if you get sand in it?,” a former Samsung Galaxy Fold owner asked. Their older Android foldable had been ruined after a trip to the beach where sand got into the hinge, causing damage to the screen. (This was not uncommon at the time.) The Duo is rated IP68, the “6” signifying higher dust resistance, making it dust-tight. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 was rated IP48, by comparison. I’m not expecting it will have the same issues, though I do hope a reviewer takes it to the beach soon!

I am certain that at least one of the handful of strangers I spoke to had never actually seen a phone that folded before. The fact that Apple has now made one means this concept will no longer be niche; it will be known to the mainstream.

The other reason I didn’t unfold it as much as I thought is that doing so feels like the start of a more intentional screen time session. When I do unfold the phone now, it’s because I’m truly engaging with what I’m doing on the phone, like watching a show on Netflix or dragging two apps side-by-side in split-screen mode for multitasking. (I love reading news in Inoreader and having X open off to the side to see what people are saying about the news, but that’s a use case that won’t apply to everyone!)

The split-screen feature is easy to use, too – with the app open, you swipe up from the bottom, then drag it to the left or right edge. Target boxes on each side help you visualize where it can move to, which is helpful. (You can also long-press on an app icon to open a split view, but I don’t do this as much.)
But as something of a “mini” phone in terms of screen size when closed, I’m somehow less drawn to what I think of as time-wasting apps like TikTok, Instagram, or casual games.

I’ve been thinking about this, and I don’t believe it’s just the lack of screen real estate when the phone is folded, or the fact that vertical apps haven’t been designed for the Duo’s unfolded landscape screen. Those concerns make sense from a practical, usability standpoint, of course, but there’s something more to this behavioral change, I believe.

For years, phones have been getting bigger, taller, thinner, and more comfortable to hold. Consequently, they easily sucked us into their digital worlds. With the Duo, the design seems to interrupt the way smartphones effortlessly pull us in, begging us to open apps and scroll endlessly.

Rather, the Duo feels like a device you open and use when you have reason to do so, not something you reflexively turn to when you’re bored or have a few minutes to spare. Because the best app use cases are when the phone is unfolded, and unfolding is something you do with careful consideration (and careful hands!), device use becomes more thoughtful.
This is not a bad thing. It also aligns with the embrace of retro tech already underway, where knobs and dials and buttons make engaging with technology feel more deliberate.
And for that reason, despite its faults, the Duo won me over. It’s a phone that’s compelling and fun — a phone I enjoyed picking up, but also found easier to put down.
