nytimes.com/2026/10/31/technology/binanc.headline: How Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Went Down

paragraphs.text: At about 4:20 p.m. on Thursday, a string of unusual transactions started to cause alarm at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Money was pouring out of the company’s accounts, a multibillion-dollar deluge of digital coins. It had all the hallmarks of a crypto heist — a high-speed bank robbery conducted over the internet.

As the news spread, Binance’s top executives put together an informal war room on Wea, the company’s internal messaging system, with about 100 participants, including specialized cryptocurrency tracers and security personnel.

They eventually transitioned to a mass conference call, with 100 boxes on the screen, where employees took turns muting and then unmuting, communicating in a mixture of English and Chinese. Among them was He Yi, Binance’s co-chief executive, who is seven months pregnant, and worked through the night from her base in Abu Dhabi, taking a call at 3 a.m. local time.

Ms. He and her colleagues were navigating one of the most damaging crises in Binance’s long and troubled history. A team of North Korean hackers had penetrated the exchange analysts said, and drained more than $6 billion in the largest crypto heist of all time. Binance was forced to halt deposits and withdrawals, and posted a series of frantic messages on X, promising that it would cover any losses.

It was a surreal situation made even more surreal by the actions of Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, who spent the evening narrating the events to his 12.9 million followers on X. He posted prayer hand emojis, publicly jousted with the site’s owner, Elon Musk, and insisted that “user funds are SAFU” — using a bit of crypto slang to reassure customers that hundreds of millions of dollars in deposits would not simply vanish into thin air.
“It hurts, but we will survive,” Mr. Zhao declared.

The impact of the Binance attack rippled across the crypto industry, from Abu Dhabi to New York, setting off a frantic effort to salvage some of the stolen funds and prompting law enforcement inquiries. This account of how the hack unfolded is based on interviews with four people with knowledge of the events, as well as analyses by crypto forensics firms and documents reviewed by The New York Times.

For years, Binance has been the most important and contentious company in the crypto world. After Mr. Zhao founded it in 2017, it quickly turned into a behemoth, the No. 1 destination for customers looking to convert traditional currencies into digital coins like Bitcoin and Ether.

It also became a haven for crime. In 2023, Binance pleaded guilty to anti-money-laundering violations that had allowed criminals to move money and paid $4.3 billion in penalties to U.S. regulators. Mr. Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison.

For all its troubles, however, Binance never lost popularity among the crypto faithful. It remains the world’s largest exchange by a distance, and Mr. Zhao, who lives in Abu Dhabi, is something of an industry folk hero. Binance’s main platform is banned in the United States. But last year, the company forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the Trump family crypto start-up. President Trump granted a pardon to Mr. Zhao last October, paving the way for Binance to expand into the U.S. market.
But on the night of Oct. 29, the company had to deal with the aftermath of the $6 billion hack.

Such attacks have become commonplace in the crypto world. In February 2025, the North Koreans stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, a rival exchange. Bybit was breached after Ben Zhou, its chief executive, approved a seemingly routine transaction that granted the thieves access to the exchange’s internal system.

It’s not clear precisely how the North Koreans got around Binance’s defenses. An initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop, Binance said Friday. But the company later said it had uncovered “additional points of breach.”

Much of the drama played out in public. Almost all crypto transactions are recorded on the blockchain, a ledger of money movements that anyone can look up. That meant crypto analysts could see funds leaving Binance in real time.

On Thursday afternoon, Jonathan Levin, the chief executive of the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, was on a video call with a former senior U.S. official, discussing the need for the U.S. government to deploy cyber attacks against adversaries. Then Mr. Levin got the news about Binance.
“I looked at my phone and was like, ‘Oh, this doesn’t look good,’” he said in an interview.

A group of Chainalysis employees gathered in a conference room in New York named “Silk Road,” after another crypto platform that was famously hacked. They worked until the early hours of Friday morning, eating Malaysian food and analyzing transactions to get a clearer picture of what had happened.

Soon both Chainalysis and another analytics firm, TRM Labs, attributed the attack to an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. North Koreans have targeted crypto companies for years, using the proceeds of those thefts to fund its nuclear program, according to Western officials.

The hackers have developed increasingly complex strategies to steal crypto and launder the proceeds, a painstaking endeavor that can take months to complete. In a blog post on Friday, Chainalysis said the attackers had deployed “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” conducting thousands of transactions over a short period, probably with the help of automation.
“The level of sophistication of these actors can’t be understated,” Mr. Levin said in the interview.

At the same time, Binance’s colleagues in the industry mobilized to intercept some of the laundered crypto. Certain digital coin issuers can freeze funds, allowing them to halt a money-laundering operation in its tracks.

Soon after the hack, Tether and Circle, two major issuers, announced that they had frozen stashes of their own coins that the hackers had seized from Binance, a combined total of more than $2 billion in crypto. Binance is now working to gain access to those funds, the company said.
But $2.4 billion in crypto is already “beyond any issuer’s reach,” according to TRM. In a social media post on Friday, Binance said that it had set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses from the hack.

How much money Binance has in reserve is not publicly known. After midnight, Mr. Musk posted a grimacing emoji underneath an X post comparing Mr. Zhao to Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced crypto mogul whose FTX exchange collapsed in 2022.
“Bad time to troll,” Mr. Zhao responded. “Please stop.” He noted that Binance owns over $1 billion in shares in SpaceX, Mr. Musk’s rocket company.

Mr. Zhao’s comment got the attention of Ms. He, Binance’s co-chief executive and his longtime romantic partner. (Mr. Zhao is Binance’s majority shareholder but doesn’t have a formal role at the company.)
“Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares,” Ms. He wrote.
With the industry reeling, Ms. He and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, told Binance employees to “stay disciplined,” according to a message reviewed by The Times.
"Do not speculate internally or externally,” the message said. “We know this is an intense moment, and we deeply appreciate everyone working overtime to make this right.”

They also tried to address the growing unease in the crypto world. Speaking in Mandarin in a video posted to X on Friday, Ms. He said that the rise of artificial intelligence had turned hacking into “a threat to the entire industry.”
“Of course, there are many things that we have done wrong,” she said. “We should have invested in security much earlier and more extensively, and established more rigorous standards.”

Word of Binance’s hack even reached Mr. Trump, who was asked about it by a reporter on Friday. “People never see the money anymore,” he said. “I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous. But they say they have it pretty much under control. We’ll see.”
Among the companies that rushed to Binance’s aid was the Trump family firm, World Liberty, the issuer of a coin known as USD1.

Zach Witkoff, the company’s chief executive and the son of one of Mr. Trump’s top advisers, announced on X that World Liberty had frozen $27 million in USD1 that was “associated with the Binance hack.”
“We stand by our industry partners,” he wrote.
“Thank you!” Mr. Zhao responded, followed by three prayer hand emojis.

nytimes.com/2026/10/31/us/politics/susan.headline: Susan Collins Is Always Keeping Score

paragraphs.text: Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. He met with Mayor Carl Sheline, a fellow Democrat, in his office and over drinks at a local Italian restaurant. They had a series of phone calls. But ultimately Mr. Sheline declined to back him.
Ms. Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent, was not in the room, at the bar, or on the line.
But she had made her presence known.

Mr. Sheline had various reasons for withholding his support, he said in an interview. Among them, he acknowledged, were a housing project, a food distribution center, and a mill museum in Lewiston. Ms. Collins had helped with the finances for all of them.
“It’s just an environment of possible retribution,” Mr. Wood said. “It is that fear she instills.”

Over nearly 30 years, Ms. Collins, a self-styled moderate in a familiar Maine mold, has cultivated a public persona as a workhorse and a fastidious maestro of constituent services and pork-barrel disbursements, using her Washington know-how to get her constituents what they need.

But for just as long, her detractors say, she has managed to mostly mask a another reality. “The gentlewoman from Maine,” as her colleagues say on the Senate floor, is a formidable power broker who can play a fierce brand of politics with a how-dare-you air. According to more than 40 interviews with Republicans and Democrats in Maine politics, former staff, colleagues and longtime observers, Ms. Collins has wielded power not so much as a Yankee Republican but as a shrewd machine politician.
“It’s almost like Tammany Hall,” said Amy Fried, a retired political scientist from the University of Maine. “You’re going to get this benefit here if you vote for me.”
Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former aide to Ms. Collins, did not disagree.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said. “She’s openly discussing the fact that Maine is going to be set back if she’s not in that position,” he added. “It puts people in the position of very clearly understanding that voting against her is a vote against their own well-being.”
Ms. Collins’s staff stresses that she has worked to bring money back to all communities in Maine — regardless of whether they support her.

Annie Clark, a longtime aide to Ms. Collins, provided The New York Times an exhaustive list of projects, from Orono and Ogunquit to Belfast and Blue Hill, for which the senator had secured funding since 2021. The senator got $234 million for 96 projects in Cumberland and Knox counties — the only two counties she lost in 2020. In Portland, where she received just 21 percent of the vote: $51.2 million for 28 projects.

“Senator Collins has been extraordinarily effective,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins. “She works tirelessly to deliver results for the state, meets with thousands of Mainers every year, and she secures billions of dollars for communities in all of Maine’s 16 counties whether they vote for her or not.”

Ms. Collins, 73, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for re-election this fall the way she always has — no clickbait TikTok posts or big, rah-rah rallies, but a relentless focus on stops in small towns where she has brought home federal dollars for boat landings, emergency operations centers and wastewater treatment facilities.
At her campaign events, supporters hold signs that underscore the point she is trying to make: “Thank You, Susan.”
In debates this month with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, Ms. Collins was unsubtle about the crux of the deal.
“In the past five years I’ve secured $1.5 billion for properties all over the state,” she said.
She was even more blunt in a radio interview this week, citing 672 projects that she had secured across the state, including 45 new fire stations.
“All that goes away,” she said, “if Troy were to be elected.”
‘I have a lot of power’
Her whole life has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power.

Ms. Collins was born and raised in Caribou in Aroostook County, the state’s most northern terrain. The Collinses didn’t just own and run the local lumber company and hardware store. They were politicos too.

“My parents,” Ms. Collins told The New York Times this past summer, “both served as mayor of Caribou. My father was in the State Senate, my grandfather, great-grandfather served in the state legislature.”

Her parents were supporters of William S. Cohen when he ran for Congress in 1972 and beyond, and Ms. Collins was a driver and an intern for Mr. Cohen when she was in college at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N.Y. After she graduated, she was hired as an aide and was on his staff for a dozen years, known by her colleagues and peers as a meticulous note-taker and over-preparer.
She ran for governor in 1994 when she was 41 and lost. She ran for Senate in 1996 and won. She said she would serve no more than two terms but then ran for re-election in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020.

Over the course of her three decades in the Senate, drafting off the renown of her cordial, consensus-building Maine forebears like Mr. Cohen and Senator George Mitchell, Ms. Collins has emphasized her image as the last of a vanishing breed. She has bucked her party, and in particular President Trump, more than enough to frustrate many Republicans — albeit not nearly enough to satisfy most Democrats.
“I’m consistently sought out by both sides for cosponsorship of bills,” she told The Times in her first year in the Senate. “I have a lot of power — I like that.”
Behind closed doors, though, she long has had a reputation as a lone wolf.

Her relationship with Olympia Snowe, the Republican who was elected to the Senate from Maine two years before Ms. Collins and served three terms, was marked by rivalries and perceived slights, according to former aides to Maine lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Publicly, they issued joint statements and often voted together. Privately, the relationship was far more fraught, as is sometimes the case when a state is represented by two senators of the same party.
“She was just hypersensitive to Olympia getting more credit than she was,” said Kurt Bardella, a former press secretary for Ms. Snowe.
“It was very machine-politicky: ‘I am owed a certain level of stature and respect,’” Mr. Bardella recalled.

Ms. Collins has a bristly relationship with Angus King, the independent junior senator from Maine, who defeated her in the governor’s race in 1994 and succeeded Ms. Snowe in 2013. While they exchange occasional text messages, the two haven’t spoken in months, according to people familiar with their communications who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. They last texted Oct. 12, according to Ms. Clark. Aides in Mr. King’s office often are instructed to let Ms. Collins get the lion’s share of the credit, they said, if that’s what it takes to get a policy initiative accomplished.
When Mr. Wood announced his candidacy for Senate, he thought he knew what he needed to know about Ms. Collins. His campaign quickly became a window into what he did not know.
Elected Democrats and political donors, Mr. Wood said, told him Ms. Collins reviewed the lists of who gives more than $1,000 to whom — and kept score.
“People told me they could not give me money because they knew she would look at the report,” he said. “Democrats.”

Ultimately, Mr. Wood’s fledgling campaign was overwhelmed by the unexpected rise of Graham Platner, whose subsequent fall precipitated Mr. Jackson’s selection as the Democratic nominee. Still, he got an eye-opening tutorial in the sway of his state’s senior senator.
Last November, when he ended his Senate campaign and switched to run instead for the Maine’s Second Congressional District, Mr. Wood couldn’t help but notice the difference.
This time, Mr. Sheline, the Lewiston mayor, endorsed him right away.
‘We should be thankful’

This month, politicking her way through the annual fall fair in Fryeburg, Maine, Ms. Collins walked from a cattle auction to a livestock barn, putting up with out-of-town press asking her questions about the president while trying to steer clear of manure.
“I know you don’t like me,” she told one reporter, “but don’t make me walk through shit.”
She quickly changed the subject — to $38 million in federal aid for heating oil.
“I was delighted,” she said, “that I was successful in expediting the funding.”
That matters a lot, said Mr. Dutson, the senator’s former aide.

“Federal money is incredibly important up here,” he said. “The choice a lot of people are facing right now is: OK, well, I can listen to the noise out of Washington or what my party tells me to do — or I can support the lady who got me a new fire truck in my 500-person town.”

In the past few weeks in Maine, as Mr. Jackson has campaigned in front of large, loud crowds alongside progressive megastars such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ms. Collins has brandished a shovel at a groundbreaking at a boat landing in Orrington and attended a grand opening of a wastewater facility in Windham.
And in the stretch run of the race, people all over the state have received targeted text messages from her campaign.
“Susan Collins delivered $33 million for Knox County …”
“Susan Collins has delivered nearly $59 million for the City of Bangor …”
“Susan Collins is delivering real results across Kennebec County — 50 projects totaling more than $109.3 million …”
Her supporters say it’s why they trust her and one of the main reasons she should be re-elected.
“What she produces is real — it’s tactile,” said Chris Gardner, the executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, who has appeared in an ad for Ms. Collins. “We should be thankful.”

Kevin Raye, a former Maine Senate president, is an anti-Trump former Republican who is now an independent — “rooting,” he said, for Democrats to take control of Congress. “But I’m in the Collins camp,” Mr. Raye said, citing her record of bipartisanship. “The thought of replacing her with a reliable partisan vote, no matter the party,” he said, “is so the wrong direction for America.”

But the calculation, her critics counter, is more complicated. Her vote to advance Mr. Trump’s big domestic policy bill before she ultimately voted against it, her initial votes against setting congressional limits to military actions in Iran followed by eventual votes to do just that — all of it costs her constituents, they say, contributing to cuts to health care and higher prices for fuel, food and more. Many remain furious about her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, a move that ultimately led to the end of Roe v. Wade.
“She’s very good at cutting ribbons,” Betsy Sweet, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and for Senate in 2020. “She’s also really good at cutting your health care.”
Moreover, as she works to fend off her challenger in a tough year for Republicans, Ms. Collins’s sharp political style has been apparent not just to political insiders but to voters as well.
In a recent interview with Politico, Ms. Collins was startlingly cutting about her opponent.
“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” she said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.” They did now.

“This is a Susan people haven’t seen,” said Tony Payne, the executive director of the Republican Party of Maine in the 1970s who became an independent after the rise of Mr. Trump and a longtime critic of Ms. Collins. “This is the peeling off of the veneer.”

Last week, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the Republican Party’s candidates, aired a radio ad about Mr. Jackson with a crude jingle alluding to the relationship. After it had made the rounds, Ms. Collins told reporters she “had nothing to do with that ad,” saying it should be removed from the air.

This week, Ms. Collins’s campaign has been airing a TV ad that many in Maine considered elitist. “We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Bill Green, a well-known, retired local sportscaster, says in the ad.

“For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance,” Sam Patten wrote in a post on social media castigating the ad. (Mr. Patten, a former aide to Ms. Collins, pleaded guilty during the first Trump administration to failing to register as a foreign agent.)
“She’s very smart, and she works very hard,” Mr. Patten told The Times. “There’s an arrogance in everyone in Washington,” he added, “but she never showed it before. She’s always been careful not to.”

Ted O’Meara, a former chief of staff of Ms. Snowe who also worked for Mr. Cohen alongside Ms. Collins, described it as a sense of entitlement. “The sense that there’s nobody else that can do this job but me or do it as well as me,” he said.
He stopped himself.
“Is this on the record?” he asked.
It was.
“She’ll be pissed,” he said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/30/climate/injured-l.headline: Conservation Efforts for Caucasian Leopards Show Promise

paragraphs.text: For years, a leopard roamed the high mountain ridges and deep gorges in the sparsely-populated region of southern Armenia. The animal had lost part of its left front leg on a land mine along the nearby border with Azerbaijan, so it hobbled a bit.

As the population of Caucasian leopards has slowly grown in Armenia, this adult male, named Aren after the village where he was often seen, had to search for new territory without the presence of other males in order to find a mate, researchers said.

So last year, Aren traveled nearly 200 miles north into Georgia where his three-legged odyssey was captured on a trail camera. To conservationists in Armenia, Aren’s remarkable cross-border trek is a small sign of progress in protecting the endangered Caucasian leopard.

Threatened plants and animals have been the focus for the past two weeks in Armenia, where delegates from around the world have gathered for the United Nations summit on biodiversity. Nations had already agreed to protect 30 percent of the planet’s land and water by 2030, among other pledges. A big question at this year’s meeting is how to get there.
Armenia, a country that is smaller than Maryland but considered a biodiversity hot spot, has protected nearly 13 percent of its territory to help native species.

In the southern province of Vayots Dzor, the government and environmental groups have linked a state-owned forest, a private nature reserve and a community-managed environmental area to create a 217-square-mile wildlife corridor for leopards and other threatened species including the Syrian brown bear, the Bezoar goat, and the mouflon, an endangered wild sheep.

With its stocky, muscular build and large paws designed to traverse snowfields, the Caucasian leopard is the world’s largest leopard subspecies. The total population is between 750 to 1,044 animals, living in four geographical areas across 11 countries.

Nearly extinct after it was hunted for decades during the former Soviet Union’s occupation of Armenia, a leopard was spotted in Armenia on a trail camera in 2005. Since then, the population has grown and experts believe as many as eight to 10 leopards might be living in Armenia.
“We now have a sustainable population of reproducing leopards in the southern Caucasus,” said Vasil Ananyan, project coordinator for the World Wild Fund for Nature Armenia.

Near the country’s southern border with Azerbaijan, residents began reporting leopard sightings around 2017, said Arus Nersisyan, director of the Arpa Environmental Foundation, a nonprofit organization that operates a 7,400-acre community reserve. The group set up trail cameras and was surprised by what they showed.
“We noticed that we didn’t have only one leopard, but two or three,” Ms. Nersisyan said in an interview.

Samvel Karapetyan, a ranger for Arpa, recalled a night in 2019 when he encountered a leopard at the bottom of a narrow gorge near the historic village of Areni. Mr. Karapetyan had been tracking a leopard’s pawprints and received a call that the animal had crossed a two-lane road.

Mr. Karapetyan and a colleague saw the animal climb a rocky cliff face. He parked his vehicle, and began filming. He left the car door open in case they had to run, and slowly approached the animal with a mixture of fear and excitement.
“I was making noise to see what kind of reaction he would give,” Mr. Karapetyan said. “He went behind the rocks. We stayed until the morning, but he never came out.”
Three months later, a trail camera in the Arpa-protected area caught an image of the same leopard, identified by the distinct pattern of spots on its fur.

It was Aren and he was limping with only three legs. He had learned to ambush instead of stalk his prey. The spot where he was located was not far from the border with Azerbaijan, a region strewn with land mines since the early 1990s conflict between the two countries. In Armenia, efforts to protect wildlife are complicated by a legacy of armed conflict.
Aren was spotted again on a trail camera in 2022 in Vayots Dzor and then in 2025 in Georgia, but there hasn’t been a sighting of him since, said World Wild Fund for Nature officials in Tbilisi.

While hunting of leopards has been reduced in the past decade by the threat of million-dollar fines, poaching of prey species like the Bezoar goat is now the biggest threat to the leopard’s survival, Hovhannes Martirosyan, head of Armenia’s environmental agency, said in an interview.

Other emerging threats to Armenia’s wildlife include a growing commercial harvest of forest plants that feed native goats, sheep and bears; a rise in hydropower that is stressing waterways; and a warming climate that has disrupted the animals’ food supply and migration patterns, according to Ruben Khachatryan, director of the Yerevan-based nonprofit Foundation for Preservation of Wildlife and Cultural Assets.
Still, it appears that Armenia’s leopards are surviving. Wildlife officials announced recently that a new male leopard was spotted twice on trail cameras earlier this month in south central Armenia.
“It can hunt and find food,” Boris Vanyan, a ranger at the privately-run Caucasus Wildlife Refuge, said about Armenia’s leopards. “It only needs a protected space and to be left alone.”

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/31/iran-fm-sa.headline: Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/31/iran-fm-sa.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a United States effort to open dialogue with Tehran is “a positive step”, but that there are currently no plans for meetings with US officials.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had studied a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance in high-level meetings, and set out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which he said would pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
Recommended Stories

He added that an Iranian delegation has travelled to Doha, a day after Qatari mediators were in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the US-Iran ceasefire. Araghchi said one of his aides is in Qatar to continue consultations.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” the foreign minister told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned: “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
‘No need to meet with the Americans’
Araghchi played down talk of upcoming meetings between the two sides.
“What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation,” he said.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” he added.
He said whether Iran would hold direct or indirect talks with the US depended on Tehran’s conditions being met.
“Mediators have presented proposals concerning the nuclear dossier, which we are currently reviewing as part of the second phase,” he said.
“Qatari and Pakistani mediators are continuing consultations regarding our conditions,” Araghchi said.
Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators had shortened the time needed to implement Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days,” he said.

“Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region,” he said, adding, “We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar.”
Iran is also demanding recognition of shipping routes through the strait that it had discussed with Oman, and the closure of other routes, he said.
‘Prepared for all scenarios’
Araghchi also said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” he said.
“We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwyv2y7g9l8o.headline: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwyv2y7g9l8o.author: Michael Teferi

paragraphs.text: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3wv311dwnlo.headline: Joseph Kabila: Former president becomes DR Congo's latest rebel leader
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3wv311dwnlo.author: Ondiro Oganga

paragraphs.text: Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.

In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.

When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.

Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.

Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.

"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.

While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.

His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.

"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.

Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.

He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.

Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.

But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.

In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.

And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.

The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.

He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.

In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.

Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.

"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.

Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.

International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.

"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.
Additional reporting by Emery Makumeno in Kinshasa
