bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crm941n0413o.headline: Ranji Smile: The forgotten chef who opened America’s first Indian restaurant
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crm941n0413o.author: Dinyar Patel

paragraphs.text: The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US.
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene.
In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name.
"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail".

Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe.
Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue.

In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah.

Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff.

At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback.
Smile, a skilled showman, thrived in this environment.
Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon".

Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him."

As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier, external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome.

Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns.

As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans.
Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad.
Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flair for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity.

Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants".

All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported.

"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof.
Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country.

In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility.
While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him.

Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant.

The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear.
Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters.
In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo".

Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf).
Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island.

Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit.

New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America.

That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.
Dinyar Patel is associate professor of history at SPJIMR in Mumbai

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckreypn92w49o.headline: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckreypn92w49o.author: Grace Dean

paragraphs.text: Sales of tinned food, radios and torches spiked in some shops after the UK government advised households what to stock up on in case of a national emergency.
While having this stash - or personal crisis kit - is new to the UK, it's common in many places across the world.
Countries facing extreme weather, natural disasters and fraught geopolitical situations regularly issue preparedness guidance - some even delivering booklets directly to homes.
So what do these emergency supplies look like for some and how do they manage it?
A 'wake-up call' but I'm not that worried - Andreas, Sweden
Thirty-year-old Andreas Wennerberg had never really thought about preparing for emergencies, until a government booklet arrived through his door two years ago.
Posted to every household in Sweden, it detailed what to stock up on and how to act "in case of crisis or war".

Andreas, who lives in Stockholm, built up a relatively small stockpile in his basement, including a crank radio, a tank with 10 litres of water and about €200 (£170) in cash. He says he already owned some of the items.
It was a "wake-up call", he says, but admits he hasn't followed the guidance in full.
"I feel secure… I'm not that worried."
I have a 'rotating pantry' so food doesn't go off - Dan, Maryland, US
Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.
"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.
In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.
Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".
I update my emergency kit every year - Ayumi, Japan
Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat.
But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.
Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide, external, which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.

In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers.
"A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.
Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.
I pick up supplies 'here and there' - Nicole, Georgia, US
Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.
The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.
Her motto is "don't panic, be prepared", she says.
As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.
To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.
My wife didn't understand but now does - Michael, Netherlands
Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.
The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.
Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.
He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.
Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire.
"Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."
In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.

At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".

Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."
Additional reporting by Hanae Takahashi and Richard Frost

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6nz4286r4o.headline: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6nz4286r4o.author: Nardine Saad

paragraphs.text: US reporter
As Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.
In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal.
"Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.
From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.
Dressing like their state
Some candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.
The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022.
She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.

Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from".
"Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.
Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.
Democratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.
She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.
During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.
The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.
Patriotism on their sleeves
Other candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.
While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.
In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.
She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June.
The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard.
"Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says.
"It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."

Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial.
"Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."
Tie off, cowboy boots on

Once a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.
On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.
"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway.
"The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."
Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas".
"Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations.
"Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."
Meanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front.
It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".

The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms.

"The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising.
"A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit.
"The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.
Personal uniforms
A uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.
It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.
Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns.
Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator.
"I always saw pearls on her," he says.
"Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."
"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.

Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.
The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics".
The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.
It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says.
"The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."
Trump, master of the image
Friedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump.
His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House.

"[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says.
"If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.
Whatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in.
"What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cknv08980d3vo.headline: Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cknv08980d3vo.author: Asma Khalid

paragraphs.text: James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.
Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.
The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour – Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

And yet despite those circumstances, the Democratic Party is also unpopular nationwide. The Real Clear Politics polling average shows the American public sees the Democrats as only marginally better than the Republicans. Recent polls show the Democratic Party still has a net unfavourability rating among Americans. Political analysts say that if the Republicans manage to buck the trend and survive these midterms, one key reason is that the Democratic Party (or the Democratic brand) is disliked by a majority of American voters too.

Behind the headlines of which party or which candidates win this Tuesday, there's also a story this election season about Democratic identity. This is a fight between institutionalists and reformists, of people who want incremental change and those who demand root-and-branch transformation. The question is, who will win out in the long run?
The not-Trump party?

I've covered every national US election in the past dozen years and this is an unusual one. When I was out interviewing voters ahead of the 2018 midterms during Donald Trump's first term, I was struck by how united many Democratic voters were in their opposition to the president. This time, I've noticed that under the facade of unity, there's a brewing fight.

There are persistent questions about what the Democratic Party stands for, and these divides erupted during the primaries this midterm cycle. "The identity of the party is pretty cloudy," said Ruy Teixeira, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a centre-right think tank. "It's all centred on reaction to the Trump administration and taking advantage of what is a thermostatic reaction against the administration... Beyond that, there's all these different factions in the party."

Part of the reason for this Democratic infighting is that the party never had a chance to have this fight during the 2024 presidential race, with the sudden departure of Joe Biden months before the election and nomination of Kamala Harris.

Analysts agree that if Democrats make big wins on election night, it still won't answer deeper, unresolved questions as they try to keep their big tent together to corral votes in Congress or eye the 2028 presidency.

In simplistic terms, the divide is between the centrist, more moderate wing of the party and its left flank. But operatives and analysts say it's also a divide between institutionalists and those who want to completely upend the existing institution. Both feel they have a better read on what voters genuinely want.

Usamah Andrabi, of the Justice Democrats, a prominent left-wing group, blames the Democratic establishment for ushering in a Republican Congress and president. "And so I think the people who led us into this mess are simply not gonna be the ones who lead us out of it," he told me.

"The affordability crisis… is a massive one, and it's not going to be resolved by tinkering at the margins," he added. Instead, he insists, it'll be solved through policies like universal healthcare and childcare, and redistributing money by cutting the Pentagon's budget to stop "endless wars". His organisation sprang up in 2017 to recruit and support the congressional members who became known as "the Squad", the furthest-left faction in the House, which includes members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar.

Healthcare will be one of the main arenas in which this fight is likely to play out, says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that forecasts the competitiveness of races.

"There is a lot of appetite for, at the very least, more transparency, more understanding of why healthcare costs are so high," said Dann. " Take a bad step, break your leg, and a huge swathe of Americans would see their worlds turned upside down by that because of the healthcare system as it is."

Several Democratic candidates this election cycle have outlined ideas to lower "out-of-pocket" costs for those who already have health insurance - being hit with additional costs on top of regular insurance payments is a common feature of the American healthcare system. But there's another flank of the party that is fed up with incremental changes and wants a national healthcare system that is free at the point of use - Medicare for All.
Recent polling suggests a majority of Democrats favour this kind of healthcare system, but a majority of Republicans oppose it.
But some Democrats say there's nuance in the issue.

"People want to have universal healthcare, and they also want to be able to keep their health insurance," says Neera Tanden, Joe Biden's former domestic policy adviser, now CEO of the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.

Mainstream establishment Democrats acknowledge that many people see healthcare as a right, but they insist that others strongly oppose a fully government-run programme, fearing lower standards of care, and insist on having the option of keeping their private health insurance.

Healthcare costs have gone up across the board - health insurance and out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, hospital expenses and prescription drug costs have all surged in recent years, rising faster than the rate of inflation. As medical expenses have increased, polls suggest the idea of universal healthcare isn't as outlandish as it once seemed, and this campaign cycle has shown that it's far less taboo for politicians to openly call for it.
Back in Georgia, it's an issue on which Tamara and James agree - they want universal healthcare.
But their most fundamental disagreement is over Israel. Tamara calls herself a Zionist. "My kids get mad at me for saying that," she said.
And they're hardly the only Democrats having this debate.

Dann, from the Cook Political Report, says one of the biggest lessons from this election cycle is that Democratic voters weren't just looking for candidates willing to fight Trump, but candidates willing to take on the establishment. Dann points to the key swing state of Michigan, where in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed - a fierce critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza - came out on top over the objections of the Democratic establishment.

"I think one reason for that was that he was not only talking about taking on Donald Trump, but taking on the Democratic establishment… the establishment in Washington writ large," she said. And part of that anti-establishment attitude is about US support for Israel.
The Israel question
Some who left the party in 2024 because they believe Biden was too supportive of Israel's actions in Gaza are now returning, energised by El-Sayed's tough tone.
"My red line has been Gaza," said Samraa Luqman, an Arab-American activist in Michigan who voted for Trump in the last presidential election, feeling betrayed by Democrats that year.

"2023 and 2024 have really taught this community a lesson that we are no longer going to be wishy-washy about the issue. It's Gaza or bust," she told me. "If you're not good on Gaza, on Israel, on Palestine, then we don't need you. We don't need you in office, and we don't need to vote for you, no matter what your party affiliation is."

But as El-Sayed has energised voters, he's also alienated others, particularly some who see support for Israel as connected to Jewish safety in the US and feel that antisemitism in their party has grown after the deadly Hamas attacks of October 7.
Zach Nessel is one of those Democrats. And he's increasingly worried about becoming politically homeless.

"We have people who don't think Zionists should have a place in our party, that they should be removed from the party," Nessel told me. "And as a proud Zionist, I don't want to be removed from the Democratic coalition just over this one issue in the Middle East."

Support for Israel became a litmus test in some Democratic primaries this season, leading to mounting resistance to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the longtime influential lobbying group.
Ideological test
But Dann tells me that it's not just Israel that's a litmus test, it's El-Sayed's race itself.

"Abdul El-Sayed's theory of the case is that he can run as an unabashed progressive in a purple state [a state that swings between the 'red' Republican party and 'blue' Democrats] and win because progressive ideas are not only popular if they're communicated correctly, but also activate voters who are not necessarily a normal part of the political process, particularly young people," she said.

If he wins, left-wing candidates will see it as a model, she adds. And if he loses, Democrats in the more centrist wing of the party will see it as evidence that left-wing ideas are out of touch with mainstream voters.

But there are others, like Jim Kessler with Third Way, a centrist think tank, who think Michigan shouldn't be the focus. He pointed out that if Democrats take control of the Senate it'll be because of more centrist candidates: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Mary Peltola in Alaska, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They, he said, are the ones expanding Democrats' odds this cycle. " So the bigger the Democratic victory, the more it seems like the centrist Democrats came through, not the DSA candidates," he said.
DSA-endorsed candidates made gains during the primaries this election cycle, but their ideas are still controversial to many.

" I don't think… the vast majority of working-class people in America are kind of mini socialists," Tanden told me, pointing to reporting that suggests the majority of people who support the DSA are college-educated voters.
" Working-class people are pretty moderate on issues like crime and immigration," she added.
Nonetheless, if Democrats gain the majority, their congressional leaders will have to navigate a group of Democrats in which there will likely be an increase in the loudest and most left-wing voices.

" The Democrats' biggest challenge is to figure out how to actually deliver on running the economy better and making things more affordable, because they've said over and over again and very loudly that's what they're going to do," said Teixeira.
Seizing the momentum
In all likelihood, people will start thinking seriously about the next presidential candidate the day after the midterms.
So, who actually has the momentum: the left flank or the centre?

"I think after the election we'll see a lot of fighting between the factions to claim credit," Teixeira said. " And that will of course feed into the jostling for the presidential nomination for 2028."
Back in Georgia, Tamara and James may disagree on some things, but they both want Democrats to win big on Tuesday.
"I'm a very pragmatic person when it comes to progressive politics," James said. He wants to make it clear he doesn't agree with everything DSA members espouse.
So much of this midterm cycle has also come down to candidate quality - not just the message but the messenger. So I asked both mother and son who their "ideal" Democrat is.
Tamara instantly answered Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator running for re-election in Georgia.
It's a point of agreement. They both really like their Georgia senator.

Ossoff is seen by many as a rising star of his party. The seat he is contesting is characterised by the Cook Political Report as "likely Democratic" - considered by analysts to be an impressive achievement in a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024.
"He knows how to speak to moderate Republicans, moderate Democrats, and members of the DSA," Tamara said. "He's not afraid to pull any punches… I appreciate how much he talks about corruption."
On Wednesday night, she joined thousands of people just outside Atlanta for a rally to cheer on the senator as former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats.
And when Ossoff took the mic, he spoke at length about what he sees as "corruption" in the Trump administration and in American politics, healthcare and corporate money.
And I heard this concern from voters in Georgia this past week, not just at the campaign rally, but at early voting sites in both Republican and Democratic counties.

"We have a corruption crisis," said Richard Schosky as he walked out of the voting booth in north Atlanta, after casting his ballot early. It's an issue that seems to be resonating deeply with voters, although the White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.
In fact, Dann with the Cook Political Report says "corruption has become one of the central issues of this election".
Still, she added, "Democrats would be foolish to believe that a very good night for them in November is a mandate for the Democratic Party," said Dann.
"They are as almost as unpopular as Republicans and the president."

Last weekend, Chaya Raichik, the popular right-wing influencer who goes by Libs of TikTok, made an ominous claim to her nearly 5 million followers on X. “In Minnesota, the USPS offices are inside mosques,” she wrote. “The people who handle mail-in ballots.. What are we doing America.” She reshared a 28-minute-long video of a man circling a brick building in Plymouth, Minnesota and accosting postal workers inside. “It’s the Islamification of the United States,” the man says. “And we have to stop it.”

Almost everything about Raichik’s post is misleading. The post office is not “inside” a mosque; they are housed in different sections of the same building. And there’s no reason to believe that the shared real estate has anything to do with the integrity of elections. In situations like this, X’s crowdsourced fact-checking feature, called “Community Notes,” is supposed to help correct the record. Users propose disclaimers for popular posts they believe are inaccurate, and if other users agree, the disclaimer gets attached to the post. Sure enough, the day after Raichik’s post, someone suggested slapping the post with a Community Note to clarify the facts, citing and linking to articles by The Minnesota Star Tribune and Minnesota Public Radio. But the note was never publicly shown on X. As of yesterday, the video had more than 1.7 million views. (Raichik did not respond to a request for comment.)

Since Elon Musk bought X four years ago, the platform has been a petri dish for rumors and propaganda. Now, having weathered a liberal exodus to other platforms, X could play a central role in the midterm elections—especially if Republicans fare poorly. X has become the go-to place for MAGA supporters to hunt for examples of voter fraud, which could be used to cast doubt on results that don’t go Republicans’ way. President Trump has endorsed this crusade—he recently announced a $1 million bounty for voter-fraud tips that lead to convictions.

Community Notes, which even some of Musk’s critics have praised as a worthwhile program, would seem to offer a bulwark against bogus claims of vote-rigging. It’s built around a clever idea: Each proposed note gets rated “helpful” or “not helpful” by users who have disagreed about related past notes. X publishes only the notes on which the users can reach consensus. Yet even though X has expanded the feature, bringing in AI note-writers to work alongside the human volunteers, it’s proving stubbornly incapable of addressing most election-related falsehoods. If Tuesday and the days afterward bring widespread claims of rigged results, expect many of them to originate on X.

Since Musk embraced Community Notes on X, crowdsourced fact-checks have gone from a niche experiment to the default on social media. After Trump’s reelection, Meta ditched its partnerships with professional fact-checking organizations in the U.S. in favor of its own version of Community Notes. (Meta still uses professional fact-checks in other countries.) YouTube and TikTok have adopted similar features. But X’s version is the most established, and it has served as the industry’s model. In some respects, it works quite well: The system routinely corrects misleading posts about topics such as sports, pop culture, and advertising.
[Read: We’re back to the well, actually internet]

The problem is that it’s rare for liberals and conservatives to agree on notes that touch on the most polarizing topics—meaning that fact-checks about politics and elections rarely get approved. That has had predictable effects on the motivation of the program’s volunteers, Mike Doris, a longtime contributor to Community Notes, told me. A group chat where active members share information and sources has become a “ghost town,” Doris said. Some have given up; he is close to doing the same.

While humans might get discouraged, bots do not. To scale up the program, X has opened fact-checking to AI, creating a purpose-built agent powered by Grok, and inviting outside researchers to build AI fact-checking tools of their own. It might seem ironic that the same technology that can generate falsehoods at scale is now being used to catch them. Yet the bots are more prolific, and X says that notes proposed by AI are also more likely to win approval from the masses, perhaps because they’re trained to use neutral language and cite reputable sources. What started as an experiment last year has quickly become the norm: In May, an analysis by The Indicator’s Alexios Mantzarlis found that half of all Community Notes shown on X are now written by just eight bot accounts. This month, the Georgetown social-media researcher Renée DiResta analyzed X’s public research and found that six of those eight are controlled by the platform itself.

This has led to a Cambrian explosion in the total number of Community Notes on X. But when it comes to politics, bots haven’t fixed the fundamental problem: Users on the left and the right just can’t find common ground. The proposed note for Raichik’s post about the post office attached to the mosque was, in fact, written by an AI agent, though not one of X’s. NewsGuard, a company that tracks misinformation, found that 93 percent of false claims about the midterms on X failed to receive a Community Note. (DiResta’s own AI fact-checking bot, she told me, has proposed 81 Community Notes; only one has been approved.)

In the weeks before the election, many of these unchecked posts have involved false claims about candidates. Fake videos targeting at least three Democratic Senate candidates have been linked to Russian disinformation campaigns. One starts with a shot of a real Cleveland local-news reporter, then cuts to fabricated footage describing nonexistent claims of sexual misconduct against Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown by women who used to work for him. Darren Linvill, a Clemson University professor who researches foreign-interference campaigns, told me that X has taken down some of the accounts behind the posts, but the same group of influencers on the platform keeps amplifying new ones. Of the 37 viral false claims about the midterms identified by NewsGuard in its ongoing tracker, 22 started as X posts, and many of them spread to larger platforms from there. Not all of them target Democratic candidates: One debunked post claims that Texas Republican Ken Paxton paid for a billboard that read, Pedos ain’t that bad.

Fact-checks were never a cure-all for social-media lies. Many conservatives distrusted mainstream fact-checking organizations, and some research has shown that Community Notes are more broadly believed. A spokesperson for X told me that the addition of AI note-writers has roughly doubled the number of Community Notes published in the past year. X, Meta, and other social-media companies also have rules against certain types of election misinformation, which they enforce through other means. For instance, X said earlier this month that it suspended more than 13,000 accounts linked to foreign-influence campaigns, and at least one viral post showing the satirical Paxton billboard now carries a “manipulated media” label.

Still, the limits of crowdsourced fact-checking might become obvious in the days to come. AI bots in particular are likely to struggle to counter fast-flying fraud claims on Election Day, DiResta pointed out. “The AI does not know what is happening on the ground unless a human has written it somewhere retrievable,” she said. In 2020, the last national election when Trump was in the White House, the president’s claims that the election had been stolen gained traction on social media and helped fuel the Capitol insurrection on January 6, 2021. Back then, Twitter applied numerous fact-checks and warning labels to posts by Trump and his allies making unsupported claims that the vote had been rigged. It’s hard to envision the platform doing that this time around.

phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-iron-age-celt.headline: Rare Iron Age Celtic helmet discovered in northeastern Poland far from its homeland
phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-iron-age-celt.author: Sandee Oster

paragraphs.text: October 31, 2026 feature
by Sandee Oster, Phys.org
edited by Sadie Harley, reviewed by Robert Egan

Around 2,400 years ago, at Łysa Góra in Poland, a group of people took a bronze helmet, crushed it, broke it into pieces and threw it into a pit with iron adzes and a scythe. Such helmets are sometimes found in lavish graves of the Celtic warrior elite, from Champagne, France, to Dürrnberg, Austria.

A new study published in Antiquity reports the discovery of a rare Berru-type helmet. Its find spot in northeast Poland makes it the only known helmet of its kind found outside its Celtic homeland in the 4th century B.C.

"Łysa Góra is one of the most exciting and mysterious archaeological sites dating to the Early Iron Age," said Bartłomiej Kaczyński, an archaeologist at the State Archaeological Museum in Warsaw. "The helmet is a symbol of power and direct evidence of long-distance contacts."
Buried in a hill

Łysa Góra was a fortified Iron Age settlement located on a sand dune between the Orzyc River and a lake. According to the study, it was inhabited between the 6th and 4th centuries B.C., possibly by people belonging to the West Baltic Barrow Culture.

Archaeologists had known about Łysa Góra for decades, with excavations conducted on and off between 1971 and 1992. However, because few of the finds from those excavations were ever published, Łysa Góra's untapped potential was never fully realized, the study reports.
On top of that, its reputation made excavators doubtful of finding anything useful. "We did not know what to expect, as the site had a reputation for being severely disturbed," Kaczyński said.
Then excavations of a ritual pit filled with charred remains revealed something unexpected. Along with adzes and a scythe, they uncovered what appeared to be an unusual bronze vessel.

"During the excavation, we uncovered an object made of bronze sheet metal, which we initially thought was a vessel," Kaczyński said. "It was only when we exposed the tip that we realized we had found a helmet of a very rare type."

Similar bronze helmets are known from sites such as Dürrnberg in Austria, located far to the south. Together with around 31 mostly fragmented La Tène brooches and ring ornaments, this suggests Łysa Góra may not have simply traded with the Celts, but may have had Celtic people living there.

The helmet could have been traded in, but the study suggests this is unlikely. Given the object's association with high status and warrior elites, a social concept very different from the local populace in northeastern Poland, it's far more likely the owner of that helmet once stayed at Łysa Góra.
Nearly 80 La Tène artifacts have been found at the site so far. "Their diversity suggests that a group of Celts lived at the site for approximately two generations," Kaczyński said.

As for why they were there, the study suggests that Łysa Góra may have been a trading post. Situated near the amber-rich Kurpie region and routes leading north toward the Sambian Peninsula, the site's location gave its occupants a strategic position to control and facilitate the movement of amber and other goods toward central Europe.
"Based on ancient written sources, we cannot rule out the possibility that enslaved people were traded there as well," Kaczyński said.

Ongoing excavations have revealed that Łysa Góra was a place bustling with trade and production, as revealed by nearly 350 metal objects, amber beads, an unfinished amber ring and a bronze coin possibly of Seuthes III, a Thracian king.

In 2025, the team even uncovered a trepanation tool, an object used to drill holes into the skull. According to Kaczyński, it suggests that "the group living at Łysa Góra included someone—possibly a druid—with medical knowledge."
"Łysa Góra is an archaeologist's dream," he said. "I hope we will discover even more exceptional artifacts there in the future."

cbsnews.com/news/residents-evacuated-ole.headline: Residents evacuated from Russia-occupied Oleshky arrive back in Ukraine amid temporary U.S.-brokered ceasefire
cbsnews.com/news/residents-evacuated-ole.author: Aidan Stretch

paragraphs.text: October 31, 2026 / 10:47 AM EDT / CBS/AP
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war. It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.

Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.

Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

phys.org/news/2026-10-gel-fuel-rocket-sa.headline: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control
phys.org/news/2026-10-gel-fuel-rocket-sa.author: Concordia University

paragraphs.text: edited by Robert Egan
A kerosene-based gel developed by Concordia researchers could make rocket and satellite fuels easier to store and control.

The material combines kerosene with lecithin, a combustible, naturally derived substance, and a small amount of calcium chloride. The researchers say it addresses a longstanding challenge in space propulsion: keeping fuel stable during storage while allowing it to flow efficiently when engines need it.

Liquid fuels can slosh inside tanks, complicating spacecraft control, while conventional gel fuels can be difficult to pump and spray into engines for combustion, they say. The new formulation is designed to balance these competing demands.

The researchers tested how the gel responds to force, temperature and chemical changes. They found that its viscosity drops by about 100 times as it is subjected to increasing force, making the gel flow more easily under the conditions needed for fuel injection. At rest, the gel behaves more like a soft solid, potentially reducing unwanted fuel movement and leakage.
The samples also remained stable for more than a year in sealed containers, with no visible separation.

The findings provide a detailed picture of how the gel behaves under different conditions and help identify the properties needed for reliable fuel storage and delivery. Its transparent appearance could also help researchers observe how fuel moves and burns.

The team says the work establishes a promising foundation for further development, but testing in actual propulsion systems will be needed to determine how well the material performs in spaceflight applications.
This study was produced by researcher Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John, associate professor of Mechanical, Industrial and Aerospace Engineering. It was published in Langmuir.

fortune.com/article/billionaire-jeff-bez.headline: Jeff Bezos once gave Eva Longoria and the admiral behind Osama bin Laden’s capture $100 million—but she says you don’t need wealth to give back
fortune.com/article/billionaire-jeff-bez.author: Orianna Rosa Royle

paragraphs.text: A lot of people talk about changing the world. But Amazon’s billionaire founder, Jeff Bezos, gave Eva Longoria $50 million to actually do it. And two years on, she says the biggest myth still surrounding philanthropy is that you have to be rich to do it.

“One of the biggest misconceptions about philanthropy is that impact is tied to wealth or scale, when in reality, impact comes in many forms,” the Desperate Housewives star told Fortune. “What I’ve learned is that impact doesn’t come from how much money you have, it comes from how you show up.”
It’s a message that feels pointed at a moment when billionaire philanthropy dominates headlines and ordinary people assume giving back is someone else’s job.

For Longoria, the most powerful—and most overlooked—form of change happens at street level. “Mentoring someone, supporting small business, sharing what you know—those things matter because not everyone has access to capital or resources, but anyone can be part of someone else’s support system,” she adds. “And I think that’s really what’s missing for a lot of people. They don’t have someone in their corner.”
What Eva Longoria did with Jeff Bezos’s $50 million

The actress is practicing what she preaches. Having built a net worth north of $80 million thanks to a sprawling business portfolio—including a luxury tequila brand Casa Del Sol, the media company Hyphenate Media Group, a stake in women’s soccer team Angel City FC, and an early investment in the multibillion-dollar John Wick franchise. Now she’s channeling paying it forward by mentoring small-business owners through a new partnership with Lenovo.

She’s also been running the Eva Longoria Foundation since 2012 to improve educational and entrepreneurial opportunities for Latinas in the U.S., as well as Eva’s Heroes, a charity that helps young adults with “intellectual special needs,” according to its website.

Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, launched the Courage and Civility Award in 2021 for individuals who make significant contributions to society. They’ve given millions (often $100 million) to help those in need. Previous recipients include CNN host and civil rights advocate Van Jones, chef and humanitarian José Andrés, and late country legend Dolly Parton—who famously helped fund Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine research.
It’s why Longoria says receiving the prize, alongside Bill McRaven, a retired Navy admiral, is much bigger than the money.

“Receiving that support was incredibly meaningful, not just because of the scale of the gift, but because it represented trust and responsibility,” Longoria said, adding that she’s been “more intentional and more strategic” in how she shows up as an advocate.

“This award has allowed me to continue investing those resources into the communities and causes I care deeply about—supporting Latina entrepreneurs, expanding access to education, and backing organizations that are driving real change on the ground,” she added. “The Courage and Civility Award makes it possible for us at the Eva Longoria Foundation to create long-term impact with transformative giving.”

McRaven, who oversaw the 2011 raid that killed al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, pledged to use his share of the money to develop education programs for future military leaders and the children of deceased veterans, as well as mental health support for those who serve.
You don’t have to be a billionaire to make a difference
Longoria isn’t the only one making the case that you don’t need to be rich and famous to make a difference.

Just look at the Giving Pledge—the commitment, cofounded by Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates, and Warren Buffett, that asks the ultrawealthy to donate at least 50% of their fortunes—has attracted more than 250 signatories since its launch in 2010.
The number who have actually followed through? A handful—fewer than 10. Most fulfilled the pledge only after their deaths.

It’s why Liz Baker, CEO of Greater Good Charities, says we “can’t afford” to wait on billionaires to solve the world’s problems.:“I think if everybody did something to help in their community, we wouldn’t have the issues that we have.”

The global nonprofit she runs has distributed more than $1 billion in impact across 121 countries since 2006—and she also told Fortune the idea that giving back has to be some grand, expensive gesture is one of the biggest things holding people back.
“Everybody can chip in—and it doesn’t even have to be money. Like, do something,” she said.
“Even if you’re like, I have one hour a week to solve this problem in my community that I care about,” Baker said. “Figure out how to do that. Most local nonprofits need help.”
A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on April 21, 2026.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6073y.headline: Harry Kane won Ballon d'Or by just 28 points from Kylian Mbappe - see how top 10 scored
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6073y.author: Craig Nelson

paragraphs.text: Harry Kane beat second-placed Kylian Mbappe to the men's Ballon d'Or by just 28 points - one of the smallest winning margins in the award's history.
Organisers released voting numbers on Saturday, showing that England captain Kane was awarded 1,055 points, compared with 1,027 for Real Madrid's France forward Mbappe.

Bayern Munich striker Kane became the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001, while France talisman Mbappe also claimed his best finish, ending up well clear of Spain forward Lamine Yamal, who was third with 881 points.

It was the smallest winning margin since Argentina great Lionel Messi beat Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk by seven points in 2019, while the men's Ballon d'Or has twice been decided by a single point.

That happened when England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton, who was later knighted, beat Portugal star Eusebio by the smallest possible margin in 1966, and Germany defender Matthias Sammer repeated the tight one-point victory when he edged out Brazil striker Ronaldo in 1996.
Mbappe may take heart from Ronaldo's Ballon d'Or experience as the legendary frontman, who presented Kane with his award in London on Monday, went on to win in 1997 and again in 2002.
Kane clinched the prize after scoring 73 goals in 65 matches last season, helping Bayern Munich to a league and cup double and leading England to a third-place finish at the World Cup.
The award is decided by votes from 100 journalists, using a weighted points system.
Top 10 in the 2026 men's Ballon d'Or:
• Harry Kane - 1,055 points
• Kylian Mbappe - 1,027 points
• Lamine Yamal - 881 points
• Rodri - 726 points
• Lionel Messi - 612 points
• Khvicha Kvaratskhelia - 541 points
• Ousmane Dembele - 418 points
• Erling Haaland - 378 points
• Michael Olise - 296 points
• Fabian Ruiz - 201 points

livescience.com/space/astronomy/astronom.headline: Astronomers may have been wrong about what ended the 'Cosmic Dark Age'
livescience.com/space/astronomy/astronom.author: Ivan Farkas

paragraphs.text: The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."
Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."
Which way the winds blow
The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.
These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.
The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.
Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/31/chelsea-.headline: Chelsea beat Man United as Martinez sent off to pile pressure on Carrick
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/31/chelsea-.author: AFP

paragraphs.text: Michael Carrick’s stay of execution as Manchester United boss may not last long after his team imploded in a 2-0 Premier League loss at Chelsea.
The visitors wasted a string of chances to take the lead at Stamford Bridge on Saturday before Morgan Rogers waltzed through the heart of the United defence to open the scoring on 50 minutes.
Recommended Stories
Lisandro Martinez then ruined any chance of a revival from Carrick’s men with two quickfire yellow cards, the second of which also conceded a penalty converted by Cole Palmer.
Winless in nine games, their defeat leaves the 20-time English champions still just one point above the relegation zone and in danger of ending the weekend in the bottom three.
Many expected Carrick to be axed following last weekend’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth.
The former United midfielder was instead given the chance to turn his side’s fortunes around and will lament a lack of ruthlessness during the first half.
Carrick recalled captain Bruno Fernandes after he was left out last weekend in the wake of criticising his manager’s tactics during the 4-1 thrashing at Como in the Champions League.
Fernandes should have marked his return with the opener when he blazed over from Bryan Mbeumo’s inviting cross.
The roles were reversed when Mbeumo could not stretch to meet Fernandes’s delivery at the back post before Amad Diallo was twice denied by Chelsea’s stand-in goalkeeper Mike Penders.
United did finally get the ball in the net when Matheus Cunha turned in Harry Maguire’s header from a corner, but the Brazilian had strayed just offside.
Carrick could not hide his frustration in a half-time interview with broadcasters and his mood soured further with a disastrous start to the second period.
Chelsea’s Rogers credits Carrick for revitalising his career during a spell together at Middlesbrough, but dealt a potentially decisive blow to his former boss.
The England international collected the ball inside the centre circle but was allowed to drive directly towards the United goal before dinking the ball over Senne Lammens.
Martinez also spoke out publicly in recent weeks to criticise United’s lack of spending in the transfer market to bolster Carrick’s squad.
But on this season’s evidence, Martinez is one of those most in need of replacing.
The Argentine international could not cope with Rogers’s strength moments later as he was penalised for hauling back the Chelsea forward.
From the resulting free-kick, Martinez then needlessly crashed into Wesley Fofana with a raised forearm.
After a VAR review, referee Peter Banks awarded a penalty and showed Martinez a second yellow card.
Lammens got hands to Palmer’s spot-kick but still allowed the ball to trickle into the bottom corner.
On a rare start since Xabi Alonso took charge of the Blues, Estevao had a third goal disallowed for offside when he crashed a pass from Palmer into the top corner.
Cries of “sacked in the morning” rained down from the Chelsea fans as their side toyed with United for the final quarter without adding to their lead.
Another big decision awaits the United hierarchy before the massive Champions League clash at home to Roma on Tuesday.
Beaten in two of their three European games so far, United face both the embarrassment and financial shock of an early exit should they fall to another defeat against the Italians at Old Trafford.

marketwatch.com/story/there-may-be-bette.headline: Our church has a $1.5 million bequest earning 3.75% in a savings account. Are we throwing money away?

paragraphs.text: 'Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently'
"Our concern is that this rate of return may barely keep pace with inflation." (Photo subjects are models.)

A Catholic church in central Massachusetts recently received a $1.5 million bequest from a generous parishioner who has passed away. Under the current arrangement, the bank holding the funds will distribute 4% annually for 25 years.

We understand that the funds are currently invested in a savings account earning 3.75%. Our concern is that this may barely keep pace with inflation, and there may be better investment options available to the church.
We would greatly appreciate your thoughts and insights on several questions:

-- How should the church consider investing these assets to balance growth, preservation of principal and the need for annual distributions? Should the church require the bank to enter into a formal fiduciary agreement, and what protections would that provide?

-- Would it be preferable for the bank to distribute the funds quarterly, semiannually or annually? What are the potential risks and advantages of having the bank continue to manage the funds compared with engaging another financial institution or investment management company?

-- Should the church arrange for periodic independent financial audits of the fund? Would it be advisable for the church to retain a CPA, financial adviser, or investment professional to provide independent oversight?
Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently and in the best interests of the parish and its future parishioners.
Don't miss: 'My main goal is to help people': I'm single, 74, with $10 million burning a hole in my pocket. What should I do?
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
No doubt this gift has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it.
Your church must have provided that parishioner with a great sense of community and spiritual healing to inspire such a generous gift.

No doubt it has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it. If that $1.5 million was put in a trust with instructions on how it should be distributed and invested over time, your church - as the beneficiary - may have less control over the interest rate. That would be up to the trustee. If, however, the money was given outright and the trustee are board members of your church, that's a different story. But you are correct: the consumer price index hit 3.7% in September.

A 3.75% interest rate is not a bad rate for a certificate of deposit (CD) or high-yield savings account, and slightly below what you might get for a 1-year Treasury bill. For a gift such as this, the church board or trustee is likely to prioritize safety over returns. Brian Katz, chief investment officer at Prosperity Wealth Management, agrees that 3.75% is a competitive rate. "The real question, which can only be answered by the church's decision makers, is how much risk they are willing to take," he told me.

"Given the long time horizon of 25 years and the relatively low disbursement rate of 4%, the portfolio has the leeway to take on more risk," he says. "One idea for a little higher yield without adding too much incremental risk would be an ultrashort bond fund. These can be found in both ETF and mutual fund structures. Currently, you can likely find something that yields 4.0% to 4.25%. As I said before, given the time horizon, building a diversified portfolio that includes equities, bonds, and cash may be considered, depending on the church's risk tolerance."
Don't miss: I'm a single 58-year-old veteran in California with $1.5 million and a VA pension. Can I retire?
Stock-market exposure

There's probably room for some stock-market exposure. "A conservative allocation of 20% equities and 80% bonds and cash wouldn't expose the portfolio to too much risk and should allow for a modestly higher return profile," Katz adds. "By focusing your equity investments on funds that favor high-quality or dividend-paying equities, the church could reduce the risk of the overall portfolio. The bond portfolio could include funds that purchase short-to-intermediate-term bonds, which would offset some of the duration risk."

The timing of distributions, if you have control over it, depends on how the church's finances are structured, but the longer you leave the money invested, the better the potential return. "The question on timing of the distributions should be made in consideration of the church's operating budget," Katz says. "From an investment standpoint, the longer the money remains invested, the more the investor benefits from compounding returns. Therefore, taking it out once at the end of the year can maximize the expected return of the portfolio."

You may also decide to use some of this money as an emergency fund, in case the church needs to replace the roof or - if you carry out broader renovations - is required to upgrade the entranceway or access to the restrooms to meet city standards. "The church should have an investment committee and a charter that defines the committee's roles and responsibilities," Katz adds. "Hiring an adviser is not a bad idea." In principle, a trust can be structured so that part of the investment income is distributed to a church while another part is reinvested.
It all depends on how the $1.5 million is held, who controls it, and what restrictions govern its use.
