bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5ynryyep2yo.headline: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5ynryyep2yo.author: Imogen James

paragraphs.text: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.
Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.
The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.
Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.
The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.
Testing and treatment is under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.
The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain.
DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said.

The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.
The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate".
Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.

In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.
In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.
Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing.
Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.
The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

fortune.com/article/why-did-us-workers-j.headline: U.S workers just took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947—and the lowest ever recorded
fortune.com/article/why-did-us-workers-j.author: Sasha Rogelberg

paragraphs.text: As corporate earnings soar and U.S. GDP balloons, the American workforce isn’t feeling the same boom. American workers are taking home less of the country’s overall income, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, and employment in the U.S. is set to continue to slow.

Labor share, or the portion of the U.S.’s economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, decreased to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, its lowest level since the BLS started recording this data in 1947, according to its labor productivity and costs report. In the previous quarter, labor share was at 53.6%. This decade, the labor share average was about 55.6%.

That’s despite corporate earnings skyrocketing, with profits for Fortune 500 companies hitting a record $2.1 trillion in 2025. The U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter last year, exceeding economists’ predictions.
That growth has not only come at the expense of how much of the pie of wealth workers are taking home, but also how many Americans are in the workforce, economists warn.

“That decline in the share of labor has got to be either falling earnings or falling numbers of people,” Raymond Robertson, a labor economist at Texas A&M’s Bush School of Government, told Fortune. “The falling share of income is having to do with the shift towards capital.”

Indeed, there are growing signs that as national income balloons, the U.S. workforce is deflating. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2% in September, and employers added just 584,000 jobs in 2025 compared to 2 million added in 2024. The U.S. added 29,000 jobs in September, about one-third of economists’ projections.

The bifurcation of corporate victories and weak labor data raises concerns among economists of jobless growth jeopardizing the U.S. workforce, as well as a K-shaped economy, where the rich get richer while the poor get poorer, becoming more exaggerated.
“Data right now is very mixed,” Robertson said. “But I think it also all consistently points to this idea that things are getting worse for workers and much better for billionaires.”
What is causing jobless growth?

Robertson attributes weakening labor share averages to the rise in automation, which he noted is displacing workers, with productivity—a metric essentially measuring worker output—continuing to rise. Second-quarter GDP data showed nonfarm productivity growth grew 1.4% last quarter, though the rate has slowed from 2.2% in the same quarter a year ago.
“All these things, bit by bit, are replacing people, and they’re concentrating income and their share of capital,” he said.

Goldman Sachs analysts Joseph Briggs and Sarah Dong estimated in a report, based on Department of Labor job numbers, that AI automation could displace 25% of all work hours. They predicted that over the course of the AI adoption period, a 15% increase in AI-driven productivity would displace 6% to 7% of jobs, and, at its peak, a 1 million increase in unemployed workers, though job displacement as a result of AI has not shown up meaningfully in any economic data.
The displacement could be substantial, the analysts said, but said the impacts of automation will be tempered by a wealth of new jobs created as a result of the technological changes.

Automation is expected to be a boon to corporate profits and GDP, projected to boost GDP by 1.5% by 2035, according to a Wharton brief published in September 2025. Early signs indicate AI could drive productivity gains, with around 80% of employees reporting AI makes them faster at specific tasks, but only 37% of companies seeing an impact of that productivity on operating profits, according to McKinsey data, and AI operating costs continue to constrain its deployment.
Robertson added that growing unemployment, which he expects to see rise over the next few months, keeps wages down, allowing margins and profits to expand.

To be sure, the recent productivity surge has been an “open question,” Morgan Stanley economists have argued, not unanimously attributed to increased adoption of AI or automation. The analysts suggested this increase would be cyclical, or vestiges of pandemic-era habits of companies making more from less.

An Oxford Economists research brief from earlier this year suggested companies are disguising overhiring-related layoffs as a result of AI, but said automation-related workforce reductions have not yet happened en masse. Additionally, while unemployment has been ticking up over the past year, it is still relatively low.
Why is an immigration crackdown backfiring on U.S. labor?

Mark Regets, senior fellow at National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), sees a different reason for a slowing workforce. He told Fortune President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown has not done what Trump administration officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, said it would in increasing the number of U.S.-born workers. Instead, according to Regets, Trump’s immigration policies have not only decimated the foreign-born workforce, but has also created fewer opportunities for domestic-born workers to find jobs.

NFAP data shows a 1.1 million to 1.4 million-person reduction in the foreign-born workforce since January 2025, consistent with the Congressional Budget Office’s report last year indicating shrinking U.S. population growth as a result of migrants being deported or refusing to come to the U.S. out of fear of hostile polities.
“The data is raising huge red flags that we are losing immigrants of all types that we otherwise would be advancing America’s economy,” Regets said.

Recent BLS data is counter-evidence to Miller’s argument that harsher immigration policy would grow the U.S. workforce. The labor participation rate for foreign-born workers fell from 66.3% to 66% from September 2025 to September 2026, and labor participation for native-born workers has similarly fallen from 61.6% to 60.9% over the same period. Fewer immigrant workers may actually make it harder for U.S.-born individuals to find work.
“A company unable to find the workers it needs for some roles could shut down operations rather than continuing,” Regets said.

He noted skillset diversity in a workplace could boost productivity and justify employing more people. Greater immigration can also increase consumer spending and stimulate businesses, as well as encourage businesses to take advantage of ample labor market availability and seek out their labor instead of offshoring jobs.
How does the U.S. reverse a shrinking labor force?
While friendlier immigration policies could help reverse an exodus of foreign-born workers, Robertson said addressing the workplace automation push would be key to growing the U.S. workforce.
“There are trades that are technology-assisted,” he said. “Those are going to be in higher demand, but you really still have to have a significant investment in skills.”

The young generation of workers are already prepared to adapt to a changing labor landscape. Gen Z are flocking to trade schools in hopes of a finding a job as a carpenter or welder not so easily outsourced by AI, and in 2024, enrollment in vocation-based community colleges increased 16%, according to data from the National Student Clearinghouse.

Companies have taken it upon themselves to provide reskilling opportunities to employees. A CareerTrainer survey from June found that 72% of hiring managers intended to reskill employees. While the U.S. Department of Labor updated guidelines to encourage states to adapt workplace development systems, Robertson argued the government hasn’t done enough in several decades to imbue the workforce with necessary skillsets for future jobs.

“Democrats and Republicans have not significantly invested in training [or] the retraining or active labor market programs that you need to match workers to jobs,” Robertson said. “That’s the obvious solution.”
Without changes, economists see the pattern of an employment slowdown continuing, but with greater concern about the ability for the U.S. economy to sustain growth.
“We need job growth to have a growing economy, and I think we need job growth to pay our debts,” Regets said. “I don’t know how you have job growth with a shrinking labor force.”
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 13, 2026.

fortune.com/2026/10/30/cisco-president-j.headline: Cisco chief found a 27-year-old ex-founder ‘buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic’—now he’s upgrading 98% of its code
fortune.com/2026/10/30/cisco-president-j.author: Orianna Rosa Royle

paragraphs.text: Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.
“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”

The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”

That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.
So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.
Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”
Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes
At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.
“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.
Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.
And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.
“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”

“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”

And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.”

His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.

He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”
She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack.

“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.
Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent
Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.
Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience.

When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”
And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI, which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation.
These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”
Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo, Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.

“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune. “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”

And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla, OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment.

Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford. “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”
And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.

“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”
“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”

bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/articles/crwydk.headline: F1: Haas bring in Ryo Hirakawa for Esteban Ocon for Mexico City Grand Prix
bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/articles/crwydk.author: Andrew Benson

paragraphs.text: Esteban Ocon has been replaced at Haas by the team's Japanese reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Ocon, who is leaving the team at the end of the year, drove in Friday practice but the team released a statement on Saturday saying Hirakawa would drive instead of the Frenchman on Saturday and Sunday.
The team gave no further details about the reasons behind the decision, although a spokesperson at Haas said it was not because the Frenchman was ill.
The move comes after Ocon had a dispute with his race engineer Laura Mueller during second practice on Friday about tyre strategy.
Mueller told him over the radio that they were switching him to use the medium tyres on his race-simulation run because team-mate Oliver Bearman's run on the soft was "not great".
After Ocon asked for clarity, Mueller told him: "We have to do medium."
Ocon replied: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."
Haas declined to comment on whether the decision to replace Ocon was related to the exchange and whatever aftermath it might have had.
Ocon is currently looking for a race seat for next year and it appears his chances are slim.
Only Cadillac and Racing Bulls have theoretical openings, but neither are said to be interested in him.
Hirakawa, 32, will be making his grand prix debut in Mexico. He is a two-time winner of the World Endurance Championship with Toyota, which is Haas' technical partner and title sponsor.
Hirakawa also drove in first practice on Friday in Mexico in Ocon's car.
Ocon is being replaced next year at Haas by Brazilian rookie Rafael Camara, a member of the Ferrari development driver programme.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cwe.headline: South Africa 17-38 Ireland: Beibhinn Parsons scores hat-trick as Irish seal back-to-back Cape Town wins
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cwe.author: BBC Sport

paragraphs.text: South Africa (10) 17
Tries: Tose, Solontsi, Ubisi Con: Cilliers
Ireland (14) 38
Tries: King, Parsons 3, Dalton 2 Cons: O'Brien 4
Beibhinn Parsons scored a hat-trick of tries as Ireland closed out their WXV Global Series campaign by securing a historic Test series win over South Africa in Cape Town.
Winger Parsons, the team's all-time leading try-scorer, crossed once in the first half and twice after half-time to lift the Irish to a hard-fought win having fallen behind with 20 minutes left.
Captain Erin King and Aoife Dalton (2) also scored to help Ireland see off the Springboks in another bruising encounter at Athlone Stadium.
Unam Tose, Sizophila Solontsi and Vainah Ubisi crossed for the hosts, who were unable to avenge last week's 40-27 loss at the same venue.
In following up last week's win with another six-try display, Scott Bemand's side become the first Irish side to win back-to-back Tests on South African soil.

cbsnews.com/news/where-to-watch-election.headline: How to watch live 2026 midterm election results on CBS News

paragraphs.text: Control of Congress and the future of President Trump's agenda are on the line in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters cast their ballots for all 435 House seats and 35 Senate races around the country. Candidates for governor are on the ballot in 39 states, along with some high-profile measures like California's proposed billionaire tax.
CBS News will have extensive live coverage of results and analysis on all platforms after the polls close on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
How to watch election coverage with cable
CBS News' "America Decides: Election 2026" live coverage on TV and cable starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. ET. (Find your local CBS station here.)

Anchors Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell will be joined on the set by "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King, "Face the Nation" moderator and chief foreign affairs correspondent Margaret Brennan, and CBS News' team of political reporters, including Robert Costa, Major Garrett, Nancy Cordes and Ed O'Keefe.

There will be live updates throughout the evening from CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and reporting from correspondents in Washington and around the country, including Weijia Jiang at the White House, Nikole Killion, Adriana Diaz, Matt Gutman, Skyler Henry, Lana Zak, Kris Van Cleave, Taurean Small, Jan Crawford and Nicole Sganga. Contributors will also include political analysts from both sides of the aisle and experts on election law and security.
How to watch election coverage without cable
Live coverage is streaming on CBS News 24/7 throughout the day Tuesday and all evening long, with election results expected to start coming in Tuesday night.
Watch on the free CBS News app on your connected TV or smartphone, on Paramount+, and all platforms where CBS News 24/7 is available, including CBSNews.com and YouTube.

Beginning at 5 p.m. ET, dive into the latest data on "Election 2026: The Nerd Show," hosted by CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and CBS News congressional correspondent Caitlin Huey-Burns, joined by Democratic and Republican pollsters and other election data experts.
Prime-time coverage anchored by Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell begins streaming live on all platforms at 7 p.m. ET.
How to watch live streaming local election coverage from CBS Stations
CBS Stations are covering the election live across 15 owned markets. Local streaming channels plan sustained live coverage with a mix of local and network coverage.
Election night live coverage plans include:
• CBS News Baltimore: Live from 4 p.m.-6:30 p.m. and 11 p.m.-11:30 p.m. ET, with updates throughout the evening.
• CBS News Bay Area: Live from 4 p.m.-11:35 p.m. PT.
• CBS News Boston: Live from 5 p.m.-6:30 p.m and 8 p.m.-11:30 p.m. ET.
• CBS News Chicago: Live from 4 p.m.-10:35 p.m. CT.
• CBS News Colorado: Live from 4 p.m.-10:35 p.m. MT.
• CBS News Detroit: Live from 4 p.m.-6:30 p.m. and 8 p.m.-11:35 p.m. ET.
• CBS News Los Angeles: Live from 4 p.m.-11:35 p.m. PT.
• CBS News Miami: Live from 7 p.m.-11:30 p.m. ET.
• CBS News Minnesota: Live from 4 p.m.-10:30 p.m. CT.

CBS News Atlanta is not streaming but local viewers can watch on WUPA Channel 69.
What time will election results come in?

Poll closing times vary from state to state, with the first batch of states closing at 7 p.m. ET, more at 7:30, and large numbers of states at 8 p.m. and 9 p.m. ET. The polls in California and several other Western states don't close until 11 p.m. ET, followed by Hawaii an hour later and finally Alaska — with a closely watched Senate race — at 1 a.m. ET.

The state says full results of the ranked-choice ballots won't be available until 15 days after the election (Nov. 18), after all eligible ballotes are reviewed and counted.

phys.org/news/2026-10-superconducting-ca.headline: Four superconducting cables link two large quantum processors into one
phys.org/news/2026-10-superconducting-ca.author: Sam Jarman

paragraphs.text: October 31, 2026 report
by Sam Jarman, Phys.org
edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

As quantum computers grow more ambitious, many researchers believe the best way forward is to build them in multiple interconnected parts. In these modular designs, separate quantum processors are linked so they can work together as one larger machine. For this to happen, however, connections must carry fragile quantum information without destroying it.

For superconducting processors, this means building reliable links around a meter (3.3 feet) long inside equipment chilled to just above absolute zero. A team at IBM Research has now achieved this for the first time: joining two large superconducting processors using four separate high-quality quantum links, all installed after both chips were already in place.
Their work is detailed in a new paper published on the arXiv preprint server.
Difficult connections

So far, quantum links between superconducting chips have mostly involved a single connection between small experimental processors. These links have allowed researchers to transfer quantum states from one chip to another, and to create quantum entanglement.

To build larger machines, however, engineers will need to install many connections between processors that are already mounted in their refrigerators. These attachments must be packed closely together, lose very little of the signal passing through them, and keep working as the system is repeatedly warmed and cooled.
Linking quantum processors
To tackle this challenge, the IBM team linked two of its 120-qubit Nighthawk R1 processors. In each link, a qubit inside one processor passed its information to a dedicated 'interface' qubit.

An adjustable coupler then fed this information into an 80 cm (31-inch) superconducting aluminum cable, which carried it to a matching set of components on the other chip. To allow for denser packing in the cables, the team plugged each one into its chip from directly above, rather than from the side.
High fidelity
With their setup complete, researchers tested how well it could pass quantum states between the chips, and carry out logic operations involving qubits on both processors.

Across the four links, quantum states were transferred with an average accuracy of 99%, reaching 99.29% on the best link. Two-qubit logic operations spanning both processors reached an average accuracy of 94.75%.

Using these operations, the team created entangled states shared across both processors, including 4- and 6-qubit states, and generated two entangled pairs at the same time through neighboring links. With the new attachment approach, all four connections remained operational through three cycles of warming and cooling.
Toward modular quantum processors

For now, further improvements will be needed before the system can become commercially practical—especially in the longevity of its quantum information. All the same, the system's achievements mark an important step forward in quantum computing.
Altogether, the team's result paves the way for computers where quantum information is stored and processed across many processors, making future machines far easier to expand and maintain.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/31/tiktoks-road-t.headline: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app
techcrunch.com/2026/10/31/tiktoks-road-t.author: Aisha Malik

paragraphs.text: TikTok announced this week that it’s adding an in-app restaurant guide, marking another step in the platform’s expansion beyond social media. The company has also recently been spotted developing a feature that would allow users to send money over direct messages.

The social media app has steadily expanded its offerings in recent years, adding TikTok Shop, a map for local discovery, more robust search features, games, and more. It appears that TikTok is taking steps to evolve into a “super app,” a single platform where users can do much more than just watch and share videos and that can actually handle a wide range of needs in one destination.

The super app model is big in China with apps like WeChat, which is kind of like Facebook, WhatsApp, Apple Pay, and an app store all rolled into a single platform. Of course, there’s the question of whether a super app model would work outside of China, but that doesn’t mean TikTok won’t try.

Instead of switching between apps, TikTok is working to become the app that people use for most of their digital activities. After taking its biggest leap with TikTok Shop, the company — which, notably, transitioned to new, primarily U.S. ownership back in January — has applied the same playbook to recent developments.
Restaurant Guides

TikTok has become a popular destination for restaurant recommendations, with viral videos often driving customers to local eateries. Now, the platform is looking to make that discovery process even easier with a new feature called “Must Eat.” The community-driven guide highlights restaurants getting attention on the platform.

“Must Eat” draws on more than 40 million posts and comments to compile restaurant recommendations and curated lists in one place. Users can browse restaurants by city and narrow their search by cuisine, price, rating, and location.

The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google Maps. It also reflects how the app is expanding its role in users’ everyday decisions, from what they buy to where they choose to go out to eat.
Payments

Bloomberg reported in August that TikTok is developing a feature that would allow users to send each other money via direct messages. If rolled out, the feature would use the social media service’s TikTok Pay offering, which is already available in Southeast Asia for TikTok Shop purchases.
Additionally, Reuters reported in March that TikTok had applied to Brazil’s central bank for approval to operate as a financial technology company offering lending and payment services.

TikTok’s potential expansion into payments marks a significant way that the company is branching out beyond a social media platform and into a digital ecosystem. By aiming to bring financial services into its app, TikTok is looking to increase user engagement, open new revenue streams, and position itself to compete with fintech startups and e-commerce platforms.
Sports

Over the years, TikTok has steadily been looking to become a place where users can come for sports highlights and content. In early June, the company launched a dedicated hub for the FIFA World Cup where users can see scores, match schedules, standings, trending videos, highlights, videos from players, and more.
If people are already watching videos on TikTok but want to keep up with the score, they can do so without leaving the app or opening a dedicated sports news app or Google.

The World Cup hub was made possible through TikTok’s Sports-focused product called “TikTok GamePlan,” which is designed to allow sports teams, leagues, and broadcasters to drive discovery and engagement on the platform. The social media giant also has partnerships with Major League Soccer (MLS) and Major League Baseball (MLB) for behind-the-scenes and exclusive content.
Hotel and attraction booking

In May, TikTok launched TikTok GO, a way for users to discover and book hotels, attractions, and experiences directly within its app in the United States. TikTok GO surfaces lodging and things to do through videos, search, and location pages. When users find something they’re interested in, they can view details, check availability, and complete a booking.

Instead of directing users to third-party websites after they find a destination or recommendation in a video, TikTok has started positioning itself as a one-stop platform where viral travel content can drive bookings and revenue.

While people have already been using TikTok as a search engine and replacement for Google, this latest step puts TikTok in more direct competition with Google’s core businesses, Search and Google Maps, because it’s working to not only be the app where you discover places, but also the platform where you purchase that trip.
TikTok Shop

It’s widely known that one of TikTok’s biggest leaps beyond social media was the launch of TikTok Shop. TikTok began testing TikTok Shop in 2021 and launched it in the U.S. in 2023. Since then, the company has been able to successfully compete with Amazon, Shein, and other online marketplaces.

According to eMarketer, TikTok Shop grew its U.S. sales by 407% in 2024 and another 108% in 2025 to reach $15.82 billion. As of last year, the company accounted for 18.2% of total social commerce in the U.S., with that number expected to reach 24.1% by 2027.

Additionally, TikTok began challenging digital marketplaces even further with the launch of TikTok Shop gift cards late last year. TikTok Shop has also recently expanded into luxury retail, after initially mainly being known for cheap goods.
Music

TikTok’s popularity has influenced the music industry and how people discover new music, and the company tried to capitalize on this by launching a streaming service called TikTok Music in 2023 to take on platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, but ended up shutting it down a year later.

The company said it would focus on driving music listening and continue partnering with music streaming services rather than competing with them. TikTok hasn’t completely abandoned its music ambitions, however, as the company recently introduced a feature that lets Apple Music subscribers play full songs in the app after discovering them on their “For You” feed.
Search and Maps

TikTok has launched a robust search experience that surfaces maps, local hashtags, and even reviews to help users discover trending restaurants, travel locations, shops, and local experiences. It has also added more detailed information about places and restaurants on dedicated pages, allowing users to quickly see things like opening hours, star ratings, price ranges, and more.

TikTok was already eating into Google’s Search business when it first launched, as it quickly surfaced videos featuring commentary and visuals of restaurant food and places. However, users may still have needed to turn to Google Search to find a place’s exact location or to read reviews. Over the past few years, however, TikTok has increasingly eliminated that need by integrating detailed information about places right within its app.
Microdramas

While TikTok is known for user-generated entertainment, the company has also begun embracing microdramas by launching an in-app Minis section and a dedicated stand-alone app for bite-sized TV shows that can be watched in a series of one-minute episodes. While TikTok already competes with streaming giants like Netflix for users’ attention, its move into scripted shows puts it in even more direct competition with them.
It’s worth noting that TikTok first took strides into entertainment with the launch of livestreaming and support for longer videos, a significant move away from its initial focus on 15-second videos.
Games

TikTok has also launched a series of casual games in its app to get users to spend even more time on its platform and engage with others in DMs. The addition of games marked TikTok’s ongoing effort to go from a social media platform to an all-in-one entertainment platform where you can not only scroll through videos, but also challenge friends to easy-to-play games.

fortune.com/article/mark-zuckerberg-meta.headline: Mark Zuckerberg’s $170 million Miami mansion is just one piece of his sprawling real estate empire that includes a 196-year-old castle
fortune.com/article/mark-zuckerberg-meta.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez

paragraphs.text: With a net worth of $222 billion, Mark Zuckerberg is one of the richest people in the world and the owner of a massive real-estate portfolio that spans the entire U.S.

His latest purchase from August is a 440-acre estate and accompanying 196-year-old castle in County Waterford, Ireland, a purchase that reportedly set him back 51.17 million euros, or about $57.1 million.

Yet, his priciest purchases dates back to earlier this year, when the Meta CEO and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, reportedly purchased a luxury mansion on Indian Creek Island in Florida near the in-progress home of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

The 300-acre, man-made Indian Creek Island is near Miami and Miami Beach and contains a mere 41 lots with approximately 84 residents, the Wall Street Journal reported. Home prices on the island start at about $60 million, and records show the billionaire paid $170 million for his waterfront home with nine bedrooms and 11 full bathrooms, the Miami Herald reported. Miami-Dade County property records note the owner as a land trust.
Even an undeveloped property on the exclusive island can fetch big bucks: One vacant lot roughly the same size as Zuckerberg’s sold for a reported $105 million in 2025.

The property Zuckerberg reportedly purchased at 2 Indian Creek Island Road puts him in the most coveted area of the already exclusive island, said Mitchell Duchon, a Miami Beach–based real estate agent with the Corcoran Group who specializes in high-end waterfront properties. On the western side of the island, where Zuckerberg’s property is reportedly located, lots are about 80,000 square feet, compared with about 50,000 square feet on the east side, according to Duchon. On this side, where Amazon founder and fellow billionaire Jeff Bezos also owns two lots, residents have better access to the open water of Biscayne Bay and a more expansive view with great sunsets, he added.
“That side of the island is perceived to be the most appealing,” Duchon said.

Bezos has been buying up properties on Indian Creek Island since he announced in 2023 he was leaving Seattle for Florida. The Amazon founder first purchased a $68 million home that would end up being just a few doors down from Zuckerberg’s in 2023. Near the end of that year, he paid another $79 million for a neighboring property with the intention of combining the lots into a single compound—a trend Duchon said is increasingly common among wealthy buyers because of the scarcity of truly expansive waterfront properties in the area. Meanwhile, Bezos is reportedly living in a third Mediterranean-style property also on Indian Creek Island, on the east side, which he snapped up for $87 million in 2024. Last year, Bezos sold one of his Seattle homes overlooking Lake Washington for a record $63 million, the Puget Sound Business Journal reported.

Indian Creek Island operates as an independent municipality with its own government and private police who patrol by air, water, and sky. Access to the island is controlled by a single gated bridge, making safety and privacy a defining feature. Most of the island’s interior comprises an 18-hole golf course and the Indian Creek Country Club, with a limited number of members owing, in part, to a difficult admissions process and a $500,000 initiation fee.

Zuckerberg is one of the latest billionaires to pick up a Florida property, especially in light of a proposed ballot initiative to be voted on in California next week that would impose a one-time 5% “billionaires tax” for any individual worth at least $1 billion dollars retroactive to Jan. 1, 2026. (To be sure, Zuckerberg still very much calls California home, having invested $50 million through Meta for a Sacramento downtown revitalization and AI-focused project earlier this year.) Google cofounder Larry Page also snagged a $71.9 million home in Miami’s Coconut Grove neighborhood in January that he plans to combine with another property to form a total $173 million waterfront compound.
Indian Creek Island, in particular, is home to a number of high-profile names, who, besides Bezos, include the financier Carl Icahn and former NFL quarterback Tom Brady.
Zuckerberg’s reported newest property is just the latest addition to the tech CEO’s growing portfolio of luxury homes across the U.S.
Palo Alto compound

Zuckerberg’s home base remains Palo Alto, where, according to the New York Times, he owns 11 properties in the Crescent Park neighborhood. Over more than a decade, Zuckerberg has poured $110 million into buying adjacent properties, in some cases drawing complaints from his neighbors.
Hawaiian estate

On the island of Kauai, about 100 miles northwest of Honolulu, Zuckerberg owns a $300 million property commonly known as Koʻolau Ranch, spanning roughly 1,400 acres. He quietly added about 1,000 additional acres to the compound last year, Architectural Digest reported, bringing his total Kauai holdings to more than 2,300 acres.

The ranch is one of Zuckerberg’s most secretive properties. Almost anyone who passes the compound security, including builders and other workers, must sign nondisclosure agreements, Wired reported. The ranch reportedly includes a 5,000-square-foot underground shelter with its own energy source.
Lake Tahoe retreat

Zuckerberg created his own mountain compound in the Lake Tahoe area through the purchase of two adjacent estates in Tahoe City on the lake’s West Shore. Lake Tahoe, in the Sierra Nevada mountains between Nevada and California, has emerged as a popular destination for billionaires seeking a retreat, with both Google cofounder Sergey Brin as well as 2020 presidential candidate Tom Steyer owning homes there.

Zuckerberg bought the properties—known as Carousel Estate and Brushwood Estate—for a total of $59 million, or $22 million and $37 million, respectively, according to multiple reports. The Brushwood Estate dates back to the early 1900s and has only had two other owners, according to SFGate. The property has six bedrooms, five full baths, and a 2,293-square-foot guesthouse.
Washington, D.C., mansion

As Meta and Zuckerberg have engaged more with policymakers in Washington, D.C. during the Trump administration, the tech CEO reportedly picked up a $23 million mansion in Washington D.C.’s exclusive Woodland-Normanstone neighborhood, Politico reported. The 15,000-square-foot mansion features brick and limestone walls and glass enclosed “walkways.”
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Feb. 12, 2026.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/31/south-af.headline: South Africa hammer Australia as Harmer takes career best bowling of 6-16
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/31/south-af.author: Reuters

paragraphs.text: Australia captain Pat Cummins said it was fair to ask questions about his side after they ⁠slipped to two heavy ⁠defeats in a row against hosts South Africa to lose the three-match series 2-1 at Newlands on Saturday.
Set 288 for victory, Australia were rocked early on and could ⁠manage only 111 to lose the third Test by 176 runs, following their defeat by an innings and 31 runs in the second match in the series.
Recommended Stories
Australia next host New Zealand, and Cummins ⁠said the series loss meant questions were inevitable as South Africa took over from them as the number one side in the Test world rankings.

“We lost two games in a row. I think it’s fair to be asking questions and we’ll be asking them internally as well,” Cummins told reporters. “We are a very good side, but I think we need to get a little bit better if we want to get back to number one [in the world].
“Maybe that’s a change of style, maybe it’s a change of personnel in some instances. We’ll work it out.”
Cummins made the surprise decision to bowl first after winning the toss on the first morning, something that had been done only 11 times before in Tests at Newlands since 1889.
As it proved, batting last was difficult on a wearing ⁠surface, and Australia fell to the spin of Simon Harmer, who took ⁠career-best figures of 10-120 in the match.
“We knew it was going to be a high-scoring game,” Cummins said. “We probably thought it was going to do a little bit more on day one than it did.
“You don’t win the toss and think you’re ⁠going to bowl the opposition out for 100 or 200, but we thought we could get 10 wickets on day one and that would ⁠put us right ahead of the game.”
Cummins said poor decisions cost ⁠his batters and that their chase was as good as over in the first half-hour of the day.
“Chasing 280-odd was never going to be easy, but we all turned up today and saw a pretty clear path forward. I thought it was achievable, but we never really gave ourselves a chance,” he said.
“There were a few really poor decisions. I know it’s a day-five wicket, but I don’t think it was drastic. There were runs to be scored out there; there were lots of balls to face.
“I think there are a few decisions the boys would like back. We have to get better. It’s happened a few times now.”

blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-.headline: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-.author: Ryan Fetterman

paragraphs.text: Saturday, October 31, 2026 08:00

• VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
• If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.

• This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.
The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.
https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions
Default model
anthropic/claude-opus-4.6
Fallback chain
moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash
0.2 — deterministic, consistent output
Request format
Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.
The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.
Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.
Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.
The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.
Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.
All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.
Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.
Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.
Sample details
9BY0tjwOc3ut.exe / yLP9m5J3i2Aw.exe

marketwatch.com/story/we-are-in-our-70s-.headline: We're in our 70s. Should we pay off our 2.5% mortgage - or put the money in a high-yield savings account?

paragraphs.text: 'Let's say 10 years from now, when I'm 84, we need a substantial amount of cash'
"Instead of making extra mortgage payments, we've decided to put that exact same money into a high-yield savings account." (Photo subject is a model.)

We're a retired couple living in Southern California. I'm 74, and my wife is 70. We are weighing up the wisdom of investing in a market driven by artificial intelligence and deciding whether to instead keep money in cash or pay off our mortgage.
I enjoyed your article about the couple with the mortgage (We have a $300,000 mortgage with a 2.75% interest rate. I want to pay it off. My husband says I'm crazy. Who's right?).
Our mortgage carries a slightly lower interest rate (2.5%) than the one in that story, and my original plan was to make extra payments and pay it off in 15 years.
But then I started asking myself a different question: If we need access to cash at some point in the future, where is that money better off - in home equity or in the bank?
Let's say that 10 years from now, when I'm 84, we need a substantial amount of cash. At that point, would I rather have the money tied up in the house or available when we need it?
So instead of making extra mortgage payments, we've decided to put that exact same money into a high-yield savings account and, as the balance grows, build a CD ladder.
As I see it, there are two primary benefits and a possible third one as well:

-- Liquidity over home equity. I'd rather have cash in hand than money tied up in the house. In other words, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush - especially as we get older and having readily available funds becomes increasingly important.

-- An added layer of title protection. Keeping a mortgage with an established lender may offer some additional safeguards, although it's not a substitute for independent title monitoring or other protective measures.
-- A potential tax benefit. Mortgage interest may still be tax-deductible. However, with the standard deduction, that benefit may be limited or nonexistent for many homeowners.
I'm simply suggesting that, particularly in retirement, having accessible cash and maintaining financial flexibility may be worth more than paying off the mortgage early.
What do you think?
Homeowner in my 70s in Temecula
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?
Given your favorable situation, especially with your low interest rate, there's no right or wrong decision.
You're in the home stretch with your financial journey, and I sure hope you are enjoying it.

With a 2.5% rate on your mortgage, you'll still be ahead if you put your money into a high-yield savings account or CDs. By all means, have an emergency fund, preferably a year's worth of expenses, but please try not to keep a large sum of money in a checking account, because inflation will eat away at that cash over time. Remember, too, that you can buy title insurance with or without a mortgage, and that a lender will always keep its own financial interests at heart.

Given your low interest rate, there's no right or wrong decision. You can get CD rates of 4.5% and HYSA rates of up to 4.25%. That's marginally above the latest consumer price index rate of 3.7%. So you'd be more or less treading water between your returns and inflation with your money stashed in cash equivalents. How much of your excess cash you put in cash or bonds versus the stock market depends on your risk tolerance and purchasing power.

With such a low mortgage rate, there's nothing inherently wrong with paying off your mortgage while building your savings, provided your returns after taxes and other costs justify it. A well-structured CD ladder, in addition to other more readily available sources, is also a good idea. This would allow you to meet unexpected expenses without having to sell investments during a market downturn or, perish the thought, borrow against your home.
Having faith in the market

When you're in your 70s, financial advisers generally recommend you have 30% to 50% of your portfolio in bonds or cash equivalents, and the rest in stocks. The idea is to avoid being held hostage by a major market correction or, worse, a recession by being forced to withdraw money during a down market. But plenty of people in your age group dance to the beat of their own financial drum and have 70% or more in stock while relying on Social Security and other forms of income.

The S&P 500 SPX, Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA and Nasdaq Composite Index (COMP) have all been on an upward trajectory this year. The Nasdaq has benefited from the AI gold rush. If you have faith in the long-term future of U.S. equities, as history would suggest you might, you could invest in an exchange-traded fund that tracks the total market, the S&P 500 or some other diversified index, perhaps a Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF VTI.

In October, Yardeni Research published a research note cautioning that the yield on the 2-year Treasury note had risen 115 basis points from its December low, indicating higher borrowing costs that could put pressure on stock valuations. However, Yardeni analysts also noted that credit conditions outside the AI sector do not yet show the widespread excessive lending that preceded some prior market downturns (which is not quite a confidence booster).

The International Monetary Fund, also in October, warned that global financial markets face elevated risks from an AI-driven market correction if the billions of dollars being spent on AI don't generate the expected economic returns. "Three key risks have been increasing, each with the potential for broader implications: an artificial intelligence-driven market correction, a sharper rise in sovereign bond yields, and cyberattacks," the IMF said.
Mulling over safer havens

For other safe havens, consider shorter-duration bonds or mutual funds and exchange-traded funds that invest in bonds with maturities of less than five years, as well as Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), which are inflation-protected bonds issued by the U.S. Treasury. Some analysts also see upside in value-oriented and defensive sectors, including consumer staples, utilities and healthcare stocks, for retired investors who seek safety over higher returns.

Ultimately, your investment strategy in retirement will depend on your lifestyle, how much money you have in your retirement-account balances, your goals, your views on the current socioeconomic backdrop and, yes, whether you think the tech boom will continue unabated (there is no consensus on that). Do you have long-term-care insurance or life insurance? How much longer do you have to pay on your mortgage? Will your passive income in retirement continue to cover your expenses?

The question you ask is timely because you can't answer it in isolation. It forces you to step back and look at your entire retirement plan. Are you, for example, comfortable withdrawing 4% from your retirement accounts in the first year and adjusting that rate for inflation in subsequent years? How much of your retirement savings are in traditional accounts versus Roth accounts? And, yes, how big are your mortgage payments? Do they account for more than 30% of your monthly income?
Once you answer these many questions, you can make your decision with relative ease.
